#33009. Industry News: A Different Hike: Camino in Reverse

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (927 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: A Different Hike: Camino in Reverse

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (927 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We took our sweet time starting out this morning.
  • By 10:00 AM, we finally walked out into the busy streets of Millandoiro to begin the day’s trek.
  • Industry observers note that the twist?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We took our sweet time starting out this morning. Like true “hiker trash,” we were determined to take full advantage of the complimentary lobby perks at our hotel: free coffees, teas, and an automated orange squeezer that freshly crushed OJ right in front of you.

By 10:00 AM, we finally walked out into the busy streets of Millandoiro to begin the day’s trek. Unlike yesterday’s intimate trail options, this morning started on one main route heavily packed with pilgrims.

Industry observers note that the twist? The entire throng was walking northbound toward Santiago de Compostela—meaning we were walking directly into the oncoming crowd.

When you hike in the same direction as everyone else, you rarely make direct eye contact with fellow walkers. Heading south against the traffic created a completely different dynamic.

For the pilgrims walking toward Santiago, encountering someone going the opposite direction was a rare novelty, so almost every single person looked up, made eye contact, and wanted to interact.

Sources indicate that at first, we greeted everyone with a friendly “Hola,” “Buen Camino,” or “Bom Camino” (since we were on the Portuguese route). But after saying it every two minutes for an hour straight, Knockerz and I were mentally exhausted.

Recent findings suggest that you simply cannot engage with hundreds—or thousands—of people every single day on a trail. We quickly vowed to drop our gaze, lock our eyes on the ground, and hike on like zombies.

Recent findings suggest that it was a gorgeous, sunny day with temperatures in the low 60s. Even with our heads down, we kept physically bumping into people.

Because northbound pilgrims never expected anyone to be walking south, they rarely saw us coming. We spent half the morning doing an awkward “side-step shuffle dance” at every pass until we decided on a strict rule: always stick to the far right edge of the path.

To a long-distance hiker accustomed to a single marked trail, walking backward through a network like this takes constant focus.

Our route wound through narrow paved roads connecting medieval hamlets tucked into the hillsides. It felt like an endless labyrinth of cobblestone alleyways.

Because every arrow blaze was painted for northbound travelers, we constantly had to stop at intersections, turn around, and hunt for marks hidden behind stone walls.

To make matters busier, this section serves as the final 100 km for pilgrims on the Portuguese route seeking their Compostela certificates:.

After our peaceful, quiet walk to Finisterre, jumping right back into the final 100 km circus was a shock to the system. We passed over a thousand people in the first two hours alone.

At one point, we took a single-track dirt path leading through a lovely forest. Noticeable red arrow blazes had replaced the blue ones, so we decided to follow them.

The path grew narrower and narrower, and soon we began spotting piles of toilet paper left behind by crowds unfamiliar with Leave No Trace (LNT) principles. Realizing we had strayed off the main route, we turned around and backtracked to the original junction.

We resumed our meander through ancient hamlets before spilling out onto a busy highway near A Escravitude, passing its grand yet worn-down cathedral along the roadside.

As the warm sun heated up the afternoon, we pushed through an eclectic mix of industrial zones, busy highways, railroad tracks, and quiet medieval villages.

Industry observers note that with three miles left, the oncoming pilgrim traffic finally thinned out. But right on cue, we got turned around again inside a tiny medieval village with narrow pathways.

Rather than backtracking, we decided to test Google Maps to navigate through the alleyways back to the official trail:.

Taking these brief detours through the “back country” turned out to be a great way to avoid the crowds, escape the trail litter, and explore off-the-beaten-path villages.

It has been revealed that before long, we reached Padrón. Because this town marks the starting point for many 100 km section-hikers heading north, we expect the heavy trail traffic to drop off significantly starting tomorrow.

Sources indicate that after dumping our packs in our room, we wandered the narrow alleyways of this small medieval town. Under heavy renovation, the main cathedral was covered in scaffolding. A river walk led to a large old Roman bridge framed by a large convent on a hill.

We picked up dinner ingredients across the street, cooked in our shared kitchen, and settled in for the night. Walking the Camino Portuguese in reverse is proving to be vastly different from the Camino Francés—and heading the “wrong way” makes every mile a unique adventure.

#33000. A Thru-Hiker Turned Her Trail Recordings Into an Interactive PCT Sound Map

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1205 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

A Thru-Hiker Turned Her Trail Recordings Into an Interactive PCT Sound Map

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1205 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When Anna “Rooster” Wozniewicz hiked the PCT in 2025, she wanted to create something that would outlast the hike itself: a record of the trail’s sounds, a snapshot of its changing ecosystems, and a way for people who might never get to hike the PCT to experience the trail for themselves.
  • Together with her friend and former business partner Haiden McGill, Wozniewicz turned hours of audio recordings taken along the PCT into Offbeat, an interactive sound map of the trail.
  • Anna “Rooster” Wozniewicz on the PCT.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Anna “Rooster” Wozniewicz hiked the PCT in 2025, she wanted to create something that would outlast the hike itself: a record of the trail’s sounds, a snapshot of its changing ecosystems, and a way for people who might never get to hike the PCT to experience the trail for themselves.

Together with her friend and former business partner Haiden McGill, Wozniewicz turned hours of audio recordings taken along the PCT into Offbeat, an interactive sound map of the trail. The project features 74 recordings spanning nearly 1,800 miles from the Mexican border to Sky Lakes Wilderness in Oregon, where an overuse injury ended Wozniewicz’s hike early.

Anna “Rooster” Wozniewicz on the PCT. Photo: Anna Wozniewicz.

McGill and Wozniewicz both have backgrounds in audio engineering. The pair met in college and founded a sound design tech giant together at age 20 and ran it successfully for four years.

“When I got back from the PCT, all I had was an SD card full of audio files and an ambitious idea, but I knew there was exactly one person who could help me turn that idea into reality,” Wozniewicz told The Trek. That person was McGill.

“When Anna first mentioned she wanted to build an experience to showcase her recordings from the trail, I immediately saw the entire thing in my head,” McGill said of the Offbeat project. “The challenge was that I wanted the user to actually ‘hike’ the trail, not fly from place to place.” They set out to design a web experience that would feel both immersive and meditative, centering the sounds themselves.

Industry observers note that wozniewicz came off the trail with 137 separate audio recordings, and the pair have spent the last year turning those raw files into something more polished. Each of the 74 sounds that made it onto the Offbeat website is carefully edited into a seamless loop with no beginning or end, and a user scrolling through the sound map finds themselves meandering northward — indeed, much like a hiker would.

According to recent reports, “Sound is subliminal, and we live in a very visual world. Throughout the build there was a constant temptation to add more visuals and UI elements to ‘enhance’ the story. This project was an exercise in restraint: keeping the listening experience calm and uncluttered. Instead of adding things, I used subtle camera movements, which I picked up from our filmmaking days, to draw listeners in and give the experience a meditative feel,” McGill said.

Forester Pass. Photo: Anna Wozniewicz.

In a recent development, “I didn’t go into my hike with the intention to create Offbeat, but whenever I stumbled upon a cool sound, I got my recorder out and started recording,” Wozniewicz stated. All she had with her was a cheap, lightweight Zoom H1essential recorder that she’d bought last-minute before her hike, but it was enough. “If you ask the UL bros, (it weighed) far too much, but in my opinion, it was surprisingly little.”.

Her guiding principle, she stated, was to capture sounds that would be hard to find in any other context — wind inside a hollow tree trunk, footsteps crunching up the icy ascent to Forester Pass, and an apocalyptic thunderstorm on Hat Creek Rim being some of her favorites. “It became kind of a game, to try and find the coolest, most unique sound I could each day.”.

According to recent reports, she aimed to capture natural sounds and, most of the time, exclude mechanical ones like traffic and airplanes. The hardest thing to capture? The silence. “Sometimes, the silence was overwhelming — no wind, no bugs, no rustling anywhere — this was the one sound (or lack thereof) that was impossible to record, that I feel isn’t represented in Offbeat, yet occurred pretty frequently on trail.”.

According to recent reports, wozniewicz with her recording device. Photo: Anna Wozniewicz.

Wozniewicz started to envision Offbeat about three months into the hike. “Hearing a specific sound can bring you back to a specific time, place, or memory. I’ve seen the PCT documented ad nauseam through images and video, but rarely have its sounds been captured, so it felt like a gap that I felt compelled to fill. My primary goal with Offbeat was to recreate the meditative experience of being in the wilderness.”.

She hoped the project would evoke that feeling for others. “Getting to spend half a year just walking is an immense privilege, and many people will never get the chance to do something like that, so my hope is that Offbeat can bring the trail a little closer to a lot more people for whom a thru-hike isn’t possible.”.

Navigating Sierra snowpack. Photo: Anna Wozniewicz.

Offbeat is also intended to preserve an auditory record of the PCT’s diverse ecosystems, many of which are threatened by climate change. “Maps are a gift from the people who went before us, and I love that as a metaphor for continuing stewardship: you inherit the way, and you leave it better for the next person. In that sense, Offbeat is an archive we may soon look back on,” said McGill.

“Also — recognizing that I’m not even close to being the first (or last) person to hike the PCT corridor was crucial to me, which is why in the Audio Library view I’ve included the names of the Native peoples whose land each recording comes from,” Wozniewicz added.

It has been revealed that climbing Mt. Whitney. Photo: Anna Wozniewicz.

Interestingly, Offbeat isn’t the only PCT sound library to come out this year. Field recordist Tom Kelly hiked the PCT in 2023 with over two pounds of recording equipment and just launched his own PCT sound map earlier this fall, featuring nearly 200 recordings up and down the trail. Like Wozniewicz and McGill, Kelly aimed to create a resource that would help people far from the PCT feel connected to the trail.

Wozniewicz and McGill could imagine doing a similar project on another long-distance trail someday. First, though, Wozniewicz wants to finish off the remaining miles of the PCT — and bring Offbeat’s audio pins as far north as the Canadian border. McGill remarked they hope to join for at least part of the remaining section.

“I’ve never felt more present in my life than on the PCT, and Offbeat is my way of packaging all those feelings up and sharing them with others,” Wozniewicz noted.

Featured image courtesy of Anna Wozniewicz.

This Traditional Archer Tagged a Major 8-Pointer With a Longbow and Stone Point Arrowhead He Made Himself

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (605 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was the evening of October 25 when Joe McConnell, a traditional bowhunter from central Ohio, climbed into a ladder stand with a backdrop of heavy cover.
  • McConnell was hunting with a longbow in a narrow strip of woods that he owns.
  • “I was really after a nice 10-point buck I had on trail cameras,” McConnell tells Outdoor Life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was the evening of October 25 when Joe McConnell, a traditional bowhunter from central Ohio, climbed into a ladder stand with a backdrop of heavy cover.

McConnell was hunting with a longbow in a narrow strip of woods that he owns. The spot was overlooking a travel lane deer were using to enter a large field of standing corn.

“I was really after a nice 10-point buck I had on trail cameras,” McConnell tells Outdoor Life. “The wind was perfect that evening, blowing right in my face. I was looking forward to filling my first landowner tag with a deer on my own property.”.

“I’d made a mock scrape in front of my stand, with a licking branch above it about 12 yards from my ladder,” states the 38-year-old archer. “I heard him in the corn about six rows in, and he came to check the scrape.

“I saw his rack above the standing corn field coming to me, and when he stopped broadside quartering away at 12 yards, I took my shot.”.

In a recent development, the buck was not the 10-point he was after. Instead, it was a dandy 8-pointer that McConnell couldn’t pass up.

McConnell drew his 64-inch, 55-pound longbow he’d made from an Osage orange tree limb. Then, shooting instinctively, he released a 26-inch arrow he’d made of cane and fletched with white turkey feathers.

His arrow hit the buck perfectly behind the shoulder, the super-sharp stone broadhead he handmade drove deep into the deer’s chest.

“I saw him race and tear through the corn field,” says McConnell, who owns a hardwood flooring and restoration business. “I heard him crashing away through corn stalks, and then nothing.”.

The bowman found a good blood trail where the buck stood, and the trail was easy to follow through the corn.

Industry observers note that “He only went about 75 yards before falling dead,” he states. “My stone broadhead did an incredible job, driving through its liver, a lung, and smashing into a rib on the opposite side of the buck. The arrow point hit bone and stopped or it would have completely gone through the buck’s hide on the opposite side.

Sources indicate that “Everything really came together for me with that deer. I’ve taken lots of animals with the bows and arrows I’ve made. But it’s the first deer I’ve taken with a stone broadhead that I knapped myself – and it was devastating.”.

It has been revealed that mcConnell has taken plenty of deer and wild hogs with traditional archery gear he’s made. He also shot a buffalo with his traditional equipment, and a stone point head he’d made specifically for the hunt.

Recent findings suggest that he called some friends who helped get his massive 8-point buck out of the field. The field-dressed buck weighed 180 pounds at the processor. It had an estimated live weight of well over 200 pounds.

He will eventually have the deer scored via Buckmasters, and his taxidermist estimated the rack to be about 140 inches.

Read Next: Killing a Grizzly the Old-Fashioned Way: With a Longbow and a Stone-Point Arrowhead.

McConnell models his canted bow shooting style after legendary archer Howard Hill. He leans forward when drawing his bow, anchors his arrow at the corner of his mouth, and uses his bare hand holding his bow as an arrow rest.

It has been revealed that “I got started in archery when I was only 14,” McConnell states. “It’s been a lot of fun learning about making bows, arrows, and now stone broadheads. Traditional equipment is remarkably efficient bowhunting gear.”.

#32981. Industry News: Tips for Hunting Mature Bucks Over Bait (Plus the Ethics of If You Should)

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1317 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Tips for Hunting Mature Bucks Over Bait (Plus the Ethics of If You Should)

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1317 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • During the 2023 deer season, I shot my biggest buck ever: a Kentucky main-frame 12-pointer with a couple extra points that scored 168 6/8 inches.
  • It has been revealed that and as I write this, I can hear blood boiling and I can see the angry comments coming.
  • Sources indicate that the National Deer Association published an article explaining how baiting deer can spread disease: “By design, baiting and supplemental feeding concentrate deer and other wildlife species for the purposes of hunting, trapping, viewing, or simply increasing nutrition available to the animals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During the 2023 deer season, I shot my biggest buck ever: a Kentucky main-frame 12-pointer with a couple extra points that scored 168 6/8 inches. And I shot that big sum-buck over a yellow pile of ear and persimmon-flavored shelled corn. I even dropped a protein block in the middle and seasoned it with scent for good measure.

It has been revealed that and as I write this, I can hear blood boiling and I can see the angry comments coming. Hunting whitetails over bait is still a controversial topic across much of deer country. It is, of course, illegal in many states in the Midwest, Northeast, and West. And even in places where baiting is legal, some argue that hunters should avoid using it.

Sources indicate that the National Deer Association published an article explaining how baiting deer can spread disease: “By design, baiting and supplemental feeding concentrate deer and other wildlife species for the purposes of hunting, trapping, viewing, or simply increasing nutrition available to the animals. Some argue baiting and feeding have positive attributes, but no one can disagree they have numerous negative implications to a deer herd, including altering animal behavior, degrading the habitat near bait and feed sites, increasing the susceptibility to predation, and greatly enhancing the opportunity for disease transmission.”.

The NDA’s formal position on baiting deer is this: “The NDA opposes the expansion of baiting where not at the moment legal. The NDA will not work to repeal baiting where currently legal, except where CWD (or other known diseases) is present. The NDA supports the use of baiting by wildlife professionals conducting scientific research. The NDA supports continued research on the effects on baiting in deer management programs.”.

Baiting is legal and very popular in many Southern states. All hell broke loose when Kansas regulators began discussing the potential of banning deer baiting. Hunting deer in Texas is synonymous with hunting over a feeder. But still, many folks don’t understand how substantial bucks relate to bait piles.

Sources indicate that two comments I always hear when the bait debate pops up go something like: “Oh, you bait, bro? Must be easy killing those big bucks.” Or, “Bait won’t kill big, mature bucks, Jack.”.

Recent findings suggest that I scoff at both of those statements. Neither are true, and it’s far easier to screw up on a mature buck with a poor baiting strategy than it is to fill a tag with one. Like other tactics, baiting is just another tool in the arsenal. It isn’t a cheat code.

It has been revealed that I know because I’ve been baiting Kentucky whitetails most of my hunting career, and it took a long time before I started experiencing success on mature deer. Here is how to bait deer and, more specifically, how to bait a monster buck—plus some considerations if you’re on the fence about legal baiting.

Recent findings suggest that the early season is my favorite time to bait a monster buck. Hunting pressure is low. There’s plenty of cover for concealment. Deer are on predictable bed-to-feed lines of movement. There’s no better time to catch a buck off-guard over a bait pile.

In a recent development, target warm-season bedding areas, such as north-facing slopes or low-lying areas near water that offer a high stem count. Then, determine what destination food source deer are targeting, such as green soybeans, fresh-cut corn, or dropping white oak acorns. Place the bait between the bedroom and dinner table.

Don’t overlook the pre-rut. This is a great time to bait a monster buck. Bucks are moving more but aren’t running wild just yet. So, capitalize on that buck’s rising testosterone levels. Often that leads to increased daylight travel.

As with the early season, it’s still all about bed-to-feed patterns. But now, deer are likely settling into their fall bedding areas and food sources. So, find these locations (which vary greatly by region and habitat type) and plant bait stations along lines of travel.

It has been revealed that once the rut hits, you might get a buck to hit a bait pile. But most of the time, a rutting buck is more interested in scent-checking does that have been through the buffet line. Because of this, bait stations are still effective during the rut, but you must hunt them differently.

Usually, I prefer to place bait piles on the downwind sides of doe bedding areas. Or locate the bait between two doe bedding areas. Bucks like to travel these locations anyway, so it’s a no-brainer game plan.

In a recent development, once the rut is over, and the late season arrives, it’s all about the food again. But still, focus on late-season bedding areas. Think solar bedding (south-facing slopes) and thermal cover (dense stands of coniferous trees). Also, consider what deer are eating now, including remaining waste grain, green plots, remaining acorns, but most importantly, woody browse.

Once again, the best bet is placing bait piles between bedding areas and destination food sources. Use these as staging areas to intercept bucks during daylight. At this point, they aren’t likely to reach destination food sources before dark. But if your bait site is located close enough to bedding, they might hit that corn pile during legal shooting hours.

Read Next: 35 Deer Hunting Tips to Read Before This Season.

Recent findings suggest that no matter the time of year, there are certain tactics that apply to virtually every baiting scenario. Of course, you have to locate a big buck before bait will help you. No volume of bait will bring in a monster buck if he doesn’t already live there. But once you’ve got a big buck located, follow these tips.

Recent findings suggest that some people say deer hunting over bait isn’t ethical. But here’s the thing: Some hunting ethics are situational. I’m not talking about taking poor shots or breaking hunting laws. Those ethics are clearly black and white.

For me, baiting deer is more of a gray area. First off, if it’s legal, it’s legal. When analyzing the differences of state-to-state guidelines on baiting, you’ll see regional discrepancies just like you will with crossbow regulations, the use of deer urine lures, and season structures. So if your area allows baiting, then it’s likely that agency wildlife managers for that area have decided baiting is not detrimental to the deer and deer hunting.

It has been revealed that second, it’s notable to realize that it’s not like you can just throw out bait at any random spot in the woods and start shooting trophy bucks. It’s far from a canned hunt. If you live in an area that permits baiting, understand that bait has several different applications. Where legal, it can be used to help you attract deer, hold deer, feed supplemental nutrition, take inventory of deer, and more.

Industry observers note that as for effectiveness, people commonly say bait stations are either fool-proof or that they turn bucks nocturnal. In my experience, neither are true.

Recent findings suggest that whitetails are smart, especially around bait piles. They learn to approach bait piles downwind and they pick up on hunters’ scent in the area. Yes, they will often hit bait at night. But no buck is 100 percent nocturnal—that’s a myth.

It has been revealed that if you suddenly start seeing a target buck avoiding bait during daylight, it’s likely because you screwed up and disrupted that deer. Or, he started bedding elsewhere. Or, he started targeting a different destination food source. Or, maybe he’s just being a wild, unpredictable deer.

The point is, hunting over bait is still deer hunting. Anything can happen, and most of the time the substantial buck wins. But if you understand how to bait deer and you execute a well-crafted game initiative, then baiting just might lead to the biggest whitetail of your life.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For winter snowshoeing on hiking trails and in the backcountry, you want a durable snowshoe with aggressive crampons for traction and a secure binding system that locks your boots to the snowshoes. If you want to get off the grid and snowshoe through backcountry terrain, here are our 10 recommended snowshoes. For more information, see our buying advice below.

Winter hiking snowshoes serve two key functions: they provide traction on icy trails and when climbing steep terrain, and they provide flotation over snow, so you don’t sink or posthole, which can be quite exhausting. While all the winter hiking snowshoes listed above meet both requirements, some excel in traction, like the MSR Lightning Ascents, MSR Evo Ascents, and Tubbs Flex VRTs, while others emphasize flotation, like the Tubbs Mountaineers.

Recent findings suggest that as a rule of thumb, teardrop-shaped snowshoes with synthetic, riveted decks tend to emphasize flotation, while rectangular snowshoes focus more on traction. If you’ll be climbing ice-covered mountains mostly, you’ll probably want a snowshoe that emphasizes traction; snowshoes that focus on flotation are better for areas where deep, powdery snow is the norm.

If you’re trying to choose between different snowshoes, there are four key properties that should guide your decision-making:.

In a recent development, most winter hikers carry multiple traction devices and switch between them during the day. If you’re hiking a packed trail, you might start in bare boots, relying on your boot treads for traction because less weight on your feet means you’ll fatigue more slowly. If you hit slick or icy terrain, you might switch to microspikes, then snowshoes if you encounter fresh, uncompacted snow or slush.

It has been revealed that to have these traction aids when you need them, you need to carry them. Microspikes are pretty easy to pack, but snowshoes aren’t because they’re big and bulky. Their bulk comes from their length, width, and thickness, which depends largely on the binding style they use. Lay-flat bindings, like the simple straps on the MSR Lightning Ascent and the MSR Evo Ascent, make snowshoes easy to attach and carry in a backpack, while snowshoes with Boa binding systems tend to be the bulkiest and hardest to pack.

Weight is also a key factor when choosing a snowshoe. Most snowshoes weigh four to five pounds, and they’re probably going to be the heaviest thing in your backpack, after water. That weight adds up over the course of a day, whether it’s in your backpack or on your feet.

According to recent reports, we’ve already considered the packability of snowshoe bindings, but you should also consider comfort, security, ease of use while wearing gloves, whether the binding can freeze and become inoperative, and how easy it is to repair if it breaks. For example, some people worry that Boa closure systems can freeze if they get wet and stop working until they thaw. It’s a valid concern. One advantage, however, is that they are easy to use while wearing gloves and provide a secure grip that’s unlikely to come undone once set. Contrast that to the flat straps used on MSR snowshoes. They’ll never freeze up, they’re easy to replace if torn or lost, but they can be hard to attach when wearing gloves, and they tend to pop open once or twice during a hike.

Snowshoes come in a wide variety of sizes. These are determined by the total weight you want to carry (body weight + pack weight) and the flotation you need. Men’s sizes are usually larger than women’s because men are taller and heavier, while women’s snowshoes tend to be narrower because their gait is narrower.

If you’re buying a more traction-oriented snowshoe, you can sometimes drop a size below the manufacturer’s recommendation, especially if you’re hiking in an area that doesn’t get much snow or on trails that other hikers have already broken out. Sizing is directly correlated to gear weight and this is a tactic you can use to lighten your load. If flotation is a priority, you can buy tails, add-on snowshoe extensions that make them longer and increase their surface area. This is another way to cut down on the weight of a snowshoe because you can bring your tails when you need more flotation, but carry a lighter-weight snowshoe in less challenging conditions.

#32979. Industry News: These Popular Bass Fishing Myths Were Debunked Decades Ago

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3177 w)

Industry News: These Popular Bass Fishing Myths Were Debunked Decades Ago

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3177 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Missed him,” I stated and groaned as I reeled in a slack line.
  • Sources indicate that “Rerig and toss it back in there,” Ralph Manns directed me.
  • The next time I set the hook I was rewarded with a pleasantly bowed rod.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Missed him,” I stated and groaned as I reeled in a slack line. Setting the hook after I had felt a gentle tap had produced nothing but a mangled plastic worm.

Sources indicate that “Rerig and toss it back in there,” Ralph Manns directed me. “Another one might hit it.”.

Manns was right. The next time I set the hook I was rewarded with a pleasantly bowed rod. After a short fight, a five-pound largemouth bass thrashed in the landing net.

“Now, you get one,” I stated and grinned as my bass splashed in the live well.

Industry observers note that manns complied with a cast that dropped his worm beside the same rotted stump. The line twitched, the rod arched and he quickly landed a twin to the first bass. Not a bad start for our first look at Texas’ Lake Livingston—especially after my traumatic and almost sleepless night.

It has been revealed that it had begun innocently enough with my arrival at Livingston’s Penwaugh Marina the previous evening for a meeting of the Texas Outdoor Writers Association. Luck of the draw had placed me in the same room with fisheries biologist Ralph Manns, a pleasant mild-mannered gentleman I was meeting for the first time. I had no idea that our meeting would alter the course of my fishing life.

In a recent development, an insatiable appetite for more facts about bass behavior had prompted Manns to become a full-time student at Southwest Texas State University after retiring from active duty in the Air Force where he had spent 20 years as an intelligence officer and a political scientist. At the time of his retirement he was a lieutenant colonel.

According to recent reports, en route to a masters of science degree in aquatic biology, which he earned in 1981, Manns conducted a study of black bass in Lake Travis in 1977 and 1978. The study team used electronic transmitter tags and receivers to track 14 bass while divers recorded the behavior of another 935 bass. Manns’ team also used angling techniques to obtain detailed reports on an additional 289 bass. Data on more than 20 different types of behavior and the environmental conditions that might influence the fish were fed into a computer to compile and analyze the results.

Manns’ exhaustive studies of scientific literature on bass and his extensive two-year study have led to rather innovative and sometimes controversial conclusions. During my first few hours with him, he crumbled the foundation of my bass fishing knowledge with solid scientific evidence that contradicted many generally accepted fishing theories.

It has been revealed that those first two bass we caught from Lake Livingston, for example, were taken from classic bass structure—a stump on the upper edge of a submerged creek bed. The bass probably had not migrated from the depths, however, to feed in the shallower water as a popular myth would have us believe.

The hypothesis that bass live in deep water, migrate to shallow water on a daily basis to feed and then return to deep water along established migration routes is generally credited to Buck Perry, the gentleman rightfully recognized as the father of structure fishing. His methods of catching bass have been so successful that other anglers and writers have perpetuated his migration theories.

Ralph Manns agreed that such structures are good places in which to fish but the analytically minded biologist could find no scientific literature to substantiate a deep-water migration theory. Manns wanted a better explanation for the appearance of bass at certain underwater structure.

It has been revealed that “Sure enough,” Manns related, “our tracking studies verified data available in at least 15 other studies that showed the predominant movements of black bass are parallel to the shorelines and contour lines and not perpendicular to them. The movement, moreover, usually is at a nearly constant depth.”.

A national magazine recently published a story entitled “When the Sun is High, the Bass Go Deep”. The author surmised that because more bass are caught in deep water during midday hours, bass obviously migrate from shallow to deep water as the sun brightens. And that’s how myths get started.

Manns’ study of Lake Travis bass revealed no such tendency.

Recent findings suggest that “Our research showed some bass at shallow depths, some at medium depths and some in deep water at all times,” he revealed. “And they tended to remain at that particular depth whether active or inactive. Bass do move vertically but not routinely. A deep fish might pop to the surface to run through a school of shad, but it will grab two or three and almost immediately dive to its original depth because that’s where it has established its equilibrium and can suspend without effort.”.

A bass can hover effortlessly at a particular depth because its air bladder is balanced at that depth and it gets out of balance if it varies much from that point. According to Manns, it takes hours for the air bladder to adjust to a major depth change. The more out of balance a bass gets, the harder it has to swim to maintain its stability.

According to recent reports, manns noted that black bass usually move along contour lines for only short distances and tend to stop at any bisecting lines of structure that obstruct their movement, such as a fence, stump or rock. By casting to a fence, an angler increases his odds simply because moving bass are likely to pause there.

Industry observers note that most anglers will catch more bass, Manns maintained, if they fish on the better bisecting structures for several minutes during activity periods. Additional schools often stop at the same structure long enough for the anglers to catch more fish.

It has been revealed that some fishermen consider schools of black bass a rarity. Limit catches might be rare but, according to Manns’ underwater observations, most bass are in either a school or an aggregation.

“There are almost no loner bass,” Manns says. “The few single fish we observed underwater were either very sick, very large or totally inactive. The sick ones obviously couldn’t keep up and the larger bass were probably unable to find compatible partners in their size range.

“Rule one,” he continued, “if you catch a bass, assume it is not alone. As a minimum, it is in a group of two to five fish. Actively striking bass are usually feeding and moving bass. They tighten up their aggregations and move in small schools.”.

Recent findings suggest that during activity periods, of course, almost anyone can catch bass by tossing an edible-looking lure in the path of a feeding school. It’s the inactive periods that separate expert from novice bass fishermen.

It has been revealed that “Fishermen should remember that bass are inactive most of the time, even if their stomachs are empty,” Manns claimed. “Unlike humans who have a predictable three square meals a day, a bass may be forced to exist for days without eating. That little bit of minnow it ate three days ago must last the bass a long time and it does not waste it!”.

The fact that a fish is inactive doesn’t mean that it won’t eat, Manns admitted. If something passes closely and in front of a bass’ mouth, it will usually eat because bass are opportunists. But an inactive bass probably won’t move more than a few inches to hit a lure. An angler who is fishing a spot that holds inactive bass may have to cast 15 or more times before the lure passes through that tiny strike zone in front of an inactive bass.

A fast-moving crankbait offers good odds of getting a lure to an active bass. Because active fish may chase lures for 10 feet or more, each cast effectively covers a wide path on each side of the bait’s track. The same lure retrieved past inactive bass, however, may pass by many fish without eliciting a strike.

The success of an angler’s technique, then, depends on how active the bass are. Anglers who cast and crank at wide intervals over inactive bass will usually get few strikes. Fishermen who flip worms or jigs to the base of cover objects where inactive bass may hold, however, get close enough to take a few fish. If the same anglers continue to flip slow lures while bass are in an active state, though, they cannot hope to hook as many as those with fast lures. Thus, an angler must match his lure and his technique to the activity level of the bass.

It has been revealed that one widely accepted myth claims that bass avoid sunlight because they have no eyelids. Manns’ underwater observations indicate otherwise.

Industry observers note that “It was clear to us that bass have no requirement to live in shade,” Manns declared. “Moving bass were as likely to stop at a sunny spot as a shaded one. Although bass have no eyelids, their eyes have pigment mechanisms that compensate for excessive light. Water is an excellent light filter, too. Unless a bass is in very shallow, calm and clear water, the water serves it well as a pair of sunglasses.”.

In a recent development, bass that anglers catch from beneath piers, boat houses and docks are probably there for cover or food rather than for shade. In fact, even slightly colored water refracts sunlight sufficiently to destroy any distinct shade line within a few feet. Even in moderately clear lakes, bass down more than 10 feet experience little or no shading from objects at the surface.

This means that bass a fisherman finds beneath floating structures will probably hold tightly to the bottom of the structure—unless, of course, there are other attractive structural elements on the bottom. Lures retrieved just beneath floating structures, then, will probably be more effective than lures retrieved along the bottom.

According to recent reports, although bass do not need to avoid sunlight, Manns’ records indicate that more bass are caught from shaded areas than from sunny ones. He stressed that this statistic is not contradictory because inactive bass may suspend in either shade or in sunny open water. But for an angler to cast his lure near enough to inactive bass to make them strike, he usually must find bass that are suspended close to an identifiable target. While the target creates shade, the shade itself is incidental and not the reason the bass are there.

Another concern of bass anglers is that bass will move when they hear noise coming from above them. Manns’ study, however, clearly demonstrated that bass learn to ignore any sounds that don’t represent a threat. Bass frequently swam beneath docks where workers were pounding with hammers or sailors were stomping in boats. Bass also ignored outboard motor noises in Lake Travis, which is heavily used by recreational boaters. Surprisingly, however, some of the lake’s bass had learned to move away from boats with electric fishing motors and it was difficult to approach such bass unless they were pushed against cover objects.

Manns suggests that a great myth of angling literature is that bass seek out preferred temperatures, water clarity, structure and so on. He stressed that the part of a bass’ brain that processes every piece of visual or physical information is about the size of a thumbnail. A bass simply does not have the ability to be intuitive.

“A bass will not run across a lake to an area that has a better temperature level,” Manns claimed, “because it doesn’t know it’s there. Now if a bass is wandering around and finds a more comfortable area, it might think, ‘Wow! Isn’t this temperature nice?’ And if it can stay there without getting hungry, it may hang around long enough for the angler with a temperature meter to catch it.”.

In Manns’ study, bass did not move to deeper water to avoid surface temperatures in the 84° to 88° range. In fact, when all other factors were equal, black bass (including smallmouths) preferred the water temperature to be between 78° and 86°, not the 72° that is popularized in most fishing literature. Manns’ findings are corroborated by at least 20 other scientific studies published during a 40-year period. Bass found in cooler water are there because of a better food supply or because they are unable to compete with larger predators present in warmer water.

Manns admits that there are optimum chemical environments for bass but in most lakes the fish must be satisfied with less. They merely move into someplace tolerable, adapt to it and once they’ve adapted to that condition, any change is a negative change to those fish.

Recent findings suggest that “Most people don’t realize that a bass is constantly adapting to its environment,” Manns declared. “The chemistry of its body adapts to temperature and water conditions and, if any factors change, the fish is temporarily out of balance. When cold fronts go through, for example, sudden drops in temperature disturb the fish’s equilibrium and it becomes slightly sick until it adapts to the new condition. That helps explain why bass normally don’t bite as well after a cold front.”.

Sources indicate that A common dream of anglers is catching bass on almost every cast from a “hotspot” where hungry largemouths eagerly await the next cast. The nearest thing I ever found to that fabled “hotspot” was on Lake Sam Rayburn back in 1968. My partner and I found a timbered flat near a river channel where every cast with our crankbaits hooked a chunky bass. We tied the boat line to a limb and promptly caught 60 largemouth bass from an area no larger than the average living room. In that era of 15-bass limits it was the first chance I had to cull bass to improve a stringer.

Our hopes for a repeat performance the next day were short lived. Our first few casts hooked bass, but the action ceased and we never relocated the bass. Nor did any of our friends ever find fish there on many subsequent trips. Manns offered an explanation for the phenomenon.

According to recent reports, “They were probably transient bass, which is a major cause of confusion to anglers. Bass are generally thought of as having one type of behavior pattern. Actually, though, there are two types of black bass: transient bass and home-range bass. The concept is an old one that shows up in scientific literature as far back as 30 years ago.”.

According to recent reports, manns theorized that the fish’s health or its ability to catch prey determines whether it is a home-range or transient bass. Healthy fish establish territories and hold them, moving as little as possible. They conserve energy by feeding rapidly and remain in the same general location unless there is a major change in water conditions or the food supply.

Large bass populations or shortages of prey create competition for food, however. Those bass that feed less efficiently must feed longer and move often to find forage. A transient is one because it is a loser.

Industry observers note that there are many transient bass in our better bass lakes and they almost always school. An angler who finds such a concentration can catch great numbers of them at one time but he should not necessarily label the area as a great fishing hole. Such catches can be the result of chance meetings with transients.

Manns notes that an angler should not spend much time returning to the site of a massive catch unless he has reason to believe, such as repeated success, that the place is a home-range area. An angler can more consistently catch bass by returning to locations where he has taken one or two fish over and over again. Those are probably spots that have enough food to hold home-range fish day after day.

Manns stressed that bass reactions vary according to how hungry they are. A very hungry fish will probably strike at any lure it can get in its mouth. A bass that has been feeding on shad for 20 minutes, however, will probably only take something that is similar to the shad.

Although bass can see colors, anglers should remember that bass do not perceive them as a human would. Manns recalled a day when he and his partner followed a large school of bass feeding heavily on shad. The two cast all of the traditional shad-color lures without a strike. As soon as Manns put on a gold lure, though, he caught fish on almost every cast.

The bass obviously responded to some flash of gold from the shad caused, perhaps, by the angle of sunlight. The bass had enough color discrimination that they triggered to the tiny variation. Manns, therefore, suggests that anglers who are unsuccessful in catching obviously active bass should change lure colors, sizes and actions until they find one that triggers the fish. Bass are not ambush predators as are halibut, angler fish and sculpin; nor are they chase predators such as tuna or striped bass. A black bass is a compromise fish designed to do a lot of things—none of them perfectly but all of them well. The bass is a seeker with a short sprint. It enters cover for protection and to rest, not to ambush prey. Cover actually limits and hinders a bass’ ability to strike and that is why prey fish hide in such areas.

The standard hunting pattern of a bass is to move around structure objects to see if anything strays far enough from cover to become vulnerable. It assesses its ability to catch individuals of prey and strikes only at those it thinks can be caught. The bass ignores prey that are likely to dodge and thus escape. A bass will ignore a lure that looks like a healthy bluegill just as it would ignore a real bluegill under the same circumstances.

Sources indicate that “Bass fishing is very mathematical, very predictable,” Manns claimed. “It is a problem to be solved. Most of the false concepts arise because writers intellectualize about bass. The reaction mechanism of bass is actually very very basic: a reaction to a stimulus and a response, nothing more.

Read Next: Old-School Tips for Catching Major Bass Right Now.

Sources indicate that “A bass can’t outsmart you. All you have to do is find something that will stimulate it, put it where it will stimulate it and you will catch a bass. There’s really nothing more to fishing than that.”.

Recent findings suggest that manns makes it sound simple and it looks simple enough when you watch him in action. He merely works the odds, covering as much favorable water as possible with a wide variety of lures. But he seems to catch many more bass than the average fisherman. The years he spent in their living quarters are paying off.

This story was originally published in the November 1983 issue of Outdoor Life.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that joe Merritt, age 41, of Middletown, Indiana had some target bucks he was after the first week of November during the state archery deer season. This is the first year he had cell cameras out to monitor multiple areas, and they proved to be a critical tool for taking the buck of a lifetime.

“On Tuesday, November 3 I got a trail camera photo of a huge buck sent to my cell phone from a very small woodlot that was my least favorite place I had to hunt,” Merritt tells Outdoor Life (he did the interview after just spending a morning hunting rabbits with his beagles). “The photos were of a huge buck that I’d never seen anywhere before.”.

Recent findings suggest that the next day the same cell phone camera got photos of the buck again. And the next morning, Nov. 5 at 3:55 a.m. he got photos of the huge buck again from the same camera in the same small wooded area.

According to recent reports, “I knew I had to go after that buck right then,” indicates Merritt, who owns a coffee distribution firm. “I left immediately and was in my saddle hanging from a  thin tree well before dawn.”.

According to recent reports, merritt listened to deer in the woods around him long before daybreak. He wanted to be in his stand early to not disturb deer. He believes the spot was a bedding area near a sanctuary of private property where no hunting is allowed.

In a recent development, as an overcast dawn broke, he had a small 8-point buck come by his stand. Almost an hour later a doe showed.

“She kept looking behind her as she moved my way,” indicates Merritt. “She kept coming to me and flopped down and bedded just 35 yards away. The whole time she was looking back, and I was a little puzzled until the giant buck I had on camera indicated up.”.

But the giant buck moved toward the doe and bedded down near her, just 37 yards away.

In a recent development, “That’s when the chess game began,” states Merritt, who is also a dedicated houndsman who’s pursued raccoons and bears with dogs. “I was hanging from a very small diameter tree, and both deer were bedded close, and there was no chance for a bow shot while they were lying down.”.

Merritt sat in his stand, quiet and still, for four hours before the doe finally got restless, stood, and walked toward Merritt. She was feeding on browse as she moved his way.

Sources indicate that “That’s when the buck stood up, and started following her,” Merritt says. “The doe was right underneath me watching back at the buck when he turned and gave me a full broadside shot at 22 yards.”.

Merritt made a perfect shot on the biggest deer of his life.

Recent findings suggest that “I saw him running and blood was blowing out everywhere,” said the bowhunter. “I didn’t see or hear him fall. But I knew the shot was perfect and the buck would be easy to find.”.

The doe was still feeding under his stand after Merritt shot and the buck ran.

Industry observers note that “I just broke down in the stand, shaking and talking to myself about what just happened,” he indicates. “It took about 10 minutes for me to de-escalate and comprehend what had just happened.”.

Sources indicate that then he climbed down to the ground and walked to where he’d last seen the buck. He walked right to the downed animal that was only 60 yards from where his arrow had struck it.

Sources indicate that “I walked up to him and placed my hands on his rack and thanked the Lord for what had just happened,” says Merritt. “Then I phoned my wife and friends.”.

Shortly, his close pal Jared Leppink joined Merritt in the woods and the two of them loaded the buck into an UTV. Then they shot photos of it, dressed the deer, and caped it.

While the buck has a massive rack, Merritt mentioned the deer only weighed about 200 pounds – not a massive animal for east-central Indiana, which regularly gives up 250 to 300-pound whitetails.

According to recent reports, “I don’t think the buck was that old,” Merritt claims. “The teeth were not very worn. I think he was between 3.5 to 5.5 years old.”.

When pictures of his buck hit social media it created a wave of folks contacting him.

“I asked him why he was thanking me. He stated, ‘Well now I know you got him, and I don’t have to keep passing other good bucks waiting for the 23-pointer to show up.’”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One summer evening, I was hiking a trail near Marias Pass in Glacier National Park, returning to the car after a few hours of wildlife photography at a lake— nothing but deer and mosquitoes to show for it—when I noticed something blondish-brown moving toward me. It barely registered. I felt relaxed, though, truthfully, I’m never fully relaxed.

And then we were on top of each other.

Recent findings suggest that A grizzly cub, substantial as an overgrown Saint Bernard. I was fascinated—until reality hit. The mother wouldn’t be far behind.

Sources indicate that “Hey, bear,” I shouted, my voice cracking. The cub woofed an alarm and took off to my left, a dark blur swallowed by the forest.

I turned toward the trail ahead. And—boom—there she was. Running at me, big and fast and flat to the ground.

I grabbed the bear spray strapped to my chest, fumbled the can free, and held it out like a pistol. She closed in. I could see the whites.

Tech Report: The Gun Industry Is Divided Over Federal’s New High-Pressure 6.5 Creedmoor Ammo. Here’s Why

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3332 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish

  • Late last month Bergara became the first gun manufacturer to explicitly state Federal’s 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak ammo is not approved for use in its bolt-action rifles.
  • The 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak, introduced this summer, has the same dimensions as a traditional brass 6.5 Creedmoor cartridge and was specifically designed by Federal Ammunition for use in existing 6.5 Creed rifles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Late last month Bergara became the first gun manufacturer to explicitly state Federal’s 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak ammo is not approved for use in its bolt-action rifles. This reverses earlier guidance that the latest high-pressure cartridge technology was compatible with Bergara’s existing 6.5 Creedmoor rifles.

The 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak, introduced this summer, has the same dimensions as a traditional brass 6.5 Creedmoor cartridge and was specifically designed by Federal Ammunition for use in existing 6.5 Creed rifles. It is not a new cartridge, but an improvement to an existing cartridge. This unusual dynamic is part of the regulatory and potential liability concerns currently vexing the gun industry.

Federal’s proprietary steel-alloy case technology contains higher pressures that drive bullets at faster speeds for better performance. Plus Peak operates at 80,000 psi, compared to about 62,000 to 65,000 psi for brass 6.5 Creed cartridges. This is possible because the Peak Alloy case material that Federal has developed is much stronger than brass. It acts as a containment vessel insulating the action and barrel from the extra pressure without inflicting extra stress on the rifle.

Related: They Built a Rifle Cartridge That Could Change Hunting and Shooting Forever.

It has been revealed that the ammunition has undergone substantial testing by Federal, a dozen gunmakers and component companies, the U.S. military (which has ordered 40 million cases), and other industry professionals.

Industry observers note that and indeed, Bergara rifles were originally deemed “compatible” with this 6.5 Creed Plus Peak ammo, according to previous guidance from Federal and media coverage of the ammo’s launch in June. But on Oct. 29 Bergara announced that the upcoming ammunition “is NOT approved for use in any Bergara rifle chambered in 6.5 Creedmoor.”.

The reason Bergara cites is spec-based:.

Recent findings suggest that “These cartridge pressures haven’t been evaluated under SAAMI’s standard development process,” reads the statement, referring to the Sporting Arms and Ammunition Manufacturing Institute. “Ammunition operating outside SAAMI pressure standards for its caliber should not be used in any rifle unless Bergara formally confirms compatibility for that model.”.

It has been revealed that SAAMI sets the gun industry’s self-imposed guardrails with voluntary performance standards for firearms, ammunition, and suppressors. Bergara did not cite any incidents of catastrophic failures or injury related to shooting the newly introduced case technology through its rifles. (No one we spoke to for this story reported being aware of a catastrophic failure while testing the Plus Peak in existing 6.5 Creed rifles.).

Bergara revealed in 2025 it would launch rifles in 7mm Backcountry, which debuted the same high-pressure cartridge technology as the Plus Peak. Various online distributors and retailers indicate Bergara’s HMR Pro and MG Lite models would be available in the 7BC, but the company doesn’t at the moment offer any rifles chambered in 7BC on its website. It’s unclear if any preproduction or production models were ever manufactured. Bergara declined to comment for this story.

In a June statement, SAAMI acknowledged the development of the 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak and the creation of a working group — at Federal’s request — to evaluate the fresh case technology on “performance, pressure, testing, and interchangeability standards.”.

SAAMI and its member companies are also discussing “the technical issues and opportunities presented by advanced cartridge case technologies and their interaction with existing firearms and suppressors.”.

The organization stopped short of taking a position on the ammunition and instead urged hunters and shooters to contact their rifle’s manufacturer before shooting Federal’s 6.5 Creed Plus Peak.

In a recent development, “At this time, SAAMI’s guidance stays the same,” SAAMI’s senior director of technical affairs, Alan Serven, tells Outdoor Life. “As this is not a standardized cartridge, we can’t really say anything definitive about it, so we are directing folks to the manufacturer of their firearm. And we do caution that an answer from one manufacturer cannot be interpreted as a blanket statement … It’s on a case-by-case basis with each of the manufacturers and potentially down to model.”.

Sources indicate that on Nov. 5 the sporting-goods retailer Scheels sent an internal memo to its employees announcing any Plus Peak ammo should not be stocked on store floors or made available to customers.

“As of yesterday morning we have added a ‘DNS’ Do not Stock rating to all SKUs of Federal 6.5 Creedmoor +Peak ammunition,” reads the memo, obtained by Outdoor Life. “The Kinetic Group [Federal’s parent firm], gun manufacturers and SAAMI are continuing to review this product. Once we have more information on their review and the stocking of the 6.5 Creedmoor +Peak, we will make a determination on how to proceed.”.

Industry observers note that scheels has put all direct orders for Plus Peak on hold, according to the memo. The retailer also instructed its ammo and gun teams to accept any returns from customers and put any received Plus Peak “somewhere where we can ensure it will not make its way to the floor to be sold.” When Outdoor Life called a Scheels store asking about Plus Peak availability and the possibility of ordering any, the employee who answered the phone replied that no, this was not possible because “corporate put the kibosh on this until SAAMI figures out the safety and pressure problems.” The store policy affects all five SKUs of Plus Peak.

Industry observers note that “Federal’s Peak Alloy case technology is the wave of the future for rifle ammunition,” Kinetic Group’s VP of marketing Jason Nash tells Outdoor Life, noting that Federal sought to work with as many rifle makers as possible in its development of high-pressure loads. “Over the past seven years Federal has manufactured millions of rounds in multiple cartridges and firearms. Federal has the utmost confidence in this latest technology and its function in today’s firearms.”.

Some gunmakers have confirmed to OL that all their existing 6.5 Creedmoor rifles are compatible with Plus Peak and they have no safety concerns whatsoever. Others have remained quiet on the advisability of using Plus Peak in their 6.5 Creedmoor rifles. Bergara remains the only rifle maker who has publicly disallowed its use in its bolt-action rifles. (Break-action rifles from CVA, Bergara’s sister manufacturer, are also not approved for Plus Peak, according to Federal’s site.).

According to recent reports, this about-face on the use of Plus Peak in Bergara rifles raises many more questions than it answers. For instance, is this hesitancy around the 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak rooted in legitimate concerns of consumer safety? Or is it ultimately driven by the potential threat that some companies see to their bottom lines? Here’s what to know.

Although the conversations around Plus Peak in SAAMI’s working group are confidential, industry insiders are keyed into the crux of the concern. Here are two of the primary camps.

It has been revealed that no one seems to be disputing the performance gains of the Plus Peak ammo. Instead, the debate is over how to standardize it.

Sources indicate that “It definitely is an interesting idea what Federal is doing,” states one gun manufacturer who spoke on the condition of anonymity. “The industry itself is not politicking against it. The industry is not against new technology. We know and understand new products are what drive business. That’s not the glitch. There’s probably some ammunition companies that are bitter or angry they didn’t think of it first, but that’s also neither here nor there.”.

Sources indicate that according to this source, the problem is the fresh technology right now puts too much onus on gunmakers without the opportunity to earn revenue. In fact, it poses a significant expense for bigger manufacturers.

It has been revealed that “For those of us who played by the rules and built guns to SAAMI’s standards, now we have an ammunition out there that’s outside that spec. And we’re at a conundrum to say, ‘Is it safe or not safe in our guns,’” claims the gunmaker. “So one [option is] we have to go back and retest all our guns at an immense cost to verify those guns will pass these pressures.”.

Some guns will inevitably pass, they say, but other guns may not. This could result in a laundry list of liability concerns in which gun companies must painstakingly note — online and in owners manuals — which rifle models are compatible and incompatible with Plus Peak.

The biggest fear is that a customer will get hurt. It’s also a bad look for any existing guns that don’t pass, given that it “may expose ‘weaknesses’ that don’t exist” in rifles that were built to spec for standard 6.5 Creed loads.

Another option for gunmakers is to simply not retest guns and not comment on (or in Bergara’s case, publicly come out against) the 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak.

It has been revealed that “It does kind of stand in the face of why we have SAAMI and why we self regulate,” indicates the source. “So it’s a legitimate concern. We won’t approve [Plus Peak] either. Will our guns pass it? Most likely. But we’re not chomping at the bit to go through all the testing to verify that. We have other things we need to worry about.”.

The right way to have handled this upcoming ammo technology, in this gunmaker’s mind, was to have rolled out a new cartridge that could have more easily received SAAMI approval and allowed gunmakers to collaborate on new rifle builds.

“We would have all happily engaged in a new caliber that did this, like the 7 Backcountry. We knew the pressures, and we could build a gun specifically to handle that caliber with those higher pressures. No problem. It’s the retro-fitting for everybody. Why should we go to a pile of work? Just build a new caliber. It’s a very cool technology. We’re all about that. We’re not dragging our feet because we’re old and crotchety. We’re trying to protect our business and this industry.”.

It has been revealed that in that scenario this ammunition wouldn’t be a 6.5 Creedmoor using Plus Peak technology — it would be a whole fresh cartridge called, for instance, the 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak. Of course, this would require shooters to buy a new rifle.

Industry observers note that “The difference is meaningful,” says Outdoor Life shooting editor John Snow of this hypothetical scenario. “And presumably, you’d have to have firearms marked with that latest cartridge name in order to be in compliance with what SAAMI has deemed acceptable.”.

Sources indicate that federal has treated the 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak not as a new cartridge, but an improvement on existing 6.5 Creed ammo. The difference, again, is that it contains higher-than-SAAMI-approved pressures that drive bullets at higher velocities.

These souped-up loads give hunters and shooters the ability to get 6.5 PRC-like performance out of their existing 6.5 Creedmoor rifles.

To some, the nature of Plus Peak is so monumental that industry disruption is natural and even necessary.

“We are embracing high-pressure technology like Peak Alloy,” says Sean Murphy, director of sales and marketing for Proof Research (and an occasional OL contributor). “It’s a development similar to switching from black to smokeless powder.”.

It has been revealed that some of the more nimble gunmakers, like Proof, have already tackled the testing they need to feel comfortable about giving customers approval to run the higher-pressure load in its guns. That’s because Proof predicts this high-pressure ammunition is going to be a major player in the future, and the manufacturer is working to develop barrel and rifle technology to complement it by maximizing accuracy and performance.

It has been revealed that “Proof Research has extensively tested Federal Peak Alloy cases in multiple cartridges, including 6.5 Creedmoor and 7 Backcountry,” indicates Murphy. “In 6.5 Creedmoor alone, thousands of rounds have been fired through hunting, target, and semi-automatic precision rifles with no case failures or firearm damage. Additionally, many thousands of rounds have been fired by Proof with Peak Alloy 5.56 ammunition, also without issue … Chamber-bore obstruction testing across every Proof Research receiver design revealed Peak Alloy cases outperforming equivalent brass cases, with a greater safety margin at 80,000 psi than brass cases at 60,000 psi.”.

The Montana-based rifle maker is also one of the most advanced barrel makers in the country. It spent years developing its PXT barrel, which Proof indicates accomodates much higher pressures and velocities without shortening the barrel’s lifespan.

“During our PXT barrel testing and development, more than 10,000 rounds of 7 Backcountry were fired — including 5,000 and 3,500 on individual receivers — with no damage, and wear levels comparable to brass-cased ammunition,” notes Murphy.

Recent findings suggest that the company also issued an apparent rebuttal to Bergara’s announcement of Oct. 29 with posts to Instagram and Facebook that same day, declaring full support and formal endorsement of Peak Alloy cartridges in its rifles.

“We have tested all our rifles — and many from other manufacturers — extensively with the Plus Peak ammunition and it’s proven to be completely safe,” notes Murphy.

According to recent reports, as part of its development and testing of the Plus Peak, Federal worked with a dozen gunmakers and related businesses. Federal confirmed to American Rifleman this summer that certain rifles from five of those companies are compatible with Plus Peak: Christensen Arms, Weatherby, Seekins Precision, Geissele, and Nemo Arms. Federal matches guidance from SAAMI that hunters and shooters should contact their gunmaker to specify which models are approved.

“Our testing has shown 6.5 Creedmoor +Peak operates in a variety of 6.5 Creedmoor firearm platforms,” Federal advises in the Plus Peak guide on its website. “Refer to your rifle manufacturer for recommendations on compatibility with high-pressure ammunition.”.

Sources indicate that christensen Arms echoes similar language on its website. However, all existing Christensen Arms rifles chambered in 6.5 Creedmoor are compatible with the Plus Peak ammo, a spokesperson confirmed to Outdoor Life. The additional seven brands who worked with Federal include Area 419, Forster Products, Proof Research, Pure Precision, Hill Country Rifles, Short Action Customs, and Springfield Armory.

SAAMI has good cause to be extra cautious, points out Snow, since it’s a voluntary organization. The gun industry has regulated itself for a century — the result of a handshake deal with the government after World War I — and would like to continue avoiding federal oversight “like that of the auto industry,” indicates Snow.

But one reason gunmakers may come out against Plus Peak in their rifles has nothing to do with safety, cost, or liability.

Sources indicate that “It’s possible that companies could see poor accuracy with the Plus Peak ammo and not recommend it,” says another industry insider, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity. “High chamber pressures, especially with some barrels and rifling designs, can cause accuracy problems that aren’t safety issues.”.

Federal has patented its high-pressure cartridge technology, which means other ammunition makers can’t leverage it without paying for the privilege.

It has been revealed that “There are rival companies that would arguably like to see this newly introduced and innovative technology put into a box and shoved off to the side,” says Snow. “Because they don’t have the ability to capitalize on this trend currently, and it’s potentially bad for their business if Plus Peak succeeds.”.

The Peak Alloy case technology used in the 6.5 Creed Plus Peak was pioneered in the relatively upcoming 7mm Backcountry, which debuted in January 2025 and was rooted in development of high-pressure ammunition for the military.

It has been revealed that when the 7mm Backcountry was introduced, we tested more of it than anyone (besides Federal’s engineers) by shooting every SKU and running it in a dozen rifles. Although the 7BC delivered on its promise of velocity and produced accuracy equivalent to factory ammo in other cartridges, we encountered one major problem with almost every rifle. After 40 to 120 rounds, the 7BC rifles developed very stiff primary and secondary extraction. It turned out this was a common concern for other testers and shooters, too.

This problem, ultimately, was rooted in the case dimensions of the cartridge — not poorly cut chambers, as some people have speculated. After receiving updated 7BC ammo and testing the fresh batches in rifles that were previously showing these issues, we’ve found that the extraction issues have been resolved.

Industry observers note that those initial extraction concerns in the 7BC were — erroneously — interpreted as effects of the increased pressure of the cartridge on the guns themselves. That doesn’t appear to be the case. In reality, most rifles chambered in 7mm Backcountry aren’t constructed differently from similar models designed for brass-cased cartridges like the 6.5 Creed.

So in other words, concerns over pressure problems from the new cartridge materials from the 7mm Backcountry to the 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak appear largely unfounded.

The 7 Backcountry was accepted by SAAMI without the current speed bumps, in part, because it’s an entirely new cartridge. It required brand-new guns manufactured specifically for the cartridge. Gunmakers could either opt to produce a gun chambered in 7BC — or not. Federal’s choice to offer the Plus Peak in an existing cartridge was a different route, but a calculated one.

In a recent development, “The reason Federal went with the 6.5 Creedmoor is because the 6.5 Creed was introduced in 2007 and is only available in modern firearms that are of recent vintage,” notes Snow. “So it is extraordinarily unlikely, I would almost say impossible, that we would see, for example, a Plus Peak .308 or .223 offered commercially. That’s because there are way too many actions and rifles of older vintages that cannot be vouched for.”.

Serven could not provide a timeline on when SAAMI’s Plus Peak working group might disclose its findings.

“Our primary mission is safety, so we are proceeding with that in mind. That concern is the overriding factor,” notes Serven. “So we are not in a hurry. The priority is that we get the right answer, not a fast answer.”.

Sources indicate that SAAMI’s acceptance of newly introduced cartridges standardizes the case and load across ammo makers. The organization’s blessing is not required for the sale and use of ammunition, and many niches of the hunting, shooting, and military world operate outside the bounds of SAAMI approval. This includes everyone from brands like Buffalo Bore Ammunition to wildcat cartridge developers to the federal government itself. It also means you can still get your hands on 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak.

According to recent reports, federal presently offers the Terminal Ascent Plus Peak for sale on its site at a limit of two boxes per customer. The four other loads are “currently unavailable.” Plenty of YouTubers have been able to get their hands on the ammo, and none we’ve seen have reported safety problems.

Recent findings suggest that “The stakes are pretty consequential,” indicates Snow of how SAAMI decides to handle the Plus Peak ammo. “On the one hand, are we going to move with less friction and resistance into the era of high-pressure, high-performance cartridges? Or are there going to be speed bumps and other impediments put in place that effectively throttle or discourage the adoption of this latest technology?”.

In a recent development, read Next: I Shot the First Elk With the New 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak Ammo. It’s an Undeniable Elk Hunting Cartridge.

The push to adopt high-pressure rounds has come from the U.S. military, which has mandated it to maintain an advantage over “near peer” adversaries (such as Russia and China) on the battlefield. The military wants rifles capable of defeating newer body armor, and the way to do that is to drive bullets from existing guns at greater speeds.

“The government has been crystal clear about what they want and expect,” indicates Snow, “which is that high-pressure cartridges are happening and need to be here sooner rather than later.”.

Excerpted from the novel Nearshore (Viking, 2026).

Recent findings suggest that palmer was midspan on the Tunitas Creek Bridge, southbound, when the boat came into view through the gunsight notch of the arroyo. It was a Whaler circling clockwise fast and tight, maybe a quarter mile beyond the surf.

According to recent reports, he’d wanted to ride a few waves at a sandbar that had been assembling itself over the past few days at Pomponio. A quick lunch-break session before the wind came up. But then he got the call about the boat, and now that he saw it spinning he also saw that his day was officially fucked. He crossed the bridge and powered up the Coast Highway to the overlook at the top of the rise. He lifted his Bushnells from the dashboard and got out of the truck and glassed the vessel.

The wake’s widening spiral told him the wheel had been hard to starboard a good long while. It looked to be stirring up some kind of suicidal whirlpool.
