  • Sources indicate that you duck hunters know exactly what I mean, but I doubt if any of you ever felt the old longing as much as I did that day in New Guinea in February, 1943.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “Ducks Can Improve Any War,” appeared in the December 1944 issue of Outdoor Life.

A duck hunter is always a duck hunter. No matter how long he’s been away from the sport, he still longs for that song of the wind on the lake reeds. He craves the acrid smell of burning powder and the comfortable feel of his favorite gun. He never forgets the beauty of the cold gray mists of dawn, the hazy silhouettes of decoys, the tense, exciting wait, and finally, the sight of fast gray wings above him.

Sources indicate that you duck hunters know exactly what I mean, but I doubt if any of you ever felt the old longing as much as I did that day in New Guinea in February, 1943. Yes, New Guinea — hot, steaming, sultry. I had been in the Pacific area for eighteen months, flying a fighter. Four of those months were combat flying. I was getting in plenty of hunting — a serious kind of hunting that I enjoyed — when late one afternoon while sitting on alert, a flock of ducks, real live ducks, passed right over our pilot’s hut and lit in a near-by swamp.

Sources indicate that when those ducks flew over, two old-time duck hunters jumped to their feet and watched ’em till they’d disappeared. Then they turned and looked at each other. They didn’t say anything; they didn’t have to. One of those duck hunters was Lieut. Fred Sibley from Maine. I was the other one. And right then and there the war we were in had improved 1,000 percent.

In a recent development, when we opened the boxes of No. 6s we found that half the shells were bloated by the damp atmosphere, and wouldn’t fit into the guns. So we had to take our knives and patiently whittle each shell down until it would slip into the chamber.

We started right in, lining things up for our next day off. We dug up a couple of old double-barrel guns from the squadron supply and, after making the rounds through several camps, found some honest-to-goodness 12 gauge ammunition a pilot had bought in Australia. We finally succeeded in heckling the officer into turning some of it over to us — by promising him a significant fat duck for dinner.

Now, this was really an effective offer, since his squadron had been practically living on bully beef for six months. It didn’t hurt our consciences to take advantage of the poor man, as we knew we could feed a lot of hungry soldiers if we could get him to come across.

In a recent development, anyway, we got back to camp with two boxes of No. 6’s. Later, when we opened them we found that half the shells were bloated by the damp atmosphere, and wouldn’t fit into the guns. So we had to take our knives and patiently whittle each shell down until it would slip into the chamber. Then we gave every shell a coat of grease to protect it from the humidity until the major day.

It has been revealed that we had found previously from wandering around in the jungle that it was absolutely imperative for a man to sprinkle himself with some kind of sulphur as a protection against the chiggers and ticks. These tiny parasites were dangerous not only because their bites caused infections which took weeks to heal in that climate, but because they were known to carry a tropical disease. We also knew it was necessary to use mosquito lotion as millions of these pests swarmed everywhere.

Our problem, then, was to concoct something that wouldn’t wash off our bodies when we were wading through swamps and marsh land after those ducks. We hit on the bright idea of mixing the sulphur powder with vaseline, and it worked like a charm. The mosquito lotion was no problem as we could carry plenty of it along in a small bottle. For extra protection we each obtained a mosquito head net and a pair of leggings. Two canteens of water completed our preparations in the way of equipment for the unique duck hunt.

According to recent reports, we still had a couple of days to go before our day off, so we decided to do some aërial scouting. We knew we’d be doing some flying in those remaining days, and that while on our landing patterns we would have an opportunity to study the swamp and determine the best possible way of getting into it from our camp.

To appreciate the importance of this, one must imagine a typical Florida swamp surrounded by the most dense undergrowth in which, every five or six feet, giant trees rear their heads. Undergrowth and trees are connected by a maze of hanging moss and tough vines, the only trails being pig runs and an occasional hidden native trail that no white man can follow. The only way a white man can get through such stuff is to cut and fight his way through. So our problem was to determine the spot where we could cut our way through with the least effort. We studied the jungle carefully during the next two days’ flying, and found that a few miles from our camp a grassy hill cut through the jungle to within about a quarter of a mile of the swamp. We could get to this hill easily from the camp, and figured that with the aid of a compass we should be able to bore through the jungle to the swamp itself in two or three hours. Our looks were now complete.

The big day came at last. It dawned misty and cool — for Latest Guinea — as near a perfect duck-hunting day as that part of the world could have provided. And it found Fred and me hacking our way into the jungle surrounding the swamp. We looked more like a couple of jungle soldiers than we did duck hunters. We had our .45’s on our belts for use on snakes or crocodiles, and also because neither of us was sure there might not be a stray Japanese pilot hiding in the brush. We knew several had recently bailed out or crash-landed in the vicinity.

According to recent reports, we looked more like a couple of jungle soldiers than we did duck hunters. We had our .45’s on our belts for use on snakes or crocodiles, and also because neither of us was sure there might not be a stray Japanese pilot hiding in the brush.

Our heads were covered by our mosquito nets, and our canteen and ammunition belts rattled as we whacked at the undergrowth with a substantial jungle knife, taking turns at hacking and resting.

It has been revealed that all through the jungle we encountered many varieties of beautiful birds. Most of them were of the parrot or pigeon families, and were of every color of the rainbow. Some were as small as wrens, others much larger than domestic pigeons. Once we caught a glimpse of an Australian jungle turkey, a magnificent bird almost as large as the American wild turkey, but were unable to get a shot at it in the thick undergrowth. We also saw a couple of dark brown jungle chickens of the grouse variety. Later, in another part of Latest Guinea, I was fortunate enough to kill several of these birds, and they were very delicious, the meat being light and tender. But this story is about duck hunting — and what duck hunting!

In exactly one hour and thirty minutes after the first swing of our jungle knife we broke into the swamp — and, believe me, it was beautiful to behold.

“Look at them, Dave, look at them!” Fred was wild with excitement.

“Gee, it’s been a long time,” I mentioned.

Ducks were everywhere — circling the swamps by the hundreds, quacking, whistling, and splashing down into the open spot among the tall reeds.

We stood there just looking for a long time. Then Fred said, “Dave, you know what we’ve got to do?”.

Ducks were everywhere — circling the swamps by the hundreds, quacking, whistling, and splashing down into the open spot among the tall reeds.

In a recent development, “Yes, I’m afraid I do,” I replied. “But it’s sure going to be hard to remember all the hungry people at camp when those singles start flying over. Boy! I wish we had plenty of shells.”.

“Yeah,” sighed Fred, “or not such a large family to feed.”.

Sources indicate that I had an idea. “I’ll tell you what let’s do,” I stated. “Let’s each of us get fifteen ducks with as few shells as possible, and then use the rest of the shells for singles. That will give us at least thirty ducks to feed the sixty guys back at camp.”.

“O.K., Dave, we’ve got to do it, I guess,” agreed Fred. “It’s going to seem real unsportsmanlike to take pot-shots, but bully beef is sure getting tiresome. Let’s go!”.

Neither of us relished shooting those beautiful birds on the water, but this was one time we had to bring home the bacon.

Sources indicate that we decided that since the length of the swamp lay north and south we would separate, Fred going south and I going north, this way keeping the ducks moving back and forth between us. So, out we started. The water in the swamp proved to be from ankle to almost waist deep. The bottom, however, was solid, so walking was not difficult. Most of the swamp was covered with thick dead reeds about six feet high that broke easily as we waded through them. In the midst of these reeds were a great many small open spots where some kind of short green water grass grew which the ducks fed upon. These openings were also the feeding grounds of many different kinds of wading birds which swarmed up with the ducks as we approached. Then there were several flocks of large white herons that seemed almost psychic, as they would take wing long before we reached their resting place, circle, climb high into the sky, and disappear into the distance. They alone seemed to leave the swamp. All other birds, including the ducks, would fly to some other clearing in the swamp and settle there.

Recent findings suggest that related: We Had a Week Off from Active Combat, So I Went Trout Fishing. I Got Pinned Down by a Sniper.

Industry observers note that hundreds of large coots were present too. They were about twice the size of any I had seen before, and looked like American birds, except they had brilliant red bills.

Sources indicate that before I had made my way very far into the swamp I heard Fred fire twice and, looking in his direction, saw hundreds of ducks getting up. A dozen black mallards passed right over my head. How I wanted to shoot! But didn’t, remembering my promise to Fred to get my first fifteen with as few shells as possible.

Most of the ducks lit about 100 yards north of me, so I began creeping in that direction, making as little noise as possible. As I crept closer through very thick reeds I came to a small opening no more than ten yards in diameter, and, lo and behold, there sat about twenty honest-to-goodness greenwing teal. They saw me and shot up like a covey of quail. I caught them just as they rose, and fired once, knocking down three. I had a tough time recovering them in the reeds, but finally found them all. At the sound of the shot the mallards got up about seventy-five yards away and circled for some ten minutes, settling back down in the same place about the time I had recovered my last teal. With the teal in my belt I crept toward the mallards, crawling through the ankle-deep water on my knees and one hand, holding my gun in the other, as the reeds were not tall in this area.

Industry observers note that how I wanted to shoot! But didn’t, remembering my promise to Fred to get my first fifteen with as few shells as possible.

When I reached the edge of the clearing where the mallards were I saw they were all about fifty yards away on the opposite side. About halfway across the clearing was a small clump of tall reeds that I thought I might be able to keep between the mallards and myself until I could get them a little more in range.

According to recent reports, I started crawling toward those reeds, making every effort to keep the ducks from seeing me but, alas, ducks seem to be as wary in one part of the world as another. Just as I got started they spotted me, and off they went in every direction. The largest bunch of them circled over the edge of the swamp and then seemed to disappear into the trees. This I believed to be an illusion — ducks don’t light on trees, especially mallards.

By this time I had decided that it was too hot for crawling and that I would let Fred do the work for awhile. So I took my station in the clump of reeds in the center of the clearing and waited for him to send some ducks my way. I took off my head net, wiped the perspiration from my face, applied some mosquito lotion, and put the net into my pocket, deciding I could shoot better without it.

Recent findings suggest that after about ten minutes’ waiting I heard Fred open up again, firing three times, and, looking in his direction, I saw them coming. There they were, hundreds of them! And from then on, things went too fast to tell about. All the ducks seemed to want to light in the clearing I commanded — and I did command every inch of it!

There they were, hundreds of them. And from then on, things went too fast to tell about. All the ducks seemed to want to light in the clearing I commanded — and I did command every inch of it.

Industry observers note that first, a major flock of mallards tried to light within ten yards of me, and I opened up with both barrels just as they were settling, getting four of them. A bunch of pintails came in right after them; then teal, and more mallards. I was firing as fast as I could reload. I could hear Fred doing the same thing and knew he was in their favorite clearing at the other end of the swamp. I had never seen so many ducks at one time, and they were flying back and forth between the two of us. The boys at camp were all going to get a real meal.

It has been revealed that after about fifteen minutes of the fastest shooting I have ever done I took inventory. I found I had seventeen ducks — and four shells left! And I actually had four black mallards, a couple of beautiful little ducks that I couldn’t identify, three pintails, and several greenwing, bluewing, and cinnamon teal. The teal were larger than any I had seen in the states, but were exactly like our teal in every other respect.

Sources indicate that since I had more than my quota of fifteen birds I felt I could use the remaining four precious shells for the tough shots that I have always loved so much. So I took my station and waited.

Sources indicate that A high flying mallard came in fast and weaving. It was one of those shots you make once in a lifetime and never forget. I led him plenty and just hoped. He came down from way up there like a rock, and I felt a thrill inside I hadn’t come close to feeling for two years.

According to recent reports, A minute later two teal came in fast and low. I caught one with the first shot, but missed the second. But the first bird came down so clean I didn’t feel badly about the miss. With my remaining shell I stopped another mallard, not as high as the first, but it was a sweet shot.

Sources indicate that I gathered up my birds and started back to meet Fred. We met just in front of our trail that led back into the jungle, and as we waded through the last few yards of swamp Fred mentioned, “Look at ’em, Dave. We’ve got thirty-five of the most beautiful ducks I ever saw!”.

“Heavy, too,” I noted, laughing.

Industry observers note that A bunch of pintails came in right after them; then teal, and more mallards. I was firing as fast as I could reload. I could hear Fred doing the same thing and knew he was in their favorite clearing at the other end of the swamp.

We reached the edge of the jungle and sat down to rest. As we sat there we beheld a most astonishing sight — about ten black mallards flew right out of the tree we were sitting under and winged their way back into the swamp. Believe it or not! Mallards do light in trees, in New Guinea anyway.

We started home and Fred said, “It’s a funny war, isn’t it? Black mallards lighting in trees; our belts loaded with ducks, and a bunch of hungry boys back at camp to appreciate them more than any ducks were ever appreciated before. I think, Dave, today has been the most wonderful day of my life.”.

Industry observers note that related: I Hunted Ducks from a U.S. Naval Destroyer During the Korean War.

In a recent development, I was glad Fred said that, because it was his last duck hunt. Fred went down fighting — doing his bit to guarantee a free and fearless future full of “wonderful days” for all of us.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Department of the Interior released a five-year strategic initiative Tuesday that outlines the federal government’s intentions to sell public lands, further reduce the workforce at its agencies, and continue to pursue natural resource development for energy dominance.
  • Industry observers note that the 28-page document lists four key goals for fiscal years 2026 through 2030.
  • “The Department will consolidate its workforce to advance operational efficiencies,” reads the plan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Department of the Interior released a five-year strategic initiative Tuesday that outlines the federal government’s intentions to sell public lands, further reduce the workforce at its agencies, and continue to pursue natural resource development for energy dominance.

Industry observers note that the 28-page document lists four key goals for fiscal years 2026 through 2030. One of the most critical sections of the document for the conservation community is nested under the fourth goal of collaborating with states, tribes, and communities:.

“The Department will consolidate its workforce to advance operational efficiencies,” reads the plan. “The Department will work to decrease the size of the federal estate by offering to states, localities and Tribes the opportunity to purchase federal lands. Through these sales, the Department will be able to focus its resources on primary federal responsibilities and nationally significant federal lands.”.

According to the Interior, the proceeds from sales of lands that aren’t considered “nationally significant” will go toward “purchasing entities to use for conservation purposes elsewhere” for “improved recreation access for American citizens, while at the same time decreasing the federal taxpayer’s financial responsibility to manage federal lands.”.

In a recent development, “From a hunting and angling perspective, we love the places that are not of national significance,” Backcountry Hunters and Anglers president and CEO Ryan Callaghan tells Outdoor Life (we interviewed him while he was deer hunting a piece of no-name BLM ground out West). “Because they don’t have a big spotlight on them, and that’s where we go to hunt and fish.”.

Selling and transferring federal lands — of any significance — is also wildly unpopular with American outdoorsmen and women.

It has been revealed that “I’d need to see the criteria for disposal, but at first blush this flies in the face of overwhelming positive appreciation and sentiment for America’s public lands,” claims Callaghan. “We’ve proved that middle-of-nowhere BLM land in Utah is of national significance during last summer’s budget reconciliation process. From an end-user standpoint, the American people want more public land and a workforce that can manage them responsibly.”.

According to recent reports, the staff cuts to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, National Park Service, Bureau of Land Management (as well as the U.S. Forest Service, which is managed by the USDA) have also been a point of contention for hunters and anglers. As we reported in September, key public land agencies have already been chronically understaffed and underfunded for decades, with an accelerated decline under the second Trump administration.

Agency Staff CutsMeasured by direct civilian full-time equivalent.

In a recent development, the only sectors where the DOI’s strategic plan promises to add staff are law enforcement and public safety — not conservation roles. That includes building a larger Park Police presence in Washington, D.C. The plan includes no staffing numbers or targets. These priorities are the heart of the objective: “Interior protects Americans and public lands.”.

Transferring federal lands to states poses both the risk of further sell-off to private entities — and greater regulation for hunters, anglers, and outdoor users in general.

According to recent reports, “People have got to understand [the restrictions of state land],” says Callaghan. “You can’t camp on state land in Colorado or Wyoming unless posted. You can’t drive on state land even on established roads unless they’re signed here in Montana. It’s illegal to shoot clay pigeons on state land in Montana. We just literally got de facto public access to our state lands in Montana about 20 years ago. State lands are private lands first, and the public access components come second to the ability to make money off those state lands. You’re not going to have [default state] public access unless it’s compatible in some way.”.

In a recent development, the initiative also merges wildland fire programs into the fresh U.S. Wildland Fire Service as part of a massive restructure of how the federal government fights wildfires.

Burgum also emphasizes the role of “super intelligence” throughout the DOI’s strategic blueprint.

Industry observers note that “For the first time in human history, we can turn electricity into intelligence,” he writes, in the only bolded line in his letter that prefaces the plan. (Nowhere in the document does the DOI use the phrase “artificial intelligence.”).

Industry observers note that the Trump administration is considering proposals for no fewer than a dozen data center projects on public land, as we reported in September. Together, those data centers could impact at least 17,600 acres of public land in the West.

Industry observers note that “At every turn, the strategy prioritizes extraction over conservation, emphasizing the need to pillage our public lands in order to power AI data centers,” Center for Western Priorities communications director Kate Groetzinger mentioned in a statement Wednesday. “Of course, that’s no surprise given Burgum’s financial ties to the AI industry. But it flies in the face of the American public, who have made their feelings about data centers abundantly clear.”.

Related: The Rush to Build Data Centers on Public Lands Is Worse Than You Thought.

Recent findings suggest that in the proposal Burgum directs DOI employees to “harness technology to power efficiency,” pointing to efforts to replace manpower with artificial intelligence. The directive comes just days after the USFWS revealed it wanted more “boots on the ground” to better manage our national wildlife refuges.

“Our team is actively expanding domestic energy production and securing our critical minerals supply chain — reducing reliance on foreign adversaries, accelerating innovation and protecting the global environment,” writes Burgum in the blueprint. “…Timber, grazing, geothermal energy, hydropower, outdoor recreation, hunting and fishing, mining, oil and gas and more contribute mightily to every facet of American life. As President Theodore Roosevelt, who helped shape and define our department, explained: ‘Conservation means development as much as it does protection.’”.

Burgum is referencing a speech then-former President Roosevelt gave in 1910, in which he spoke forcefully against private interests. The full quote from Roosevelt reads:.

“Conservation means development as much as it does protection. I recognize the right and duty of this generation to develop and use the natural resources of our land; but I do not recognize the right to waste them, or to rob, by wasteful use, the generations that come after us.”.

“Releasing this [proposal] anytime would not get positive feedback. Releasing this during the middle of hunting season is absolute proof the people administrating our public lands right now are extremely out of touch with the American people and their needs,” says Callaghan. “You’re not going to stop at a diner, a truck stop, a bar in America right now and find someone wearing hunter orange who says, ‘You know what? I want less of this. What would be good for me, and my kids, and my hunting season now and in the future, would be less land.”.

The DOI’s strategic proposal was released on the same day the BLM proposed a rule that would make the goals defined in this plan easier to execute.

The potential rule is rooted in public-land rule making, but it would essentially overhaul the guidelines for writing BLM resource management looks. That includes eliminating the 90-day public comment period for major plans, throw out the currently required draft plan for public comment period, and potentially replace public comment periods with public meetings.

Related: Public Comment Periods Don’t Usually Matter Much to the Feds. Duck Hunters Made a Difference Anyway — for Now.

According to recent reports, “Those plans decide where drilling, mining, and grazing can happen on public lands, and which lands can be sold,” according to the Center for Western Priorities. “Under the Federal Land Policy Management Act, BLM can sell land only after a resource management plan identifies it for disposal.”.

The proposed BLM rule is open for public comment through Jan. 11, 2027.

Two Hikers Were Killed by a Sow Grizzly with Cubs in ‘Very Rare’ Predatory Attack

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two women and four grizzlies are dead near Bella Coola, British Columbia after an unusual and horrific predatory attack.
  • Industry observers note that “It’s surreal.
  • It has been revealed that the remains of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, were found November 2.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two women and four grizzlies are dead near Bella Coola, British Columbia after an unusual and horrific predatory attack. A sow with three cubs killed two hikers, a mother-daughter pair who had been missing since November 1. DNA tests confirm the women were killed by the bears.

Industry observers note that “It’s surreal. It doesn’t seem real,” Josh Balcarras, a family member, told CBC News. “The way it starts is a few hours of not hearing from them. That turns into a day, and then a night. Then a second night comes and it becomes a real thing.”.

It has been revealed that the remains of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, were found November 2. The remains of her daughter, 20-year-old Selah Reed, were found November 3. The two were not far from a trail  in the steep and heavily-wooded Snooka Trail System. Both were buried in caches, something bears often do to hide their food from other animals. Investigators consider the attack to be motivated by predation.

Recent findings suggest that “This attack involved predatory behavior, which I can tell you is very rare,” Jeff Tyre, British Columbia Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS) inspector said in a recorded statement issued November 10. “That is to say, we don’t know how it started but we know how it ended. Out of respect for the family, I’m going to decline to answer what predatory behavior looks like specifically in this case.”.

The mother grizzly bear was in her late teens. Her three cubs were born this year. BCCOS announced November 10 that all four were captured and euthanized for their predatory behavior. A week after finding the remains of the second woman, the case is considered closed and trapping equipment has been removed. Nuxalk Nation cultural leaders will decide how the bear remains will be used.

It has been revealed that “They all had to be destroyed because bears that are involved in attacks on people cannot be rehabilitated or relocated,” Tyre mentioned. “This type of behavior presents an extreme risk to the public and such bears are dispatched to protect the public and prevent similar attacks in the future.”.

This most recent attack happened nearly a year after a grizzly attacked a group of tribal school children who were having lunch in the same region last November. In that case covered by OL, three students and one adult were hospitalized after a grizzly raided their picnic.

Despite the two high-profile incidents, investigators say grizzly bear attacks are not increasing near Bella Coola. They also cross-checked DNA from bears involved in both cases. None of the grizzlies euthanized this year were involved in the group attack last year. That bear was never located.

The tribe renewed its safety protocol during this year’s investigation. It has since lifted curfew but continues nightly patrols and offers escorts to take kids to school.

“This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year’s attack,” stated Samuel Schooner, Nuxalk Nation elected chief. “Our focus continues to be on taking care of our community members.”.

It has been revealed that bella Coola is in the coastal region of British Columbia. Coastal bears and interior bears are genetically the same grizzly species, but their size and diet are different. Coastal bears have access to salmon, a nutrient-rich food source.

In a recent development, “Individual bears with increased access to salmon tend to be larger, have bigger litters, have lower stress hormone levels, and exist at higher densities at a population level,” reads an October 2025 study by Lauren Henson and Kris Christensen published in the scientific journal G3: Genes, Genomes and Genetics. “Interior grizzlies [have] smaller body mass and skull size than coastal individuals.”.

Read Next: These Alaskans Stopped a Charging Grizzly at 5 Yards with Their 10mm Pistols.

BC’s combined coastal and interior grizzly bear population has increased from 6,600 in the 1970s to 15,000 in 2018. In 2017, BC implemented a controversial grizzly bear hunting ban. Those in favor of the ban believe that a lack of grizzly hunting does not lead to more human fatalities, but organizations opposing the ban refer to recent attacks as reason to re-open the hunt.

According to recent reports, “We have to do something,” Jesse Zeman, B.C. Wildlife Federation executive director told CBC News. “What we’re right now doing is very clearly not working.”.

#32963. To Win the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, Try Being … Vulnerable?

To Win the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, Try Being … Vulnerable?

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2213 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Author Dan England spoke with five members of Team USA after they won the 2026 Significant’s Backyard Ultra World Team Championship on October 22.
  • Industry observers note that early into the second night of the 2026 Significant’s Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, Mark Dowdle turned to U.S.
  • Sources indicate that before the start, Harvey Lewis, a two-time individual backyard ultra world champion whom many on the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Author Dan England spoke with five members of Team USA after they won the 2026 Significant’s Backyard Ultra World Team Championship on October 22. A rough start forced the team to abandon the fundamentals of competition and ask for help, be honest about their problems, and sacrifice for others. It paid off: the U.S. came from behind to defeat Australia and Belgium, who took second and third, respectively.

Industry observers note that early into the second night of the 2026 Significant’s Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, Mark Dowdle turned to U.S. teammate Levi Yoder and admitted that he was so tired he might fall asleep and into the nearby ditch. Yoder replied that he was so tired he was hallucinating and might wind up in that same ditch.

Sources indicate that before the start, Harvey Lewis, a two-time individual backyard ultra world champion whom many on the U.S. squad thought of as their de facto captain, told his teammates to lean on one another. But Dowdle hesitated the first day, and so, he thought, did many others. It made sense: Backyard ultras are usually individual events predicated on you staying strong while others give up.

For the uninitiated, backyard ultra rules are pretty simple: Run a 4.167-mile loop on the hour, every hour, until only one remains. (That runner must complete one final loop, also called a yard, to be declared the winner.) At the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, which alternates every other year with the individual championship, each participating country simultaneously hosts its own backyard ultra with 15 runners. The team with the most cumulative laps wins.

Typically at backyard ultras, competitors are wolves looking for the elk with a limp. No one wants to look weak. No one demonstrated this formidable exterior better than Dowdle in the Last Soul Ultra this April, when his gamesmanship created the event’s most talked-about moment. But his competitive side was ubiquitous among the 15 elite backyard runners on Team USA. They each won backyard ultras to qualify; they were wolves, not elk.

Sources indicate that yet Team USA struggled from the start. With daytime temperatures in the 70s Fahrenheit, it felt warmer than they thought it would. The course was hilly, with over 400 feet of climbing per loop, costing them a minute or two per loop in a format where extra seconds are precious. Indeed, over the first 40 laps when all runners from all 67 countries were still in the race, the U.S. had the slowest average lap speed of 52:21—nearly seven minutes slower than the fastest country, Slovakia.

Sources indicate that struggling through that second night, the U.S. decided to try a different tactic. They decided to be vulnerable.

Lewis urged the team to be honest about how they were feeling because there was a good chance others could help. It took Dowdle a bit to believe, even after watching how others supported each other.

“It did take encouragement from my team to even be more of a teammate,” Dowdle told Trail Runner.

But Dowdle was enthused when, after his admission that he was struggling, Yoder suggested that they look out for each other over the next 3 miles they had to complete to keep going. Dowdle got the message: This would be a different backyard than he’d ever run before. They talked to each other through the loop and by the end they had caught up to their teammates.

“That turned the corner for me,” Dowdle said. “In a normal race, I would never say that I was falling asleep to another runner. You just would never give up that information. But that opened the door for me to be more vocal about how I was doing.”.

Several other members of the U.S. squad admitted that being honest with each other and asking for help when they needed it was key to them winning the world title. Instead of acting like individuals in a last-man-standing race, they were a unit. That helped many of them run farther than they ever had before—eight Americans ran over 80 yards, or 333.3 miles—when it looked like Australia might literally run away with victory.

Industry observers note that “When some were feeling strong, we would help those who were not feeling OK,” said Megan Smyth, who set a PR with 82 yards and was the last woman standing. “I’m pretty sure that’s how so many of us got over 80 yards.”.

The backyard, despite its do-or-die nature, lends itself to camaraderie because of the way runners all start the next 4.167-mile loop together on the hour, every hour. Jon Noll qualified for Team USA by running over 440 miles at the individual world championship last year. Even there most competitors congratulated each other after each lap. “The ultra community, in general, is not exactly a cutthroat environment for the most part,” Noll said. He especially felt that sense of camaraderie this time as the miles piled up.

This is why Smyth loves the backyard format.

“There’s no incentive to win a lap, so you really do wind up cheering for each other,” Smyth said.

Recent findings suggest that still, Team USA had to get comfortable with each other in a hurry. Even with seven returning members from the third-place 2024 team it was a little awkward at first: Some had previously competed against each other, and some called each other friends. Some were rivals. Other first-timers felt a sense of awe: Smyth had imposter syndrome, which doesn’t make it easy to talk about, say, a sore ankle.

But she also welcomed the unique race set up. If a typical backyard ultra can feel crowded and chaotic, the team race with its 15 competitors feels sparse, even intimate. Smyth got her wish right away.

Recent findings suggest that “I haven’t gotten to do true team running since my cross-country days,” she said. “It was just a magical experience.”.

A couple team meetings over Zoom, as well as an in-person meeting before the race, helped shoo away some of the awkwardness, Lewis thought. But Smyth remarked Lewis helped bring the team together during the event, too, with little (even corny) things like running in a fighter jet formation and chanting “U.S.A!” for a lap.

According to recent reports, smyth remembers walking at night and nearly falling asleep before the Ron Express came up behind her. Ron Wireman, competing in his second team championship, struggled early in the race and needed help from others. That first night, he was eager to pay his teammates back and named himself after a train to help them through the dark.

“He stated, ‘MEGAN ARE YOU AWAKE?,’” Smyth said.

Smyth, just like Dowdle, learned how to ask for help. Later in the race, as the prospect of doing another lap on the steep trail, she requested a “hill sherpa.”.

The team cohesion would be tested right away as Lewis insisted they answer a question democratically: Should they run the road or the trail?

Team USA competes on the original Big’s Backyard Ultra course in mastermind Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell’s literal backyard in Bell Buckle, Tennessee. On odd years during the individual championship, racers run a trail loop during the day and a road loop at night. This time it was runners’ choice throughout the race.

Sources indicate that the road was flatter and easier, but the hard, smooth surface can be problematic for trail runners. Smyth, for instance, said she didn’t bring many pairs of road shoes. But Laz recently made “improvements” to the trail loop that made it steeper, tougher, and slower. The precious minutes saved on the road loop could be the difference between having time to recover, fuel, sleep, and even go to the bathroom, and to DNF.

“There isn’t a lot of wiggle room in a backyard,” Lewis mentioned.

Communication was key as the team tried to accommodate runners struggling with the trail by adding more laps on the road.

Recent findings suggest that “We were changing things as the race went on,” Noll remarked. “Sometimes you didn’t know what course you were doing [on the next lap]. Mentally that can be hard.”.

According to recent reports, ultimately, the back and forth paid off. Eventually emphasizing the road over the trail helped the team squeeze yards from people who may not have been able to continue otherwise.

“If we hadn’t moved to the road, I don’t know if we would have won the race,” Lewis said.

As the third day burned off its final few hours, Australia had a commanding lead of 58 yards over the U.S. The Aussies still had 11 runners in the race; the U.S. was down to 9. Nicholas Steel kept announcing to his U.S. teammates just how far behind they were. More than one American admitted later that they found these updates annoying. Dowdle told himself he didn’t care and tried to enjoy the experience.

But backyard veterans will tell you that the race doesn’t end at hour 70; that’s really when it starts. One Aussie dropped at yard 70, another at 72, two at 73, and two more at 75. By yard 80, nine Aussies had dropped. They had only two runners left—a precarious place to be, given the final runner can only complete one additional lap after the penultimate runner drops. Sure enough, Australia was out by yard 88. We’re not being judgy about this: They were on their third day of running without sleep. But that brutal attrition gave the U.S. a shot.

According to recent reports, suddenly Steel’s updates were inspiring. They would need Dowdle and Noll, the workhorses, to keep doing their magic. But the Americans realized that they could win if they got at least half their runners to yard 75 and several past yard 80.

“The possibility that we could catch up lit a fire under my belly,” Dowdle said, “and I remember thinking, ‘Oh, maybe I do care.’”.

Even the Americans who dropped relatively early decided to stay at the campsite to cheer. This was substantial: Dowdle finished one lap with 15 seconds to go, riding the wave of exhortation to get him across the line in time.

Lewis did what he could to keep as many runners out there as possible. He ran with those who were close to dropping, even to his detriment. At times he finished the lap with less than three minutes to go. Lewis, famously, sleeps for a few minutes after every loop, but running with others meant he wasn’t able to do that. Ultimately, he went out for yard 84 but didn’t finish it, a result that Lewis found disappointing.

It has been revealed that “I didn’t have my own rhythm because I was helping others,” Lewis said. “My ultimate goal was to be there for the team, so I sacrificed myself and my own best race for that.”.

Industry observers note that that kind of support from teammates, along with the competitive boost the Americans got chasing down Australia, helped push some to their backyard ultra PRs. Nick Petterson made it to 84 yards, 19 more than his previous best. That’s nearly a full day more of running.

“The team needed you, and that was a really easy thing to grab onto,” Petterson stated. “We needed everyone to crank up the numbers. That motivation outside of just myself was really helpful.”.

Petterson thrives off that external focus anyway. During backyards, he enjoys asking others how they’re doing, even though it’s not always reciprocated.

“The team factor was a major driver when times got hard for me,” he noted. “I might have gone out earlier if it wasn’t for that.”.

According to recent reports, yoder made it 86 yards, 11 more than his qualifying mark. Ryan Snickles went 69 yards after qualifying with 55. Smyth set a PR by five yards and quit only after her ankle swelled like a balloon. Jeff Walker got 75 yards, 30 more than his qualifier. Even Steel seemed inspired by his own updates. He went 94 yards—177% of his 53-yard qualifier.

Ultimately the U.S. won by a landslide with 1,120 yards to Australia’s 1,069.

It’s the second world title for Team USA in this rapidly developing sub-sport. When the U.S. won in 2022, it was with only 860 yards. Belgium, which has won the other two team titles, took third this year—although two of their runners set the individual backyard ultra world record of 124 yards, or 516.7 miles over five days of running.

“When other runners are hanging on longer,” Lewis said, “it impacts everyone to hang on longer.”.

It has been revealed that ultimately, Dowdle was the last American standing with 107 yards—a personal best by 13 yards, or 54 miles. Noll got the assist with 106 yards. Despite his initial reticence, Dowdle notes he values moments with his teammates more than his individual national title.

“There was one lap where I broke down crying,” Dowdle stated, “and Nick Petterson saw me and put his arm around me and was just with me during that time.”.

Dowdle wouldn’t want the backyard format to be flooded with team events, but he wants to go back:.

“I’m bummed that you have to wait two years for it again.”.

#32961. A Deer for My Dad: It Was the Biggest Buck of My Life — But Would It Mean Anything to My Fading Father?

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2122 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

A Deer for My Dad: It Was the Biggest Buck of My Life — But Would It Mean Anything to My Fading Father?

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2122 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The first three deer to come by me were ridge-flat regulars—I’d seen them before, both on trail camera and in person.
  • It has been revealed that but I never thought that the cool-looking little deer would be capable of running the gauntlet of hunters during general firearms season, so it was good to see him in this final hour of the final day.
  • It’s always exciting to see deer on the last day of the season, but missing was any rush of adrenaline—for good reason.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The first three deer to come by me were ridge-flat regulars—I’d seen them before, both on trail camera and in person. The lead whitetail, a piebald button buck, was a welcome sight, even though I had cursed him so many times these past few weeks. At first a curiosity, the little buck had become something of a nuisance during bow season due to his ravenous appetite for the apples that covered the leaves near my stone-wall ground stand and his proclivity for busting every good setup.

It has been revealed that but I never thought that the cool-looking little deer would be capable of running the gauntlet of hunters during general firearms season, so it was good to see him in this final hour of the final day. A doe and an I’d-probably-shoot-him-on-any-other-day 8-pointer followed, each glowering at their backtrails as they picked their way toward my food plots several hundred yards down the hill.

It’s always exciting to see deer on the last day of the season, but missing was any rush of adrenaline—for good reason. There was another deer around, or at least I hoped that he was still around. It was a buck the likes of which I’d waited my entire life to take. It’s why I never even thought to flick the safety off on the 8-point.

According to recent reports, that other buck had haunted my trail camera for a solid month and left me day- (and night) dreaming of killing him. In a land of dinks and almost-shooters, this was a bona fide stud. Hell, he’d qualify as such in Kansas. He was a perfect 10-point, so symmetrical that I thought my buddies were playing some sort of cruel practical joke on me when I first saw the photos. What would he score? Who knew? Who cared? I surely didn’t. But what I did know was that I’d never seen a larger rack on any buck on my family’s property in all the years of living there—nor had anyone else who hunted our little patch of Fresh England deer woods.

I barely had time to wonder why those first three deer might be so unnerved when a single thought screamed in my brain….

According to recent reports, that simple word and a thin smile were pretty much the only signs of acknowledgement Dad had been capable of during Thanksgiving dinner two weeks earlier. In addition to some snapshots I’d taken of our deer camp, I had downloaded a couple dozen trail-camera photos to my phone to show him in the hope that seeing a photo of that buck on his property might ignite a spark of recognition in his brain—that he’d somehow come back to me even if only for a moment or two. You see, that’s mostly what we—families of Alzheimer’s sufferers—pray for. Something. Anything. A glimpse or a glint, some little part of the old Dad would do. And I got that little gift.

If there’s a more insidious disease than Alzheimer’s, I certainly can’t conceive of it. What other ailment kills a host’s loved ones years before actually killing the host? And make no mistake, my family (no different from any other Alzheimer’s family) has been dying in fits and starts for more than a decade. No one is capable of standing by helplessly while watching a father, a spouse, or a dear friend fight their own mind without losing a part of themselves. Even harder is watching a once-brilliant engineer, capable of taking anything apart and putting it back together, struggle for hours on end to solve simple word-search puzzles.

In a recent development, truth be known, Dad wasn’t really a deer nut—never shot one, actually—but he did hunt with me each season and both tolerated and nurtured my addiction to chasing whitetails. He bought me my first deer-hunting coat when I was 15, and he lugged an extension ladder a half mile through the woods to build my first treestand. We drove three hours through a ferocious ice storm in his brown Buick LeSabre one Thanksgiving night just because I told him that the bowhunting the next morning would be incredible after such a weather event. He gave me my first sip of whiskey after I spent too many hours in that same stand during a blizzard. Even though it’s been years since Dad has hunted, he always liked to hear my stories of deer missed or deer killed and other adventures at our family’s little hunting camp—or at least it seemed as if he did.

Recent findings suggest that somehow, the trail-camera photo of the huge buck brought that particular Dad back to me, if only for a moment before he went away again. But it was enough—I knew that he knew. And so it was that after 1 ½ months of frustration during bow season, and much of the same during the firearms hunt, I felt the sort of motivation I remember feeling two decades ago, when he and I used to sit within sight of each other in the deer woods and I wished for a buck to walk by so that I could do my dad proud. I decided that I needed to show Dad one more photo—the one in which I’m holding that buck’s rack in my hands in front of the camp where he and I had spent the greatest days of our lives.

Just five minutes or so after the last of the three deer walked out of sight, I finally spotted the reason for their preoccupation. Even at 80 yards there was no mistaking him—that magnificent rack, burly body, and gait of dominance. It was the one I had come to think of as Dad’s deer. Whether it was the cautiousness of his years or my impatience, I still can’t be sure, but the damned buck seemed not to move no matter how hard I wished him to—neither­ would he give me a broadside shot. This stasis lasted long minutes and was physically draining. I didn’t dare stare him directly in the eyes, but I didn’t dare look away either. When he’d finally take a noiseless step, he’d stop to scrutinize the frozen woods, and it seemed his intensity bored right into me. He closed from 80 to 50 yards but I still hadn’t heard a footfall on the frost-brittle leaves. He still would not turn broadside.

Industry observers note that okay, I’ll shoot you dead-on facing me if I need to, you big bastard, I thought. It’s not ideal, but if you get too close I’m going to shoot. I’m not gonna blow this one.

It has been revealed that as if eavesdropping on my conversation with myself, the buck somehow cut the distance to 35 yards, though I swear I didn’t see him take a step. And then he turned. Using my knee as a solid rest, I snicked the safety forward, put the shotgun’s bead on his chest, and squeezed it off. The significant buck kicked high with his rear legs—a good thing—before tearing off for parts unknown—a very bad thing. Then the woods became still again. I sat there in agony listening for many soundless minutes and fighting off the urge to run to the place where the buck last stood. As much as I wished to see him lying there dead in the light skiff of snow, to run my hands along his main beams, I feared more the agonizing what-ifs.

What if he was still alive and I pushed him to a nearby hunter, who shot him?

What if he was still alive and I pushed him into some far-off thicket, never to be recovered?

What if I missed him completely?

What if I wouldn’t be able to show Dad that single, all-revealing photograph?

Diminishing daylight made the decision to give the buck time a bit easier. Judging from his size on the trail camera, I’d need help getting him out of the woods anyway. I’d go back to camp, have a beer or two to calm down, and make a few phone calls.

Three torment-filled hours later, I finally received a return call.

Industry observers note that “You got him,” mentioned a familiar voice on the other end of the line, not in the form of a question, but rather a statement. “We’re all at a Christmas party, but give me 20 minutes and I’ll be there.” I never got the chance to respond before the phone clicked. The cavalry was on its way. If anyone could help me find the buck, it was my friend Rich Hamilton.

In typical subdued fashion, Rich walked through the door, asked to hear the story, then wasted no time heading out the door again. Although he’d not been there with me, he took the lead in our search for blood.

“Well, this ain’t worth a sh&$,” he said when the beam of his flashlight hit a single drop on the snow. “Not worth a sh&$ at all.”.

And he was right. Even with the skiff of snow on the ground, it was difficult to find a second drop. The hoped-for salvation of all sunset shooters—a blood trail a blind man could follow—was not revealing itself. My heart sank.

Industry observers note that “Well, he fell here,” Rich deadpanned, now following the running tracks in the windblown spots of snow. “Fell here, too.”.

According to recent reports, our flashlight beams fell on the giant rack simultaneously. He hadn’t gone more than 50 yards.

It has been revealed that “Look at that giant son of a bitch,” Rich noted. “Oh…my…God.”.

Industry observers note that I’d never before seen a more magnificent sight. Dad’s deer had come to rest in a boggy thicket amid a jungle of briars, his rack seemingly floating 5 feet above the ground. Under the moonlight, we could see the faint lights of camp and billowing woodsmoke pouring from the chimney. We unashamedly hugged and shouted, then struggled to get the significant deer onto a dry hummock for field dressing. In all honesty, I was of no help.

“Here, hold the flashlight,” Rich mentioned after my first header into the muck. “I need to gut this deer. I want to gut this deer.”.

In a recent development, an hour later, and too tired to move him any farther, much less hang him up, Rich and I wrestled the buck to the top of the basement woodpile. We stepped back a few feet to simply stare at the deer for the first time in full light—at a complete loss for words.

After Rich left, I stood and stared some more—long into the night—just me with the buck and thoughts of a hunting season incomparable and unreproducible. And of my Dad. By the next day, everyone who cared to hear the story, and some who didn’t, came by the house. After a while, 10 of us—each grabbing an antler, a hoof, a leg, or the tail—carried the buck outside and into the sunshine. Embarrassingly unprepared for a photo session, I handed my camera phone to one of the kids and asked him to click off a few pictures. I really only needed one.

Instead of fading with time, my exhilaration seemed to grow in the days that followed. I told the story countless dozens of times and emailed photos to friends around the country, but it wouldn’t be until Christmas Day, two weeks later, that I would see Mom and Dad.

“He’s not having such a good day today,” my mom stated when she hugged me at the front door. “Just sit with him for a while.”.

And I did. I told him our story and revealed him our buck, but his eyes remained focused on the word-search puzzle book in his lap, as he haltingly circled letters—the sound of my voice either unheard or completely foreign.

Somehow, my daughter, Amy, has always been able to garner Dad’s instant attention, and she did again on Christmas Day.

“Merry Christmas,” Dad noted as Amy hugged him in his chair, word-search book falling to the floor. The hours Mom spent rehearsing those two words with him had paid off. Tears welled in his eyes as he smiled at a face he fought his own brain to recognize.

Read Next: ‘The Safety Was On!’ I Nearly Missed My Chance at a Significant Adirondack Buck.

Industry observers note that I picked up his book as they hugged, Amy trying in vain to engage Dad in conversation but getting no response. Glancing down at the crumpled page, my eyes focused on three circled letters: D-O-E.

My Dad was back, if only for a moment or two, before he was gone again.

It was cold and rainy the morning of November 6th in northwest Missouri. But the bucks were in rut chasing does, and dedicated bowhunter James Fleener was in his tree saddle long before daylight on a 320-acre hunting lease he has with his brother-in-law.

It has been revealed that “I hunted the spot the evening before, and it was ideal,” Fleener tells Outdoor Life. “I knew there was a giant buck in the area. I had lots of trail camera photos of him. I felt good about that place. I left my saddle stand, climbing sticks and bow in the woods that night to return the next morning prepared for an all-day sit.”.

Recent findings suggest that well before daylight he was in a Latitude Outdoors saddle that he used for the first time this year. For him it’s been a hunting game-changer.

“I’d hunted that deer about a dozen times, and moved slowly and quietly into the area where I figured the bucks were pushing does,” indicates the 26-year-old bowhunter from Lawson, Mo. “I’d hunt a spot, then move 100 yards or so to another place, and get my saddle up in another tree fast and quiet.”.

The little maple tree that Fleener hunted from that November 6 morning was near a small pond with a grassy ditch feeding it. That created a natural funnel for deer, and at first light he started seeing does and small bucks.

It has been revealed that “I cracked together my rattling antlers and pretty soon a small buck came my way,” he indicates. “I was watching him come to about 50 yards and I looked beyond him and I saw the significant buck through my binoculars about 200 yards off.”.

Sources indicate that the buck was on the prowl, apparently looking for does. Fleener grunted loudly at the substantial buck, but he was far off and it was raining so the deer never heard it.

“I grabbed my rattling antlers and cracked them together as loud as I could,” says Fleener, who owns Mid-Mo Trucking Services. “When I did, his head whipped around and he came right to me at a trot. He came fast around a bean field edge. He looked like a moose coming to me at a trot.”.

Fleener knew the buck was huge, and looked away for a moment to gather himself, so as not to make a mistake when the deer got in range.

“He was coming right to me and fast, so I drew my bow when he was almost 100 yards away so he wouldn’t see me move to draw,” he indicates. “At 10 yards he slowed down to cross the grassy ditch, and I let my arrow fly.

In a recent development, “He jumped but never knew what hit him. He moved away at a fast walk, got behind some cover and I thought I heard him crash, but it was wet and rainy, so I wasn’t sure.”.

Fleener contacted his good friend Mason Chapman and told him he’d shot a great buck. Chapman was hunting nearby, but he immediately went to help his buddy.

About 30 minutes later Chapman met with Fleener and they tracked the buck, which ran only 40 yards before falling dead.

“When I first saw him up close I was in disbelief,” Fleener says. “This was the first year I’d hunted that lease, and although I knew he was on the property, I had no idea he was really that big.”.

In a recent development, since our very first issue published in 1898, Outdoor Life has covered outdoor gear with independence and rigor. From Jack O’Connor’s old gun columns to today’s in-depth video reviews, field testing gear and reporting the results has always been part of our publication’s DNA.

In a recent development, which is why I am excited to now introduce our newly introduced online gear shop, which represents the culmination of more than a century of gear coverage. This new online retail site will carry a wide variety of quality outdoor products, and purchases made from the site will help to power the Outdoor Life you know and love into the future. There are a few key points that longtime OL readers should know.

If you’ve followed Outdoor Life closely, you know that we’re not scared to piss off folks on occasion. This often includes manufacturers who have overhyped their products. That’s because we believe that reader trust is OL’s single most notable asset. If we report the truth, good or bad, we have faith that you will keep coming back. This has been the promise that the OL editors made at the very beginning, and it’s the contract we uphold today.

In all of our gear reviews and buying guides, we will continue to celebrate the top-performing products (whether they are carried in the Outdoor Life shop or not). Likewise, if a product falls short, we’ll continue to call out those flaws.

It has been revealed that unlike some other media outlets in our space, we have no editorial obligation to a single brand. We shoot, hunt with, and wear whatever is new and noteworthy, because that makes the most interesting content. This will continue, regardless of which brands are carried in the shop. Simply scan a few of our recent gear reviews (like our rifle scope test or binocular test) and you will find this to be true.

Over time, the shop will begin to host content from the hundreds of gear reviews we’ve written through the years. Beyond basic specs and product descriptions, the Outdoor Life shop will include details about how the products actually performed during testing. Our “editor’s picks” will highlight the top performing items in a category. Video reviews will show how products work (or don’t work) in the field.

Our aim will be to educate the reader, or potential customer, about the gear they are considering buying, whether they end up buying it from us or someone else.

According to recent reports, the OL team is proud that we already spend a ton of time and effort producing the most in-depth gun and gear reviews in the outdoor space. We have been able to fund these efforts by linking to online retailers who sell the gear that we cover. If one of our readers purchases a product from these online retailers, we made a small commission. Added up over the course of the year, these commissions become a meaningful source of revenue that powers our editorial team to create more content.

At its best, it’s a system of meritocracy. Those who create the best content grow the biggest audiences and, in turn, make the most money — to make more content.

But that system has been corrupted with the popularization of Artificial Intelligence. Now, more and more folks are simply asking ChatGPT or Claude, “what’s the best wader for duck hunting?” These chatbots scrape online articles to produce an answer for the user, who then makes their purchase. That hunter will rarely see the original source material. In other words they will never come to our reviews and field tests at Outdoor Life.

It has been revealed that and the chatbots don’t much care if they are lifting content from OutdoorLife.com or someone’s basement blog, or even a manufacturer’s own website. In time, this will lead to the degradation (I believe the modern term is “enshittification”) of  gear reviews, and, well, first-hand expert information in general.

Our way to combat this is to own the online shop ourselves. We believe that so long as we have the best and most thorough information, and the best available products, the reader will end up with us.

In the weeks and months to come, we will be adding many more brands and gear categories to the shop. We’ll be offering deals on select products that have performed admirably in our field testing. And we’ll be turning out a lot more stories and videos.

Industry observers note that if you’re looking to purchase some fresh gear, I do hope you check out the OL shop. But the truth is, there are many reasons to love the outdoors and our passion for quality gear is only a sliver of Outdoor Life. So, after all these years, thank you for reading, following, and watching.

It has been revealed that some people dream of assembling a long-range rifle capable of ringing one-MOA targets at 1,000 yards. Others dream of an ultralight mountain rifle that’s easy to carry for miles and can make a single precision shot. I dream of an ultra-quiet, accurate, and handy rifle for dropping squirrels out of trees. Here’s how I turned a CZ 457 into my dream gun and how it performed in my testing this fall.

The base rifle for this build is a CZ 457 American. I kept the American’s stock because I love a wood stock on a hunting rifle, and its ergonomics work great for squirrel hunting. There are a ton of ultralight chassis you can go with, but wood and squirrel hunting just go together. I did have to sand down the inside of the stock to create room for the newly introduced barrel, but that’s easy to do with a palm sander, a dowel wrapped in sandpaper, or every garage gunsmith’s favorite tool: a Dremel.

Read Next: CZ 457 American Review.

According to recent reports, lilja makes CZ 457 pre-fit barrels that are fantastic for competition shooting, but I wanted something lighter. That’s why I went with a 16-inch Proof Research pre-fit barrel. One of the great things about the CZ 457 is that the barrel changes are a piece of cake. You simply loosen two set screws to remove the barrel and the new one slides right into the action.

According to recent reports, the entire Nightforce NX6 line is fantastic, and the 2-12x F1 variant is perfect for a versatile rimfire. It can take a 50-yard head shot on a squirrel or snap shoot one up close. It also makes this rifle excellent for shooting long range. Dialing in to 300 yards and ringing steel is quite easy with this setup. The scope is fairly light and short, so I don’t think I’m giving up much in terms of weight compared to a traditional 3-9x, but I’m gaining a lot of capability and versatility.

In a recent development, this suppressor is quiet, light, relatively affordable, and easy to clean — everything I look for in a .22 can. There are plenty of other great options like the Dead Air RXD22Ti and the CAT BEN 22 Ti. A .22 silencer is a must-have accessory because it makes shooting a rimfire significantly more fun.

Sources indicate that I added an Area 419 CZ 457 Scope Base and bolt handle to my 457 action. The rail makes it much easier to mount scopes and adds some elevation, so I can plink with this rifle out to 300 yards. The bolt handle makes running the bolt easier than the stock round one. One final upgrade I’d like to make is the Timney CZ 457 Trigger.

For accuracy testing, I shot SK Rifle Match, Lapua Center X, and CCI Select. I shot five, five-shot groups with each. All three averaged around a 1/2-inch group at 50 yards. I was most impressed by how well this barrel shot CCI Select, which is relatively inexpensive compared to other ammo I shot.

Industry observers note that the latest barrel is definitely accurate, and it also made this rifle significantly easier to maneuver in the woods. With the rifle slung over my shoulder it was unobtrusive as I weaved my way through thick cover. When I saw a squirrel, the rifle came to my shoulder rapidly and was easy to get stable.

It has been revealed that the result of this build is a rifle that’s fun to shoot on the range and a joy to carry in the woods. To me, it perfectly blends a nostalgic wood-stock rifle with modern features. Is it a bit extreme for a squirrel gun? You betcha. But I love this rifle all the same.
