Skida Alpine Fleece-Lined Headband.

DryGuy Travel Dry DX Boot & Shoe Dryer.

Nocs Provisions Portal AFN7 Camera.

Hardcore skiers can be difficult to shop for.

In a recent development, the more involved you become as a skier, the more specific your wants and needs get. Suddenly, the standard goggles no longer apply, and you choose your jacket not based on what looks cool but on what functions in the ways you need. If you have a dedicated skier in your life, it’s not always obvious what to gift them, especially since you’ll want them to use it and love it.

To help ease your mind, we’ve rounded up some of our favorite gift ideas for the people in our lives who eat, sleep, and breathe skiing: from powderhounds to corduroy snobs, this list has a little something for everyone. And we can guarantee it—we’re somewhat of ski hardos ourselves.

We all have that one friend who complains a little too much about being cold. But when your butt freezes the second you sit on the lift, can you blame them? That’s where insulated knickers come in. Throw them on over your base layers for extra protection your derrière didn’t know it needed. Wear them over your base layer for some extra warmth or on their own for a more loose-fitting base under your ski pants. These are the perfect gift for the skier you know who likes to get a lot of days in and stay nice and toasty on the hill. —Giorgia Menetre, Senior Social Media Strategist.

Good goggles don’t need to cost a fortune. Dependable click-in, click-out interchangeable lenses are a staple for a reason—they’ll get you through just about every condition. Smith’s OG reliable goggles offer a wide field of vision, ChromaPop lenses that make the view pop, and a flexible, comfortable frame. Lenses swap easily, with no worry of a magnetic slip-up. Don’t let another ski day go by letting the skier you love squint through bad light. —GM.

According to recent reports, these booties come with a high price tag, but they’ll be the gift hardcore skiers never forget. This updated compression boot from Normatec takes the pressurized, full-length boot system that has proven recovery patterns and adds heat. Dynamic air circulation throughout the boot’s treatment session helps muscles recover faster and reduces soreness. Remember how good it feels to put an achy and tired calf next to a hot tub jet? Now, imagine that level of recovery from the comfort of your couch. Boots come in three sizes and can fit a wide range of heights.

Please note that boots will ship the week of 11/23. —Jamie Aranoff, SKI Senior Editor.

Recent findings suggest that hestra’s Fall Line mittens are consistently ranked as some of the warmest by our testers. The mittens have a cozy inner layer of brushed polyester and foam to keep hands insulated without overheating. The outside is leather that, once broken in, is soft and dexterous. Wrist straps ensure that the mittens stay with the skier, and not at the bottom of a chairlift. The mittens are on the pricier side, but will surely be a gift that skiers cherish for years. The same warmth also comes in a glove. —JA.

Read our full review and browse other warm gloves and mittens here.

According to recent reports, vests are underrated heroes for skiers: they’re a great midlayer for touring and warmer days, easy to layer, and stylish enough to wear around. The Helium Utility down vest from Peak Performance checks all three of these boxes and more. The vest is incredibly lightweight and packs down into its pocket. More importantly, it’s windproof and water-repellent. A cinch at the bottom allows for customization for the right fit. —JA.

In a recent development, if you’ve got an impossible-to-shop-for skier on your list, then look no further: this adventure camera from Nocs Provisions (yes, the same brand that makes binoculars) is sure to please. The camera is incredibly easy to use, even with thick gloves or mittens. Its simple one-button technology allows skiers to easily whip it out of a pocket and hit record (it takes both photos and videos). There’s no SD card needed, and content is easy to transfer to either a phone or computer with cords included. The camera takes retro-style photos and videos and comes with a lifetime “no matter what” policy. —JA.

For any serious skier, Dermatone chapstick is the ultimate stocking stuffer. Not only will Dermatone protect lips from chapping, but the SPF keeps skin from burning. It also belongs in every first aid kit; it’s proven to help stop frostbite on extremities like lips, noses, and cheeks. Most ski resorts sell Dermatone somewhere in the shop, but here’s your chance to stock up and avoid inflated prices. Your lips, nose, cheeks, and just about everywhere else will thank you. —JA.

Fleeces are always a solid gift, but Ridge Merino’s Alpha Wool Insulated jacket goes the extra mile. This fleece is designed to act as an outer layer for warmer days or uphilling, and a midlayer for when temperatures drop. What makes this fleece different is a mix of strategically placed wool to wick away moisture in places you sweat most, matched with a water-resistant Pertex Quantum Air that acts more like a shell than a fleece. The fleece is complete with a hood, so no matter the weather, you’ll be prepared.—JA.

The North Face just inked a deal with U.S. Ski & Snowboard to outfit the men’s and women’s alpine and freestyle teams for the next eight years. Bonus: They just released a version of the kit for the skiing public. The Comp Team Gore-Tex 2L Freeride and 3L Alpine jackets and pants come in alpine and freestyle designs, but the tech is the same: fully wind- and waterproof with plenty of features such as helmet-compatible hoods,  pit and thigh zips, and a multitude of smartly placed pockets. Don’t forget about the U.S. Ski Team crest on the right chest and all of the relevant sponsor badges to complete the look for your U.S. Ski Team superfan. —Samantha Berman, SKI Executive Editor.

Industry observers note that here’s the perfect stocking stuffer for the uphiller on your list—or anyone who wants to add a little flair to their kit. Skida’s Pursuit Headband features the newly introduced Alpenbloom print, designed by U.S. Ski Teamer Paula Moltzan as part of the brand’s 2026–’27 collaboration with U.S. Ski & Snowboard. Beyond the athlete-designed pattern, the headband is a genuinely useful piece, made with a moisture-wicking, quick-drying fabric that regulates temperature without trapping too much heat and cozy fleece lining for comfort. A secure, nonslip fit keeps it in place whether you’re skiing, skinning, or working up a sweat on a cold-weather run. For guys, check out Ryan Cochran-Siegle’s Under the Lights print, which comes in a hat and a neckwarmer in addition to a headband.—SB.

Recent findings suggest that the Black Diamond Spark Mitts have been a tester favorite for years, and for good reason: you can’t go wrong with a short gauntlet mitt with a full leather outer. But the Spark goes beyond boring old performance. Every few seasons, Black Diamond drops a colorway with a fun, embroidered design on the inner side of the index finger. The Angel Collinson mustache model was our longtime favorite, but the current model with shark teeth is just as fun—and a good reminder that skiing isn’t so serious. —Jenny Wiegand, Outside Associate Gear Director.

According to recent reports, for the skier who skis in all conditions, this is the midlayer to give. At just 9.8 ounces, the Lightstream Full Zip stays unbulky while delivering serious warmth from -10 to 50 degrees. Vivo Extreme insulation is zoned for the job: 60 grams in the body and collar, 40 in the hood and sleeves, and 25 in the underarms and side seams. The 15-denier stretch nylon/PU ripstop shell is tough enough for daily abuse, and it also works as an outer layer for fall bike commutes and dog walks. Pair it with the Lightstream Insulated Short, made for skiers who run cold but won’t give up their shell pants, even on resort days. Full-length side zips let you take the shorts off when things heat up, without removing your ski pants. Light and packable, they’re also the ultimate emergency layer to stash in your boot bag. Available for men and women. —JW.

In a recent development, carv is the perfect gift for the skier who has everything, mostly because it’s the kind of gadget they’d struggle to justify buying for themselves. But if someone gave it to them? Game on. I’ll admit, I was skeptical of this digital ski coach, which uses sensors attached to your boots to analyze your technique and deliver real-time feedback. But after a few seasons, I’m hooked. It turns improving your skiing into a game, and it’s surprisingly addictive. Ted Ligety once told me his secret to topping the Carv leaderboard: find a stretch of groomer where you can make 10 perfect turns, then ski it over and over until you top the leaderboard. Personally, I might get distracted looking for powder, but I’ve found Carv makes even an ordinary groomer day more interesting. It’s fun, genuinely useful, and exactly the sort of gift someone might not know they wanted. Editor’s note: The list price includes a 12-month membership; continued coaching requires renewal. —Sierra Shafer, Editorial Director, Lifestyle.

Industry observers note that few things in skiing are more universally useful than a Voilé Strap. These simple, stretchy polyurethane straps are the duct tape of the ski world, minus the sticky residue. Need to secure your skis together? Voilé Strap. Something breaks on your pack? Voilé Strap. Need to attach something to something else in a way the manufacturer probably didn’t intend? You get the idea. Made in Utah, these little problem-solvers come in a variety of lengths and colors and are practically indestructible. Every skier should have a couple tucked into their pack. Or, if you’re like me, scattered around the garage, the gear room, and the back of the car. You never know when you’ll need one, but trust me, you will. —SS.

In a recent development, why do we organize entire lives around sliding down snowy mountains? It’s a fair question, especially when you consider the expense, questionable career decisions, and occasional sleeping arrangements involved in chasing winter. In Powder Days, journalist Heather Hansman sets out to understand the people who’ve made skiing more than a hobby, exploring the history of ski-bum culture and what happens when the mountain towns that made it possible become increasingly difficult places to live. It’s funny, thoughtful, and at times uncomfortable in the best way, asking major questions about access, affordability, and the future of a sport we love. Give it to the skier who prepares their life around winter, or anyone who’s ever seriously considered quitting their job to ski more. —SS.

I didn’t win a single race in Alta’s town race series last winter, but I did win this boot dryer in the end-of-season raffle, and frankly, I count that as a victory. Wet ski boots aren’t just smelly. Moisture in your liners compromises insulation, making your feet cold even on mild days and potentially cutting a perfectly good ski day short. And if that moisture freezes overnight? Even worse. This compact dryer uses gentle heat and forced air to dry your boots without damaging their liners. What I love most is that it plugs into both a standard outlet and your car’s 12-volt adapter, so you can start drying your boots on the drive home. It’s also small enough to toss in your ski bag for a trip. Not glamorous, but genuinely one of the most useful things I own. —SS.

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Oh October, the month of mystery. Here in Boulder, Colorado, it’s when you wake up in the dark not knowing if it will be warm, cold, raining, or windy. The only thing you do know every morning is there will be even more much-larger-than-life-sized skeletons poking out of peoples’ lawns. (Why has this become a thing? As my friend Clare remarked on a run the other day, “people are desecrating their lawns with plastic trash!”).

Anyway, it’s a tricky time of year for running. Head out the door overdressed and you will end up a puddle of sweat that, depending on the weather, ultimately makes you cold. Leave underdressed, as I did for a tempo run two weeks ago, and your limbs will feel like they’ve been cursed by a witch who’s turned them to immovable ice.

But tricky conditions can be solved with treats. My trusty associate editor is, in his words, “going to the desert to do something stupid.” (Go Cade!) That leaves just me to round up our gear of the month. Here are the five items I kept packed in my Janji Ultrahauler (another piece of gear I can’t live without!) so I was ready for whatever I woke up to:.

Industry observers note that kilian Jornet’s fledgling shoe and apparel company has stuck to relatively technical alpine equipment—until now with the Nnormal Cadi. This do-everything trail shoe is exceptionally comfortable thanks to a padded heel collar and tongue and a cushy midsole with 37 mm stack in the heel, 31 mm in the forefoot. It’s got a nice wide toe box (an obsession of mine as I work on my foot strength and toe splay). And with a Vibram Megagrip outsole it’s tacky on all terrain and in all conditions. I also appreciate the mesh upper, which is breathable on hot days and dries swiftly on wet ones. It’s the only shoe I brought on a trip recently, which means I found myself wearing it for a 12-mile run around the Charles River in Boston—definitely not as energetic as your typical road trainer these days, but it got the job done just fine. It’s just a solid, dependable shoe.

It has been revealed that it’s rained A LOT in Boulder this month. And by a lot, I mean more than zero times. I know I’ve lived here for too long because I’ve gotten soft and the only thing that got me through more than zero very dark, very wet mornings was this rain jacket from Arc’teryx. That’s because it’s actually waterproof. But it’s also super lightweight and breathable, meaning you don’t incinerate in your own body heat and end up wet anyway. Plus one for the cinch on the hood so you can actually keep it on your head while you’re running and another bonus for the vents under the armpits, which help moderate body heat. I know $450 is an obscene amount to spend on anything, but this is definitely a case of you get what you pay for.

It has been revealed that when it comes to running pants and tights I am very, very picky. They can’t suffocate my waist, but they also need to stay put. They can’t bunch around the knees, but they also can’t be so baggy that the pant legs rub into each other. The Janji Altas Multi Pant is one of the few pieces that passes my stringent test. They are supremely comfortable thanks to a wide elastic waistband, and a drawstring lets you dial in the fit. They’re loose enough to allow for full range of motion, but they’re streamlined enough that I can wear them for harder efforts without getting annoyed. Why I really love them for this time of year is they are lightweight and breathable, providing just the right amount of insulation. And even better, they have nearly knee-length ankle zips so I often wear them for the warm up and zip them off for intervals—no shoe removal required.

There is something so comforting and luxurious about tucking into a comfy vest for a fall outing. Enter this fleece-lined vest from 7Mesh. It’s super breathable yet cozy thanks to a soft, woven outer layer paired with the light and ultrasoft fleece lining. I’ve been loving it for colder runs when a jacket feels like too much but a long sleeve isn’t quite enough. And I’ve also been loving it on the bike—especially because the vest folds into itself via a significant back pocket, revealing little straps that let you fix it to your bike frame when you’re not wearing it.

Recent findings suggest that not too cold and not too warm, snug but not tight, these gloves are  a shoulder-season star. They’re so lightweight that I don’t think twice about wearing them for the start of a run before the sun rises and stashing them in a pocket as I warm up with the ground. I can use my phone with them on, carry my ballot (the midterms are on Tuesday!), as well as maneuver zippers and, if desperate, tie shoes. Plus the colors and patterns instantly boost my mood. (They came in so many fun options!).

One-star review for the name. Zero stars for the logo branded on the top of the collar. And yet, five stars for these socks. They are just that comfy and moisture-wicking. I am pretty skeptical of overengineered gear, but CEP has me thinking maybe there is something to developing stuff in a lab. These socks provide a gentle amount of compression and arch support while also being ventilated in all the places you want it. In other words: they stay put, and they keep my feet comfortable for a wide range of temperatures—perfect for fall running. Most importantly, my feet do not slip in my shoes. I repeat: no slippage here. My friend saw me running in them the other day and he remarked he also loves these socks so much that he ordered five pairs. Oh and they come in approximately one billion colorways.

I know, I know, it’s a crime to spend more than $50 on a hair product—much less two products. But hear me out: Colorado is savage on my wavy hair. When left unchecked, the dry air and harsh sun leech out every last drop of moisture, turning my hair into a wiry mess. Add in the rainy days of October (or my annual pilgrimage to Hawaii) and in years past I am ripping out chunks of matted hair every time I shower. Enter this fancy shampoo and conditioner. I am not exaggerating when I say this stuff has revolutionized my hair’s life. For the first time in 13 years since I moved here, my hair feels soft. And I can actually get a brush through it when I get out of the shower! You better believe I will be buying it again.

#32943. Latest Update: Traversing the Saiga Silk Road

📅 26 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2098 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adventure-journal ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Traversing the Saiga Silk Road

📅 26 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2098 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adventure-journal

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As we skidded off the main road and onto a mud path maintained only by tire treads, lines began to blur.
  • Flanking our two-track trail were a series of parallel lanes no more than a foot wide, which forked, merged, and crisscrossed our own.
  • Recent findings suggest that through borrowed binoculars, I soon got my first glimpse of an ancient tableau, seemingly untouched since Neanderthals roamed the earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As we skidded off the main road and onto a mud path maintained only by tire treads, lines began to blur.

Flanking our two-track trail were a series of parallel lanes no more than a foot wide, which forked, merged, and crisscrossed our own. In the distance, I saw what looked like a ghost train, faintly visible and thrust forward by howling Siberian winds.

Recent findings suggest that through borrowed binoculars, I soon got my first glimpse of an ancient tableau, seemingly untouched since Neanderthals roamed the earth. On the far horizon, hundreds of nomadic travelers pierced the frigid air with their ringed horns, inhaling the brittle shards through Snuffleupagus snouts as they sprinted across the desolate steppe.

Watching them charge through the treeless plain at full bore, I was reminded of a saying I’d heard shortly before arriving in this remote corner of Kazakhstan: “The saiga is a freedom-loving animal.”.

In a recent development, since time immemorial, saiga antelope have blazed trails across Central Asia while other civilizations rose and fell around them. They once inhabited a world dominated by woolly mammoths, saber-toothed cats, and giant deer with antlers 12 feet across—and outlived them all. When pioneering human caravans first attempted to navigate this unforgiving land, they considered the saigas to be their guides.

Recent findings suggest that ahead of my arrival, seasonal rains transformed once-green grasslands into sludge punctuated by tufts of withering brush. Driving through such muck is, I would soon discover, akin to controlled hydroplaning. The steering wheel bucked wildly as our tires swerved, shredding deep into the gunk and desperately gripping anything remotely solid enough to push off from.

Sources indicate that in the front seats were Alexandr and Albert, two team members from the Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan, or ACBK. Between them, they have more than twenty-five years of experience following saigas across the steppe, and I’d arranged to join them for the western leg of one of their field audits.

Sources indicate that our visit was timed to coincide with the rutting season, a critical part of the year for saigas. This is a gathering time, when antelope from across the region sprint together in massive single-file lines, before congregating for a series of competitive battles and subsequent mating rituals.

Recent findings suggest that for males, it’s a time for strutting and headbutting to demonstrate one’s physical prowess to female onlookers—an activity so energy-intensive that many will forget to eat and keel over from extreme physical exhaustion. For females, this is a time of choosing. In addition to assessing fitness, they pay particular attention to one distinctive feature: a potential mate’s floppy, elongated nose. The saigas’ sniffers are essential for filtering out dust in the semidesert plains and for warming frigid winter air before it reaches their lungs. A large nose is the ultimate sign of virility, so as the males marched into these annual gatherings, they were doing everything they could to accentuate their schnozzes.

In a recent development, because of the saigas’ preference for large-scale migrations across a landscape almost entirely devoid of trees, they have long been a favorite of global wildlife trackers. The isolation and starkness of the saiga world is a strength when it comes to GPS collars, which deliver a reliable stream of daily pings without risk of visual obstruction. Prior to such breakthroughs, conservationists would sometimes spend weeks roaming the boundless steppe unsuccessfully trying to locate the nomadic herds.

The wildlife sanctuary we were traveling through was created only a year prior, with its boundaries informed by tracking data that Albert and his team personally collected. He seemed pleased that the animals were continuing to use the newly designated space as intended. Standing along the roadside, Alexandr spotted a stream of the famously skittish ungulates wrapping around the contours of the earth. As he did, ripping wind and snow started blowing in sideways—the outer ring of an encroaching storm.

These were no fluffy flakes. This was the harsh, crunchy ice of a walk-in freezer, which instantly hardened our truck’s caked-on mud like liquid nitrogen.

Industry observers note that seemingly unperturbed by the dropping barometer, Albert chirped, “Who’s hungry?” Setting up an impromptu picnic, he and Alexandr dug into a prepared meal of fresh bread, tea, and dried meats of unknown provenance. In a muted attempt to thaw my face, I opted to guzzle spicy instant noodles.

A tradition of nomadism has loomed large in this corner of the world since at least the Early Iron Age. The very word kazakh is thought to be derived from the Turkic word qaz, which means “wanderer” or “vagabond.” For millennia, small human groups routinely migrated to higher altitudes in the hot summer months, where melting snow made for abundant water and greenery, before returning to sheltered valleys ahead of winter’s whipping winds. At various times of the year, disparate nomads would also congregate for formal meetings and large cultural festivals, complete with physical challenges like wrestling and tug-of-war. When the gatherings were finished, the nomads dispersed once again.

In a recent development, historical analysis has shown that nomads’ seasonal migrations and time-honed transit corridors may have helped pave the way for portions of the Great Silk Road, which was less a singular route than an ever-evolving web of pathways and bypasses that linked together reliable stopovers. At the Silk Road’s peak, this corner of western Kazakhstan along the fertile banks of the Ural River became a vital transcontinental crossroads. To this day, the river still serves as a natural boundary between Asia and Europe, meaning this part of Kazakhstan is, quite literally, where East meets West.

Industry observers note that the land above the Caspian Sea also served as a main artery that linked together key transit points. Strategic settlements along the riverbank allowed weary caravans to rest their heads, unwind in large public baths, exchange knowledge, stock up on essential supplies, and regroup before moving onward.

Among overland voyagers traversing the continental divide, saigas have long been spoken of with an almost mythical reverence. Cave paintings of the antelope created as far back as the seventh century BCE depict them as resilient, elusive, and charismatic. Expert navigators who embody the true spirit of a most inhospitable terrain.

According to recent reports, in human society, traditional nomadic practices persisted even as the land itself was variously claimed and reclaimed by Turkic tribes, Genghis Khan, and the Russian Empire. Only with the rise of the Soviet Union in the twentieth century did mandatory sedentarization efforts successfully manage to lock nomadic people in place, force them to farm, and extinguish a cultural flame that had burned brightly for millennia. Denied the ability to live in perpetual motion, people’s navigational muscles began to atrophy.

Industry observers note that this transition was viewed by many as an inevitable shift toward “modernization,” but it also represented a significant diversion from our own history as a species. Of the roughly 300,000 years that Homo sapiens have existed, we spent the first 288,000 of them living in small, mobile groups that followed the migratory patterns of other animals. Forcing nomads into agricultural plots was also a colossal failure because much of the steppe soil was unsuitable for growing crops, which is why so many people were nomadic in the first place. Iconic filmmaker Werner Herzog once remarked that “whatever went wrong and makes our civilization something doomed is the departure from the nomadic life.”.

It has been revealed that whether by choice or necessity, most Kazakh people now lead stationary lives in urban centers. The world that nomads once freely roamed has also been feverishly transformed, not only by agriculture but through the construction of new roads and railways.

For the saigas, whose nomadic days never ceased, these upcoming layers now represent an existential threat.

Recent findings suggest that with the weather taking a turn for the worse, Albert and Alexandr ultimately decided to call it a day and start fresh in the morning. After a blistering drive through whiteout conditions, we hunkered down in a tiny village less than 10 miles from the Russian border, where Albert pulled out his laptop and showed me how saiga movements have changed over the years.

“They would routinely trek hundreds of miles as part of an expansive migratory route across the Eurasian steppe,” he said. “Saigas could be found from the Caucasus Mountains to Mongolia, and everywhere in between.”.

According to recent reports, for millennia, they lived with few barriers and obstructions on the landscape. Then, seemingly overnight, rattling railways and roaring roads began to crisscross the region, fragmenting the saigas into smaller, more isolated groups. As the interior steppe got more accessible to vehicles and passengers, development begat more development.

Sources indicate that on his screen, Albert clicked open a recent map that highlighted how a population of GPS-collared saigas once routinely traveled deep into Uzbekistan before being unceremoniously clipped off by a new rail line in 2014. The data from the years prior to the railway’s construction showed a flurry of squiggly lines representing individual animals zipping back and forth with the seasons. The post-construction slide showed those same animals spinning around despondently on the northern side of the tracks, while the fresh grasses and water they had come to rely on withered away to the south.

Such interruptions can lead to a complete collapse in spatial knowledge—a loss that science writer Ben Goldfarb once wrote is “as thorough as the erasure of a language.” Just as human nomads forced to stay in one place eventually lost connection to the physical landmarks of their ancestors’ journeys, young saigas learn where they can reliably find food and shelter, as well as places to stay away from, through active participation and observation. This cultural exchange keeps their world in orbit and is one of the reasons they have been successful at navigating a terrain fatal to so many before them. As the land they know is cleaved and partitioned, whole stretches of the Saiga Silk Road begin to fade from memory.

Sources indicate that to unwind this damage, Albert’s team has partnered with the Kazakh government to construct dozens of saiga-friendly crossing points, where slightly sloping dirt ramps rise up to match the height of the train tracks, making it appear from a distance as though there’s a natural gap in the rail line. Cattle-guard fences positioned far away from the crossings ensure that trains and saigas never actually run into each other at these intersections, which would shatter the illusion of safety.

ACBK has also worked with the Uzbek government to reshape its border fences from a barbed-wire wall to an X-shaped barricade that blocks vehicles from driving through but leaves just enough space for saigas to pass. Over time, Albert hopes such efforts can rebuild the trust necessary for them to confidently return to a plateau they once relied on.

The next morning, I was astonished by how austere the steppe looked compared with the day before. Gone was the slippery muck and browning grasses of shifting seasons, replaced by a blanket of crunchy snow. Against this stark black-and-white backdrop, the fresh crystals functioned like fingerprint dust, illuminating the only remaining pops of color: the rust-red streaks of human and nonhuman pathways in the dirt.

Parked in an otherwise empty tract of prairie land, we watched in stunned silence as thousands of saigas seized the day, flying like banshees across the periphery, their hooves gouging the frozen crust and stamping pigment into an earthen canvas.

As I gazed east toward the colorless horizon, I tried to envision how it might have looked in the thirteenth century, when this corner of the world boasted a vast network of caravanserai, or road inns, where exhausted travelers could rest and recover before continuing onward into the great unknown.

It has been revealed that I pondered what it must have felt like for an intrepid merchant to know that they would not see another human being for many days, maybe weeks. To be fearful of what you may soon encounter, but take solace that the space between is not wholly empty. For there is life beyond humanity’s margins, and among nonhuman communities, that in-between space is the center of everything. That, I imagined, must have offered some measure of assurance that the road ahead, perilous though it may be, is well traveled.

This essay was adapted from the new nonfiction travelogue The Hidden Nations of Animals and is published here exclusively for Adventure Journal, with permission from Penguin Random House.

Sources indicate that narrow down the huge list of possibilities by focusing on his core interests. If dad likes fishing, get him a gift that supports that passion. If he has a lot of hobbies, you can’t go wrong with a gift that goes well with all of them.

Once you have the list narrowed down, the difference between a good gift and a great gift is buying something that dad wouldn’t buy from himself or something that he can make memories with for a long time.

In the “Key Features” section for each product, I’ve written what type of hobbies the gift is good for and given you an idea of the price range. The amount of dollar symbols corresponds to how many digits there are in the gift’s price tag. So, something that’s $100 will have three dollar symbols and something that’s $5 will have one dollar symbol. To also help you find a gift in the right price range, I’ve listed them from the most expensive to the least expensive. I’ve also hyperlinked an article where you can read more about the product if you want to dive in deeper.

I don’t know a dad who doesn’t love flashlights, and if you’re buying a gift for a father who spends his weekends at the range, the Inforce ARC is a great choice. It’s a modular weapon light that mounts to any M-LOK handguard (Picatinny adapter sold separately).

Recent findings suggest that why do they want it? Weapon lights have become a must-have accessory for defensive shotguns, pistol-caliber carbines and AR-style rifles. You’ll be helping dad complete his next build with one of the best weapon lights out there. This light is exceptionally bright with a focused center beam and good spill. It’s MIL-STD-810H certified for durability and IPX8 certified for waterproofness. It uses a rechargeable 18650 battery and has a lengthy run time for such a powerful flashlight.

Sources indicate that the world is awash with thermal-curious dads, who want to try the technology, but don’t want to start off with a $10,000 scope. The Athlon Cronus ATS P-Mini is a thermal monocular that won’t break the bank and has a ton of cool uses. From projects around the house to finding the dog in the backyard to game recovery. It’s a fun and useful optic that is guaranteed to get a great reaction from any outdoorsy dad.

It’s also easy to use with a touchscreen display and app connectivity. Even a luddite will be able to turn it on and start using it right away. The kids can help with changing the color palettes and recording videos.

In a recent development, this is the ultimate carry-on luggage. Pelican manufacturers everything from gun cases to coolers, and one thing that’s consistent in their product lines is durability. The ATX luggage is no different and it has a hard exterior that’s built similarly to Pelican’s legendary Air cases. I’ve traveled thousands of miles with mine and it’s held up to abuse as a carry on and a checked bag. The Pelican ATX is a well-made piece of luggage that’s the ideal gift for the frequent traveler. Read my full review.

Dad needs something practical that he can wear while mowing the grass, reeling in a bass, grilling burgers, or scouting for hunting season. One shirt that fills all those roles is the Kuiu Gila Hoodie. I’ve worn mine doing all of the above and while chasing my toddler around the yard. It’s a comfortable shirt that protects skin from sunburn and keeps you cool through oppressive heat.

The fit is loose, but not too loose and runs true to size. The hood lays flat when not in use and doesn’t obstruct your peripheral vision when it’s up. The SPF protection prevented burns, even when I spent over 8 hours in the sun. I live in the southeast where the humidity stays above 80 percent all summer, and the Gila wicks the inevitable sweat and keeps me comfortable in triple-digit heat. Another noteworthy feature is that the shirt’s material doesn’t hold odor like some synthetics, so you can probably give dad a hug when he gets home from the lake.

It has been revealed that the Gila Pro hoodie is another good option. It has a built in facemask for additional SPF protection or concealment while hunting. Its has a more athletic fit so that it can be worn as a base layer. One of my favorite features is the vented arm pits, which is like having central air built into a shirt.

Every outdoorsman needs a good fixed-blade knife and the Victorinox Venture Pro is a perfect option that won’t break the bank. This is a full-tang knife that’s designed for bushcraft but is versatile enough for camplife, hunting, or anything else your dad likes to do outdoors.

It has been revealed that the design of the protruding tang makes it easy to start a fire with the included ferro rod. There’s jimping far forward on the blade’s spine (near the tip), which allows you to choke up on the blade for more control when carving, whittling, or feather-sticking.

The Venture Pro’s handle has a comfortable thumb rest for extra control when using specialized carving techniques like the sternum pull cut, pinch-grip, or power cut.

It has a polymer handle, which will work well in all weather conditions. The knife clicks positively into its MOLLE-compatible sheath, which also holds a tweezers, ferro rod, and pressurized ballpoint pen.

Trail cameras are practical hunting tools that provide a wealth of insight. But, they’re also a ton of fun. That’s why a trail camera, particularly a cellular trail camera is a fantastic gift. It’s something dad has a practical use for and he’ll have a ton of fun watching photos of deer and other animals appear in the app.

The Reveal Pro 3.0 won our 2024 trail camera test because of its stellar performance and easy to use app. The key differences between the 3.0 and the 3.0 Pro are that the Pro has an LCD screen and no-glow flash. Both would make excellent gifts for the whitetail fanatic.

If dad loves the sweet smell of hickory smoke in the morning, then this is the perfect gift for him. It’s under $500, small enough to easily move around, and substantial enough to cook up a feast. It’s ideal for making delicious BBQ, but doesn’t require the work needed to maintain a consistent temperature of a propane or offset smoker. Keep in mind that the max temp is 450 degrees so this grill will be great for low and slow brisket and beer can chicken, but not ideal for searing steaks.

In a recent development, the Johnny Morris CarbonLite 2.0 is a baitcasting rod and reel setup that will make dad’s day and keep him smiling all summer. It’s a high performance rod and reel that looks as good as it fishes. You can get it in number of configurations, but you can’t go wrong with a 7 foot, medium heavy. If dad fishes a lot of places with thick vegetation, a the 7 foot 3 inch, heavy will allow him to muscle fish out of the cover. Or if he’s a smallmouth angler, the medium or medium light power rods are excellent options.

If the $230 price tag is too steep for your budget, also consider the awesome Bass Pro Shops Pro Qualifier Baitcast Combo, which is $100 less.

According to recent reports, today’s air rifles aren’t Ralphy’s Red Rider or inaccurate pellet guns. They’re powerful and wicked accurate. If dad likes squirrel hunting, hates squirrels, or just likes plinking, the Air Venturi Avenger is a great first reintroduction to the world of airguns. When Jim Chapman did his Air Venturi Avenger review, his rifle shot a 16-shot group at 40 yards that could be covered by a quarter. He also noted that the air rifle was backyard quiet, so it won’t disturb the neighbors. It’s no wonder he chose it as one the best air rifles.

Something any hunter will appreciate is the price of shooting an air rifle, which costs pennies in comparison to the ammo a centerfire or even rimfire uses. Also, at well under $500 it’s a gift a few people can chip in on and provide dad with a ton of fun or a new hobby.

It was very difficult choosing a knife for this best gifts for dads list, but my selection ultimately landed on the Benchmade Mini Adamas, which won best overall in The Best Pocket Knives review. The Mini Adamas is a tough, rugged blade that is also convenient to carry. Anyone from hikers, anglers, to backcountry hunters will love this pocket knife. Dad will carry his new pocket knife on all his adventures and create new memories with it everywhere he goes. An heirloom piece like this is a special gift that any dad would be lucky to have.

If you’re buying for a dad that loves sharp flying objects, a throwing ax is a fun yet practical gift he’ll love. The Council Tool Flying Fox is balanced for throwing, and sticks in ax targets with ease. But, it is also a great ax for turning logs into firewood and kindling. It makes a great gift because it is an utilitarian tool and backyard fun all in one. At under $60 it won’t break the bank either. If you want to see more ax options check out Drew Conover’s article, The Best Camping Axes.

Recent findings suggest that the Abel Vaya is a functional work of art. In fact Monte Burke chose it as one the best fly fishing reels in his review. Its performance is stellar, but it also comes in a wide variety of colors and paint schemes. You can even order a custom reel from Abel. And that added touch makes the Vaya stand out as a great gift for a fly fisherman.

If mosquitoes and gnats are preventing dad from enjoying time outdoors, a Thermacell is a must-have backyard accessory. I’ve tested them extensively while hunting in buggy places and for my best mosquito repellents article. They’re highly recommended and they really do a great job at keeping mosquitoes away.

The EX90 uses a rechargeable battery and just one consumptive refill. While the EX90 isn’t ideal for taking on a backpacking trip or a hike due to its size, it is a great option for RVing, car camping, and the backyard. The device takes 15 minutes to create a protective bubble and will provide protection for nine hours on a single charge. After the heat-up time you’ll have a 20 foot mosquito-free zone.

If you really love dad or you and other family members want to chip in on something really special, then an heirloom-grade hunting rifle will make an unbeatable gift for any hunter. You might actually make dad cry when he opens the box and finds a rifle with a beautifully figured wood stock.

It has been revealed that buying a Winchester Model 70 Super Grade is the easy decision, but choosing the cartridge it will shoot is a tough one. If dad is a deer hunter you can’t go wrong with the .308 Winchester or the 6.5 Creedmoor. If you live west of the Mississippi and he hunts elk, mule deer, and antelope you might consider going with the 6.5 PRC or .300 Winchester Magnum. If he’s an old school dude, then get him the 30-06 Springfield or .308 Winchester, which are both great for hunting anything in North America. Outdoor Life’s editor-in-chief, Alex Robinson, wrote The Case for Fresh, Wood-Stocked Deer Hunting Rifles, which makes a compelling case for these timeless rifles.

A hunting rifle, really nice hunting clothing, or a quality knife are all great gifts for a dad that likes hunting.

Dads want a gift that helps them enjoy their hobby and is something they can use for years to come.

A tie is the most common gift and one of the worst gifts for an outdoors dad.

Dad deserves something great this year, and the best gift for dad is one that helps him enjoy his favorite outdoor hobby even more.

  • Still, he had been a boy of the Great Depression, and Dad’s early years had instilled the necessities of marksmanship, fencerow rabbits, and freshly caught bullheads.
  • It has been revealed that so on that Christmas Day, Dad drove me outside town, handed me a cardboard box with a Magic Marker bull’s-eye, and told me to put it 30 yards away in the snowy woods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that MY FATHER wasn’t trying to ensure hunting’s future or even create a newly introduced hunter when he slid that Savage 24S-E in .22/.410 beneath our Christmas tree in 1971. Dad had quit hunting by the time I was 14, and honestly, he probably wasn’t the best teacher or role model to take me and my three brothers out for rabbits or squirrels. Dad was a crack shot, but he was impatient with hunting and its painstaking tactics.

Still, he had been a boy of the Great Depression, and Dad’s early years had instilled the necessities of marksmanship, fencerow rabbits, and freshly caught bullheads. He enlisted in the Army at age 17, as World War II ended.

It has been revealed that so on that Christmas Day, Dad drove me outside town, handed me a cardboard box with a Magic Marker bull’s-eye, and told me to put it 30 yards away in the snowy woods. I then shot, first with the .22 barrel and then with the .410 bore. After we returned home, Dad handed me two latest Hoppe’s cleaning kits, one for rifles and the other for shotguns. He showed me how to swab the barrels with nitro solvent and rub the exterior with light oil.

In a recent development, his mentoring tasks complete, Dad never again offered another hunting or shooting tip. Even so, with that little gun, my love and obsession for hunting grew. With neither intent nor forethought, Dad had recruited me into hunting’s largest demographic group: white males from families with rural or near-rural backgrounds, born between 1946 and 1964. We baby boomers swelled hunting’s ranks to record numbers by the 1980s, and by 1991 there were still more than 14 million estimated hunters in America.

Today, baby boomers are 56 to 75 years old. We’re no longer the majority of -America’s hunters, and our numbers are declining fast. Research indicates folks typically retire from hunting around age 70, which means most of my generation will hang up our bows, rifles, and shotguns for good in the next 10 years, if we haven’t already.

Recent findings suggest that I’m not all that sentimental about this. Baby boomers, after all, didn’t invent hunting. Hunters roamed North America eons before 1946, and they’ll keep roaming long after boomers and our heirs are gone. But my generation’s pending end prompts a question: What, exactly, is the legacy we’re leaving behind?

To answer that question, it’s important to understand how we got started. As kids, we boomers shot BB guns, watched Daniel Boone and Davy Crockett on TV, died daily atop imaginary Alamo walls, and quietly inspected unlocked guns and Remington Peters ammo we removed from our fathers’ Sears, Roebuck gun racks.

We mostly taught ourselves to hunt while envying friends whose fathers, uncles, and brothers also hunted. We weren’t farmers, but we bicycled often to farms and rural woodlots with our recurves or shotguns lashed to our rear baskets. We hunted those places until the landowners shooed us away for November’s gun season, but we returned in December after they again judged us harmless.

Sources indicate that by the mid-1970s, we saw whitetail deer herds surge across the eastern two-thirds of the U.S. That explosion occurred rapidly and mysteriously.

When I returned home from the Navy in 1980, after missing four years’ worth of deer seasons, I hunted the same woods as before, but I found a far different herd. It seemed the Department of Natural Resources had corralled the results of five years of whitetail reproduction onto one 100-acre woods.

Recent findings suggest that A friend’s dad owned that property and invited me to hunt it after he counted 56 deer on opening morning and shot a -6-pointer before noon. Other friends made claims of 70 to 80 sightings that weekend, 10 times what I’d seen on opening weekend only five years before.

Sources indicate that I didn’t shoot any of the many deer I saw in three days of hunting after Thanksgiving 1980, but only because the DNR hadn’t yet invented bonus antlerless tags. Once it did, my freezer was always full of venison.

With so many whitetails on the landscape, hunters adopted a range of beliefs about deer and their management. By the early 1990s, I was passing up yearling bucks regularly, filling free or cheap antlerless tags, and packing our freezers full of six deer each fall. Unfortunately for the herd and its habitat, most other hunters weren’t so eager to shoot does.

According to recent reports, with bucks aplenty in the swollen herds, many hunters waited out “their” buck—any buck—and then shot it and went home. Others also ignored does and fawns, as well as yearling bucks, and proudly held out for a “150-class” buck. They pledged allegiance to QDM, and didn’t get the humor when asked if they meant “quantity,” not quality, deer management, which is what they achieved by refusing to shoot female deer.

Sources indicate that that combination of surging deer herds and growing boomers sparked the mass production of compound bows, portable tree-stands, and anodized aluminum arrows throughout the 1970s. We boomers weren’t wealthy individually, but collectively we squirreled away fortunes to fund outdoor store layaway programs.

Throughout the 1980s, manufacturers made increasingly fast bows, better-performing bullets, more convincing camouflage, clearer and brighter riflescopes, and warmer and drier hunting clothes. Hunters also began driving ATVs and building increasingly tall and cushy box stands. Hunting media boomed too, with hunters renting VHS tapes and buying three-year subscriptions to a variety of different hunting magazines.

Whitetails kept pace, overwhelming farmers from North Dakota to Georgia.

Sources indicate that hunting gear kept improving and multiplying through the 1990s, with calls, grunt tubes, rangefinders, rattling devices, GPS units, pop-up ground blinds, substantial-game decoys, inline muzzleloaders, and much, much more. Boomers were there for it all.

According to recent reports, maybe I’m a product of my generation, as I still use much of that gear today and especially like the better boots and clothes, which keep me happier on stand in all weather. I also admire the straight-​shooting bows and broadheads, which consistently deliver cleaner kills and clearer consciences.

Sources indicate that but what about all those gadgets, the ones that Aldo Leopold warned about in the 1940s? Aldo called them “aids to self-reliance, hardihood, woodcraft, or marksmanship, but too often functioning as substitutes for them” and claimed their “aggregate poundage becomes tonnage” when hunters go afield.

I hold no man in higher regard than Leopold, a member of the Lost Generation, but he overstated things. Yes, hunting’s gadgeteers are making more toys than ever 75 years post-Leopold, but hunters often limit their “tonnage,” promptly abandoning gear that is useless. Also, I haven’t found much evidence that our gadgetry provides an unfair advantage over the game we hunt or makes it difficult for game agencies to regulate harvests.

We boomers excelled at creating and maintaining hunting gear, but we flopped at creating and sustaining latest hunters. As early as the late 1980s, industry analysts, university sociologists, and wildlife agency administrators knew our children weren’t following us afield at the pace we’d once set. When demographers plotted hunters’ birth years and projected them on graphs, the baby boomer bulge moved like a basketball through a python. What would happen when hunting’s dominant generation passed on?

A rural sociologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison in 1991 warned of massive changes. Professor Tom Heberlein mentioned “hunting as we know it” in Wisconsin could cease by 2050. He speculated the state might have to manage its deer herd with 100,000 well-trained animal control officers.

Heberlein, however, said his “straight-line projection” of declining hunter numbers wasn’t a prediction, given the unknowns of future technology, social trends, and natural events. Still, all evidence in 1991 demonstrated hunting interest had peaked with the then-middle-aged boomers and would only fall as they aged, became more urban and white collar, and led smaller, less structured families.

Most media outlets skipped such nuance and caveats as Heberlein’s warning generated national headlines and debates.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, wildlife agencies and universities wondered how institutions would fund habitat work, scientific studies, and hunting programs. They were learning firsthand the risks of relying on one type of crop for survival. In effect, hunting’s boom had relied on four specific elements:.

Sources indicate that A 2016 analysis by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service underscored the whitetail’s dominance. It highlighted that of the nation’s documented 13.7 million hunters in 2011, 79 percent (10.9 million) were deer hunters, primarily whitetail hunters. Although the accuracy of this oft-cited survey is unclear, it’s the best data we currently have for understanding national hunting trends.

While hunting depended on whitetails for a species, it depended even more heavily on white males for participants. Roughly 10 percent of U.S. hunters today are female, but they form a slow-growing group with great “churn,” meaning they move in and out of hunting’s ranks at higher rates than males.

And of the 11.5 million Americans who hunted in 2016, 96 percent (11.1 million) were white.

In a recent development, in addition, even though states fund wildlife programs largely with license fees, sales of hunting licenses across much of the eastern two-thirds of the U.S. are declining, even though few states have raised prices. Western states are keeping resident fees modest, but regularly jab nonresidents with license prices 10 times higher than what residents pay.

According to recent reports, the agencies’ other chief funding source is the federal excise taxes levied under the Pittman-Robertson Act on sales of ammo and firearms for hunting, self-defense, and recreational shooting. Many of today’s popular products didn’t exist when hunting boomed a half-century ago, and the P-R Act hasn’t been updated since Fred Bear and the archery industry persuaded Congress to impose excise taxes on bows, arrows, and accessories in 1972. Therefore, sales of scents, decoys, ATVs, tree-stands, hunting optics, rangefinders, trail cameras, ground blinds, game calls, GPS-driven smartphone apps, and high-tech clothing and footwear don’t -contribute to conservation.

Despite the challenges, I’m hopeful for the future of post-boomer hunting. Today, many younger hunters are just as hardcore as any grizzled boomer. Serious hunters, no matter their age, aren’t easily discouraged. We boomers eagerly toughed out state-mandated age requirements, some of which still stand, that forbade youngsters to hunt until ages 12, 14, or 16. And some fathers didn’t welcome boomers to deer camp until high school or after.

According to recent reports, “It was an honor to finally go to deer camp at 17 or 18,” notes Rich Stedman, a rural sociologist at Cornell University and chairman of the school’s Department of Natural Resources and the Environment. Even though Stedman is a Gen Xer by two years, he hunts mostly with an older generation.

“There was something masculine about an early-1980s deer camp,” Stedman claims. “I was finally grown up enough to hunt with the men who survived a world war and the Great Depression. The boomers’ parents had a sense of optimism, a deep belief they could do the hard things. In comparison, our lives were relatively easy, so when we finally got to hunt with them, we tried hard to make the grade.”.

Stedman and his group cherished deer camp, and he laments the fading -multigenerational-​deer-​camp traditions but claims it’s not the last institution that hunting will spawn, alter, or abandon.

Sources indicate that “I still feel connections to our camp, but I’m also haunted by its ghosts,” Stedman notes. “It’s the repository of many stories that make you who you are. The flip side is that almost all those men are now gone. It’s time to make upcoming memories, but I can’t make my kids see deer camp through my eyes. They don’t buy into challenges I welcomed. New things jar some of my traditions, but that’s how things change.”.

Will hunting’s younger generations find ways to fund the nation’s conservation programs with fewer hunters? Will they agree to pay more themselves, lobby for broader funding systems, or insist on both? Stedman, Caren Cooper, and other Cornell researchers found in 2015 that hunters, bird-watchers, and other nature-based outdoor recreationists were four to five times more likely than nonrecreationists to donate to conservation and wildlife initiatives.

Sources indicate that even so, Congress and voters haven’t tried to expand the Pittman-​Robertson Act beyond ammo, firearms, and archery for more than 50 years. Likewise, bird-watchers and other “nonconsumptive” recreationists fight suggestions to include binoculars, birdseed, bird feeders, or camping gear in the P-R Act.

Industry observers note that future generations of hunters might also have to broaden their passions beyond whitetails, whose overabundance in many areas has caused extensive over-browsing for the past 20 years, reducing the land’s carrying capacity. Meanwhile, chronic wasting disease has increased slowly but steadily, and if researchers are right, CWD-infected herds will decline without reductions in hunting harvest.

Will hunters then focus more on small-game species? Yes, history suggests. Even though deer dominated the boomers’ era, most boomers learned the craft by hunting small game and “graduating” to deer. Not until whitetails became so numerous in the 1980s and ’90s did most beginners start with deer.

According to recent reports, most importantly, the hunting community will need to broaden its population. Family-​driven hunter “recruitment” has fallen short, claims Wisconsin’s Christine Thomas, former dean of the College of Natural Resources at UW Stevens Point and founder of the Becoming an Outdoors-Woman program. Thomas says programs like BOW help fill voids, and she predicts more women will populate hunting’s ranks. So does Linda Bylander, who coordinates Minnesota’s BOW program.

Sources indicate that “Our students are typically women who are just getting done with young-child–rearing duties, so they’re often between 30 and 40,” she says. “They want to hunt, and they like the locavore movement.”.

Likewise, a 2020 nationwide study of university students found that potential hunters, compared to active hunters, were more likely to be women or racial/ethnic minorities and less likely to have social support for hunting.

Rue Mapp, founder and CEO of Outdoor Afro, and Jimmy Flatt, Lydia Parker, and Thomas Tyner, co-founders of Hunters of Color, are helping to drive the conversation. They say many Blacks, Hispanics, Native Americans, and members of other ethnic groups are intrigued by hunting. Few come from hunting families, however, so few can ask relatives or friends for help.

“If you separate people for one generation from anything, it’s hard for them to reacquire those skills,” Parker says. “You can learn some things by reading and watching YouTube videos, but you need repetitive lessons with others who hunt regularly. By matching our members with mentors and trying to create surrogate families, we hope to get beyond the R3 programs. We want hunting’s participation rates to eventually match society’s demographics.”.

Mapp has similar hopes but emphasizes she doesn’t want hunting to be colorblind.

“I’d like it to be an American quilt, where each person is a patch sewn together into one community,” she claims. “Hunting unites us.”.

Latest York’s Jim Tantillo is a baby boomer and Cornell University professor who teaches environmental ethics and history and the philosophy and morality of hunting. He thinks hunting will likely benefit from the many programs now trying to recruit hunters.

“These programs help us learn which paths are closing and which ones are widening for hunters,” Tantillo indicates. -“Banquet-​based fundraisers and the traditional hunter-education model are probably past their expiration dates. No one should’ve thought they’d work forever.

In a recent development, “This perception that we need to recruit hunters is fresh, but hunting is as old as mankind,” Tantillo continues. “I’m optimistic about hunting because Americans always turn to it as a way to be in the outdoors. Each generation finds its way.”.

#32939. Why the Post-Rut Is Actually the Best Time to Hunt Whitetails

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1561 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Why the Post-Rut Is Actually the Best Time to Hunt Whitetails

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1561 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A few years ago in North Dakota, the entire month of November was warm, with hardly any snow.
  • According to recent reports, plautz hunted hard for weeks without seeing a shooter buck.
  • He didn’t have a tree stand in the area, so he built a little brush blind behind a fallen tree and climbed in for the evening hunt.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A few years ago in North Dakota, the entire month of November was warm, with hardly any snow. “Needless to say, the rut was tough,” says resident bowhunter Derek Plautz.

According to recent reports, plautz hunted hard for weeks without seeing a shooter buck. But in early December, the weather cooled down, snow flew, and the deer started moving. With two days left in the season, Plautz checked his trail camera. Finally, a significant 10-point.

He didn’t have a tree stand in the area, so he built a little brush blind behind a fallen tree and climbed in for the evening hunt. Deer started moving and soon here came Big Ten, bronze antlers glinting in the fading light. When the buck crossed at 30 yards, Derek let fly. The deer kicked like a mule and ran, but it didn’t go far.

“What a great way to end a weird season,” Derek says. “I got to hunt for weeks and then cap it off with a massive buck at the very end!”.

A hunt like Derek’s is becoming the norm rather than the exception across North America. My observation and theory: As temperatures have gotten warmer in late October and November, deer patterns are gradually changing. While does and bucks still breed in mid-November as they always have, they tend to move less in daylight and more during cooler nights.

Sources indicate that in December, it starts to cool down for longer stretches at a time—for days or weeks—and deer start moving with more vigor. Bucks are still rutty, prowling, and looking for the last receptive does of the year.

Each year I hunt in several states in early to mid-December, from Kansas to Oklahoma to Virginia. I am witnessing good to great deer movement, and more late rutting activity than ever before. Such good activity, in fact, that the early post-rut is becoming my most productive time to hunt.

One of the country’s top whitetail hunters agrees. “The weeks following the rut are my favorite time without a doubt,” indicates Midwestern hunter and Outdoor Channel personality Mark Drury. “I see more mature bucks in the post-rut period beginning in early December than at any other time of year. Significant bucks are on the hunt for food and the last does.” Here are some ways to capitalize.

Sources indicate that your strategy from early December through the end of the season should center around the limited food sources that remain for deer. Both does and bucks are run down from the primary rut, and they have to eat. The colder (and snowier) it is in December, the harder deer move to and from the feed, and the more visible they will be in daylight.

You’ll see the most animals if you have access to corn and soybeans, or alfalfa in the West. A patch of standing corn is especially good, as it provides both eats and cover for deer.

Recent findings suggest that in a harvested bean field, scout edges and corners where a few strips of standing beans were missed by harvest. Those will be a magnet for deer. One chilly December evening, I killed one of my biggest Iowa bucks, a 150-inch 10-point, by finding a few leftover beans and taking a ground setup nearby.

Industry observers note that the less gun pressure in and around a field during the hunting season, the more bucks you will see active in daylight. Pray for snow and temps from the teens to mid-30s. A hungry buck might pop out into the crops morning or afternoon, or even briefly in the middle of the day. Bundle up and be out there till the end.

If you hunt significant woods, public or private, miles from the nearest crops, you won’t see nearly as many deer, none some days. To have a chance of punching your buck tag you must find and watch what little food/cover mix is left for a buck: greenery on the edge of a clear-cut or power line, second-growth oak flat near a cedar swamp (maybe a few last nuts and green vines and leaves), grape or honeysuckle thicket…you get the picture. Set a stand or make a blind on the fringe of a pine, cedar, or honeysuckle thicket. Bucks love to travel a green edge in the woods.

A great bonus now is that most of the rut hunters who crowded the woods in November are long gone. A few of them got their bucks; others have lost interest or had to go back to work. Whatever, the reason, there’s less competition. Hunt Monday through Thursday and you’ll have the woods to yourself most days. Bucks move best on days when there’s less pressure, so you’re in great shape.

Read Next: Best Deer Attractants.

In early December, bucks are tired and battered but still running on a last jolt of testosterone. Sometimes a buck makes fresh rubs, so look for them. While bucks generally don’t paw scrapes this late, they often cruise back through creek bottoms and draws where they scraped and rubbed trees a month ago, and hooked up with does. Go back and hunt a stand that you hung in a sign-blazed funnel in early November, you might catch a buck cruising there now.

In a recent development, one cold, still morning in early December, we hiked down into a canyon near the Cimarron River in western Oklahoma and set up on a rocky outcropping. As pink dawn was breaking, my friend Kenny hissed, “Buck in the river.”.

I peeked at the deer, an old fellow with a bull chest, thin hips, and a gray face. I hadn’t looked at his rack, but I knew he was a shooter, at least 5 ½ years old.

“Eight pointer, gnarly,” Kenny remarked while checking him out with his binocular. “He’ll be on our side of the river in a few steps.”.

The buck stepped out of the misty river and disappeared into thick brush. He popped out 250 yards away, and I was fixing to try a poke….

Whack, thwack, whack…grrppp, urrrrppp….

I peeked over at Kenny, who worked his horns and grunter with a gleam in his eye.

The buck turned our way and marched in, back hair bristling and face a white halo in the morning sun. My 140-grain bullet drove him into the sandbar, and he never moved again.

Sources indicate that top whitetail scientist Mickey Hellickson conducted an intensive three-year study in Texas on the movements and behaviors of mature bucks. Part of that research project produced groundbreaking research on antler rattling.

It has been revealed that “The first weeks of the post-rut, when old bucks cruise for the last hot does, are a good time to keep rattling,” says Hellickson. This was the phase when the researchers rattled up the most mature bucks. Of the 29 bucks that responded to their 51 post-rut rattling sequences in the study, 10 were 5 ½ years old or more, and another 10 were 3 ½ to 4 ½.

According to recent reports, don’t give up on rattling too soon. Here are a few things to keep in mind:.

Recent findings suggest that one December day in Kansas, B.J. Clement bowhunted from a ground blind in an old abandoned farmyard where he’d found lots of rubs and scrapes in late October. He saw some young bucks and does, but nothing he wanted to shoot.

Sources indicate that to help his Dad out, his son Todd sneaked into the farmyard the next day and stunk up the joint. “I made several mock scrapes, and laid scent trails all through the area with both doe and dominant buck urine,” Todd says.

A few days later, Todd returned and freshened the scrapes and trails.

On the way to his blind the next day, B.J. found the yard torn up with significant rubs and fresh scrapes.

Around 4 p.m., B.J. spotted a big rack. The buck marched into the farmyard and thrashed a tree. As the deer worked closer, Clement drew his bow when he could and fired a lethal arrow. The rack scored 181 inches.

Read Next: 7 Deer Hunting Tactics You’ve Never Tried Before But Should.

In a recent development, you’ve already read here that in early December adult does that didn’t conceive the first time around cycle into a second estrus. As a bonus, in an agricultural state like Kansas or Iowa where there is good year-round nutrition for deer, a few 7-month-old doe fawns might pop into heat for the first time later on in the month. Whatever the case, these sweet-smelling does can and will draw in bucks.

Back in early November, you probably tried scent lures. But sometimes scent works better the first two weeks of the post-rut. Think about it. During the peak rut, a lot of estrus does mist the woods, and bucks had lots of choices. But now, with only a few estrous does left, the sweet scent of one can bring a buck running to you on a string.

Sources indicate that where legal, lay a doe-in-heat trail into your stand or blind each day. Try doctoring old scrapes with both estrus and tarsal as a challenge to other bucks. Stink up the December woods. The bucks are still out there and moving, and you might get one yet.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Recent findings suggest that the SOLGW Mk 1 made waves last year for rising to the top during a grueling selection process in which one of our Tier One SOCOM units selected to field it. This 11.5-inch carbine chambered in 5.56 NATO demonstrated the best reliability and performance among its peers.

Not surprisingly, it has since become one of the most desirable AR-platform rifles in the commercial market, though many would-be buyers have balked at its hefty price, which is just shy of three grand.

I’ve spent the last several months running the carbine to see whether the juice is worth the squeeze and you can see it in action in the video here.

Recent findings suggest that my experience with the SOLGW Mk1 has been universally positive. I’ve run it in several configurations, in terms of the optics I’ve mounted on it and with respect to the types of muzzle devices I’ve employed. In all cases, the rifle has run without any glitches.

More impressively, my hands-on time with the rifle has shown how it rises to the occasion when called on to perform different tasks.

For instance, in a multi-gun capacity I ran it with a Vortex 1-10 Gen III Razor LPVO and a Holosun 507C in an offset Area 419 mount. Not only did this setup perform well at distance with the LPVO at 10X, but I was able to swiftly transition between far and near targets by rotating the rifle 45 degrees to bring the Holosun’s halo-style reticle rapidly into view.

In another configuration, I ran the rifle with an EOTech holographic sight and 3x magnifier paired with Unity FAST mounts and EOTech’s OGL weapon-mounted laser and IR designator. This setup is much closer to how SOCOM assaulters kit-out the gun. Unsurprisingly, the rifle worked like a charm here too.

It has been revealed that A final thing worth noting is the primary muzzle device I used is the Huxwrx Flow 556 Ti, which is also similar to the military’s selection for the Mk1. The rifle has a non-adjustable gas block that balances extremely well with this suppressor, and cuts the gas going back into the shooter’s face to basically zero.

In conjunction with the bolt-carrier group and buffer system, the gas block and suppressor, enhance the SOLGW Mk1’s reliability and soften the recoil impulse in a way that makes the rifle very easy to control.

Reports from the operators who field the rifle indicate that its lethality, performance and reliability are outstanding.

Based on all this, it looks like the Mk 1 delivers in a way that justifies its price, and then some.
