The Ephemeral Global Climbing School Amid China’s Epic Limestone

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (915 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that on October 22, hundreds of climbers of all skill levels descended upon Yangshuo, China, for the long-awaited  2026 Arc’teryx Climb Academy.
  • It has been revealed that the Arc’teryx Climb Academy is a roving international climbing school—and one that offers some of the most advanced mountain education in the world.
  • While there are tons of events in the climbing universe, Arc’teryx Climb Academies stand out for just how seamlessly they’re run and how well integrated they are into the local community.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that on October 22, hundreds of climbers of all skill levels descended upon Yangshuo, China, for the long-awaited  2026 Arc’teryx Climb Academy. Participants say the remarkable thing about the weekend wasn’t just the climbing or even the upcoming skills they learned—it was the magic of the remote, fantastical landscape, and the opportunity to connect with people across cultures and continents.

It has been revealed that the Arc’teryx Climb Academy is a roving international climbing school—and one that offers some of the most advanced mountain education in the world. Since 2007, academies have been held in global climbing epicenters like Squamish, Chamonix, and Mammoth Lakes. Some focus on climbing while others offer backcountry or freeride skiing education. Each installment is a complex undertaking, bringing together world-class guides and athletes to pass on their knowledge in a highly efficient, structured format. Dozens of courses—ranging from alpine overnights to big wall workshops to mental resilience clinics—are designed to meet participants where they’re at. At each academy, students can learn skills from scratch, drill fundamentals, or significantly boost their skills, even within just a few days of instruction.

While there are tons of events in the climbing universe, Arc’teryx Climb Academies stand out for just how seamlessly they’re run and how well integrated they are into the local community. Unlike some climbing festivals, which tend to put more emphasis on socialization than education, Arc’teryx has figured out how to nail both without compromising either. All day long, participants of every skill level take hands-on courses on some of the best rock in the world, each one packed with pro-level hacks, technique drills, and actionable tips for continuing your education after the trip ends. Each evening, a five-star lineup of films, speakers, music, and parties makes it impossible to tear yourself away. Every chapter of the event buoys you along to the next. The weekend passes in a flash. And you return home with more phone numbers, more latest climbing partners, and more stoke than you could have imagined possible.

In 2023, the series brought this special blend of inspiration and education to the limestone cliffs of Yangshuo, China—and the event was a runaway hit. In 2024, the Academy returned with even more courses crafted specifically for the local community, including rescue and evacuation clinics tailored to China’s uniquely rocky landscapes. The 2026 Academy further expanded the course menu, offering beginner trad clinics, bolting workshops, and masterclasses in big wall climbing. Over four days, hundreds of climbers participated in 37 clinics at more than a dozen crags across the stunning Guangxi region. It was the region’s biggest Arc’teryx Climb Academy yet.

While many of the Academy’s participants came specifically to experience Yangshuo’s world-renowned karst spires, the crags aren’t just a backdrop here; they’re the heart of a thriving and longstanding community of climbers, route developers, and outdoor businesses. Since international climbers first arrived in the late 1980s, the zone has grown to nearly 2,000 routes across 74 crags on world-class limestone.

“Yangshuo means a lot to me,” says Peng Zhou, renowned Chinese mountaineer and Arc’teryx athlete. “I completed both my first 5.12 and 5.14 routes here, and it has left me with many wonderful memories.” He loves getting an opportunity to share this place with newcomers; it’s one of the reasons he comes back to teach year after year.

Given Yangshuo’s robust existing climbing scene, the event offers more cultural exchange than top-down discourse. Here, international visitors learn just as much from their Chinese counterparts as locals learn from the global pros.

It has been revealed that take it from Arc’teryx athlete Quentin Roberts. This year, he taught his third Yangshuo Big Wall Climbing clinic in a row. Each time, he’s astonished by how much the climbing community has grown since his last visit. “Every year I feel like I have had to level up to meet the growing ambitions and skills of the participants,” he indicates. “It’s exciting to see how eager everyone is.”.

But for Roberts, the best part about climbing in China is the profound and indescribable warmth of the Yangshuo community.

It has been revealed that “We always have a major, Chinese-style, round-table dinner with all the instructors before the event,” he says. It’s an evening filled with laughter between old friends. Jokes and stories fly across the table like sparks, and Roberts leaves feeling filled up at a soul level. “Many of the people in that room are at the forefront of climbing in China. It’s special to feel that sense of family, and to see the passion everyone has for what they’re doing.”.

It’s that sense of connection that makes the Yangshuo event—and the other installments of the Arc’teryx Climb Academy—so invaluable.

Sources indicate that “Coming to China over the years and connecting with people through climbing has really reinforced something I believe deeply: we are all more similar than we are different,” says Roberts. “Climbing has an incredible ability to bring people together. Sharing a rope, trusting one another, sharing our experiences—those connections transcend language and culture.”.

Arc’teryx is a Canadian organization based in the Coast Mountains. Our design process is connected to the real world, focused on delivering unrivaled durability and performance in extreme conditions. Our products are distributed through over 160 branded stores and more than 2,400 retail locations worldwide. We are problem solvers, evolving and searching for a better way to deliver resolved, minimalist designs. Good design that matters makes lives better.

#32872. Rodents Keep Destroying Your Hiking Gear? Here’s How to Keep It Safe

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (847 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

Rodents Keep Destroying Your Hiking Gear? Here’s How to Keep It Safe

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (847 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A chipmunk chews its way into a hiker's backpack.
  • Sources indicate that one of my favorite parts of being outdoors is the wildlife, and that includes rodents.
  • Recent findings suggest that this is a common occurrence in the backcountry, whether you’re hiking a populated trail or posted up at some far-flung campsite.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A chipmunk chews its way into a hiker's backpack. (Photo: Stanislav Sablin/Getty Images).

Sources indicate that one of my favorite parts of being outdoors is the wildlife, and that includes rodents. I love watching squirrels chase each other around tree trunks, and I may or may not have had a “pet” chipmunk in one of my cabins during a horseback guiding season. I talk to marmots when I’m alone, and hearing the chirp of a pika makes my day. But I draw the line at the little buggers crawling over my face in a shelter, chewing through my trekking pole straps, or getting into my food bag.

Recent findings suggest that this is a common occurrence in the backcountry, whether you’re hiking a populated trail or posted up at some far-flung campsite. While no one I know has a perfect mouse-proofing strategy, here are a few tips and tricks to help keep rodents at bay and protect your pack pockets, straps, and food.

Recent findings suggest that the most vulnerable parts of your gear are the deliciously salty pack straps, trekking pole straps, and pockets where you’ve forgotten you left food. While keeping your straps clean is easier said than done after days of sweaty hiking, reducing the tantalizing salty odors will work wonders in keeping sodium-fiending rodents away. If you can, dunk your straps in running water a few times throughout the day, and especially at night when you get to camp.

You can also drip a few drops of hand sanitizer onto trekking pole straps to make them less appealing, and tucking a dryer sheet into salty pockets or around hammock straps can also work as a rodent deterrent. Finally, always stash your trekking poles upright in the ground to keep the straps less accessible.

The bear hang is a time-honored backcountry art form, but if you’ve ever seen an acrobatic mouse shimmy down the rope and land a perfect 10 on your backpack, you know this protective measure doesn’t translate perfectly to rodent-proofing. The solution, as many of us have seen in high-traffic trail shelters, is something I call the Mouse Swing. This is simply your standard piece of paracord or bear-hang rope, but with a barrier tied in the middle.

It has been revealed that I’ve used everything from a (clean!!) tuna can to a quart-size yogurt container lid. Punch a hole in the can or plastic lid, run your string through the hole with knots to secure it in place, and you’ll have a lightweight, highly functional barrier between your pack and the string. Make sure your bag is a few feet above the ground or shelter floor to prevent high jumpers from making the leap.

Along with salty straps, mice, rats, and squirrels are highly attracted to food smells. The worst pocket destruction I encountered was when I carefully hung my pack from the rafters of a shelter but forgot to remove the remains of an energy bar from the pocket, and an industrious mouse chewed right through the material. Don’t forget to check your pockets for lip balm, energy gels, or the remains of your lunchtime protein bar.

In a recent development, while a hard-sided bear canister is the best protection against animals getting into your food supply, I prefer not to carry the bulky, heavy contraption unless it’s required in the area. The next best thing is the Ursack Allmitey, a heavy-duty food bag made from Spectra, a specialized material with one of the highest strength-to-weight ratios out there. Once tied properly closed, it’s next to impossible for critters to chew through or squeeze through the opening. If you’re in an area where rodents are the only concern, you can size down in bulk to the Ursack Minor, a Kevlar bag that isn’t tough enough to stand up to bears, but can keep smaller toothy critters at bay.

I’ve also used RatSacks for food drops in the desert. They’re heavier than the Ursack Minor, but have proven virtually indestructible against desert rodents, and some national parks like Canyonlands lend them out for free. These are made from stainless steel mesh with a heavy-duty Velcro closure at the top, and while they aren’t bearproof, I’ve never had a smaller animal bust through the dense metal mesh.

Sources indicate that finally, if scent control is your primary priority, you can further streamline your gear with LokSak OPSAK bags. These won’t prevent sharp little teeth from chewing through them, but the polyethylene material and secure zip tops are completely odorproof and can keep curious squirrels and chipmunks from testing them in the first place.

In a recent development, I hesitate to write this since it’s such a Big If, but if you’re camping somewhere that the risk of running into a bear is zero, you can bring smelly items into your tent. This isn’t foolproof—you run a risk of an unusually bold mouse chewing into your tent—but by and large, most small rodents will be deterred by your massive sleeping form and won’t bother trying to break in.

That’s because my Smartwool half-zip is perfect for just about every brisk-weather activity.

Made from Smartwool’s reclaimed Merino wool scraps blended with recycled polyester, with a 100-percent recycled polyester overlay, the entire top is sourced from rescued material. And, important for wearers like me who rarely take it off, the material offers that classic no-stink wool perk. After months of regular washes, I haven’t noticed any pilling, either.

Right now, my number-one fleece is on sale for 25 percent off at Backcountry, marking down the price from $160 to $120.

The high neck is long enough to protect against cold mountain gusts but not so high that it rubs my chin too much. It’s also extra wide, so it doesn’t feel constricting as some turtlenecks do.

According to recent reports, in fact, the entire cut feels roomy in the best way. The Second Cut is large enough to fit more than just a base layer under it for those extra cold mornings. Plus, its boxy fit is Gen-Z cool without making this millennial feel like she’s trying too hard.

I own the charcoal color, which matches any pair of pants in my closet—jeans, colorful track pants, or even workout leggings. And it’s a good thing this fleece so versatile, because at this point, it’s basically attached to my body.

The Second Cut got me through the fall, and now, as snow starts to dust the peaks near my home, I know I’ll keep wearing it: cross-country skiing with my family, under a shell to skin up the local ski hill, and for every errand and outdoor mission in between.

Two Hikers Rescued from Wet Snow and Freezing Temperatures Deep in the White Mountains

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (361 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A view west from Mount Bond in New Hampshire's Pemigewasset Wilderness.
  • Two hikers were rescued on Saturday near the summit of 4,698-foot Mount Bond in New Hampshire’s Pemigewasset Wilderness after they encountered deep, wet snow and freezing temperatures along their hike.
  • Hikers typically climb Mount Bond via one of two routes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A view west from Mount Bond in New Hampshire's Pemigewasset Wilderness. (Photo: MikeCherim / Getty Images).

Two hikers were rescued on Saturday near the summit of 4,698-foot Mount Bond in New Hampshire’s Pemigewasset Wilderness after they encountered deep, wet snow and freezing temperatures along their hike.

Hikers typically climb Mount Bond via one of two routes. The first involves taking the Lincoln Woods Trail, which is generally a 19.9 mile round-trip hike with 3,959 feet of elevation gain and currently partially closed. The second route takes hikers up the Zealand Trail, covering 19 miles and up to 4,947 feet of elevation gain.

While it isn’t clear which route the duo took to Mount Bond, 23-year-old Ethan Fena and 21-year-old Matthew Nakota were more than 10 miles into their hike near the summit when they encountered winter trail conditions.

Although they’d packed lights, food, and water, New Hampshire Fish and Game (NHFG) said the pair had hiked the route without overnight and winter equipment, leaving them struggling to warm themselves. By the time the duo called for help, they’d assembled a makeshift shelter in an attempt to warm up and allow their gear to dry.

Industry observers note that NHFG said that conservation officers initiated a rescue operation, using ATVs to transport volunteers with the Pemi Valley Search and Rescue Team to the area. Rescuers reached the pair at about 11:45 p.m., and helped them begin the descent back to the trailhead. The whole party arrived safely at the parking lot at about 2 a.m. on Sunday, November 15th.

In the wake of the incident, Upcoming Hampshire Fish and Game officials reminded hikers to consider factors like shortened daylight hours and failing temperatures before heading into the mountains.

This incident comes just 11 days after two 18-year-olds became stranded on Mount Washington after getting caught on the peak without headlamps. The two hikers reached the Lakes of the Clouds AMC Hut and discovered that it had been closed for the season when they realized they needed help. The group used an emergency shelter located at the hut until rescuers reached the hikers and helped them descend the mountain.

Nobody knows this better than skiers and snowboarders. You want goggles that give you unparalleled visibility and comfort that can also vibe with the look of your kit.

ROKA hits that trifecta with their two newly introduced models, the Niseko and the Bridger. They deliver crisp clarity and stylish comfort for all kinds of riders and riding conditions. See the difference these goggles can make on the mountain.

It has been revealed that elite performance, precision engineering, and sleek design are all rolled up into one lightweight package in these built-for-anything googles. Industry observers note that one of our top mountaineering boots of the year, the G-Summit climbing boot accomplishes a small but significant miracle: It’s a double boot that climbs like a single boot. #32859. Editor’s Letter: Why Do Hard Things Outside? Our Outsiders of the Year Answer

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (746 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

Editor’s Letter: Why Do Hard Things Outside? Our Outsiders of the Year Answer

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (746 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anyone who does hard things outside has heard it.
  • It has been revealed that this year Alex Honnold free soloed a 1,667-foot skyscraper live on Netflix, after being explained away as a brain-scan curiosity for two decades.
  • Industry observers note that jim Morrison and his partner Hilaree Nelson shared a dream no one had pulled off: to climb Everest’s North Face and ski it back down.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anyone who does hard things outside has heard it. Why climb a mountain that’s already been climbed? Why run 253 miles across a desert? To test the limits of human potential is the tidy answer. The real one, as our Outsiders of the Year show, shifts like snow on a massive face: it’s different for everyone, and never quite the same twice.

It has been revealed that this year Alex Honnold free soloed a 1,667-foot skyscraper live on Netflix, after being explained away as a brain-scan curiosity for two decades. Now 40, with two preschoolers, he fits climbing in where he can. Some days that means getting up at 2 a.m. to climb a thousand-foot granite wall to still make it home for dinner. Why bother? “In some ways, climbing is my only opportunity to feel like I’m good at something,” he tells Features Editor Frederick Dreier. Any parent who has squeezed in a run between school pickups knows the feeling.

Industry observers note that jim Morrison and his partner Hilaree Nelson shared a dream no one had pulled off: to climb Everest’s North Face and ski it back down. In 2022, Nelson died on Manaslu, and Morrison swore off the mountains. Then his dog started pulling him back up the trail, a little higher every day. In 2025, with Jimmy Chin filming beside him for Everest: The Other Side, Morrison skied 9,000 feet off the top of the world. At the bottom, he screamed, “That one’s for you, Hil.”.

Sources indicate that not everyone on Everest gets to ask why. Sherpas still take the biggest risks so others can reach the top. This spring, Hillary Dawa Sherpa, a 57-year-old cook, was pushed toward the summit when his outfitter came up a guide short. Descending with eight empty oxygen bottles (lose one and he’d be docked $250), he ran out of air and was assumed dead. Six days later, he dragged himself out of the Khumbu Icefall on a broken leg. He’d only gone because someone else’s summit needed him.

Sources indicate that for Christina Koch, the answer was bigger than herself. In April, she flew around the moon on Artemis II under a patch her crew designed so “A II” read as “all.” When she heard the whole planet was watching, she cried, and in zero gravity, the tears had nowhere to fall.

Sources indicate that rachel Entrekin’s answer is the hardest-won of all. As a teenager, she nearly didn’t survive. In treatment for an eating disorder, she learned a rule she still runs by: do the very thing you least want to do. This year she ran 253 miles across Arizona and became the first woman to win the Cocodona outright. “Running helps me practice who I want to be when things get tough,” she indicates.

Adventure has never had a bigger audience. Millions watched Honnold’s climb in real time, and this fall, Everest is all over movie screens. Almost none of those viewers will ski Everest or solo a skyscraper. But every one of those moments sends someone out the door to find their own answer. Ask anyone at a trailhead on a Sunday morning why they came: to do something hard, to carry someone with them, to feel small in front of something vast, to become who they want to be.

According to recent reports, the Northflag gets that the best travel gear does its job without asking for attention. The name nods to the 1950s British North Greenland Expedition, where the explorers wore Tudors, but its smartest feature is modern: a true GMT, so you can set local time the moment you land and still know the time back home. It’ll keep running for almost three days after you take it off, and it looks as right at a trailhead as at the dinner table.

Every trip has a weather day, and this is the shoe I pack for it. The Gore-Tex membrane keeps my feet dry, and the gravel-tuned outsole and bouncy foam handle pavement and light trail equally well. I’ve logged about 50 miles of Italy’s Via Francigena in it, both hiking and running, and ran all over London and Paris. Best part: it doesn’t look ridiculous with civilian clothes. One shoe, three jobs, and more room in my carry-on.

#32855. This 30-Mile-Long Canyonlands Art Gallery Might Be Utah’s Best Backpacking Trip

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1290 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

This 30-Mile-Long Canyonlands Art Gallery Might Be Utah’s Best Backpacking Trip

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1290 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when you think of ancient rock art, what comes to mind?
  • But there’s one canyon in Utah that blows those expectations out of the water.
  • Hidden deep inside Canyonlands National Park, Salt Creek Canyon holds some of the most impressive pictographs I’ve ever seen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when you think of ancient rock art, what comes to mind? Handprints? Stick figures? Maybe a long-limbed man holding something? For the most part, you’d be right. The petroglyphs and pictographs of the southwest are beautiful, but they aren’t known for their intricate details.

But there’s one canyon in Utah that blows those expectations out of the water.

Hidden deep inside Canyonlands National Park, Salt Creek Canyon holds some of the most impressive pictographs I’ve ever seen. Enormous human figures, elaborate patterns, and colorful paintings that have survived for hundreds of years. It’s an open-air art museum, and one that’s slowly weathering away.

According to recent reports, and the museum doesn’t stop at rock art. There are Ancestral Puebloan granaries, settlers’ abandoned ranch buildings, and reminders of the conservationists who helped protect this landscape.

A walk through Salt Creek Canyon is a walk through history. Over two days and more than 30 miles, it became one of my biggest backpacking surprises of the year.

Trail: Salt Creek Trail + Angel Arch Detour Start: Cathedral Butte / Salt Creek Canyon Trailhead Finish: Cave Spring / Salt Creek Gate Distance: 30.78 miles (my GPS; mapped distance may differ) Elevation gain: 1,054 feet (my GPS) Type: Point-to-point, vehicle shuttle required Permits: Required for overnight trips Highlight: The All American Man pictograph.

The trail begins high in the contested Bears Ears National Monument, in the shadow of Cathedral Butte. Typically, this is the sort of view you’d have to earn after hours of climbing. Instead, you start at the highest point, looking down into a canyon that stretches toward the horizon.

It’s mostly downhill from here, but don’t mistake that for easy. Thirty miles with a loaded backpack is still 30 miles, especially when much of it is through deep sand.

About two miles in, we crossed into Canyonlands National Park. My Gaia GPS map was littered with waypoints and “Don’t miss!” markers, the first of which were Kirk Spring and Kirk’s Cabin.

In an otherwise dusty landscape of sagebrush and juniper, a little oasis appeared. Reeds, cottonwoods, and bright green vegetation surrounded a small spring. We filtered some water and continued toward the cabin, an 1890s-era log home with a fieldstone chimney.

Sources indicate that outside the weathered log structure sat the wheels and axles of an old wagon. Inside, bear traps and antlers hung on the walls. It looked like something out of a history museum, only sandier, dustier, and considerably more authentic.

This was our first introduction to one of Salt Creek’s defining qualities: Layers of human history occupy nearly every corner of the canyon.

Long before ranchers arrived, Indigenous people—Ancestral Puebloans and Fremont, then Ute, Paiute, and Diné—lived, hunted, and farmed here. Later came European explorers, conservationists, and eventually backpackers like us. Different people, different centuries, but all drawn to the same remarkable place.

One of the biggest reasons was water. Unlike much of Canyonlands, Salt Creek supports a surprisingly lush corridor of vegetation, even in a dry year. We encountered several places to filter water, although sources became scarcer farther down the canyon. (Water here is seasonal and never guaranteed, so come prepared to carry plenty.).

Industry observers note that around mile six, a small spur trail led us beneath a sandstone overhang. Tucked into the alcove were several stone structures, likely granaries used by Ancestral Puebloan people to store their harvests. Just below them, dark-green vines spilled across the sand. They looked like squash plants, still thriving in the shadow of structures built centuries ago.

I’d come to Salt Creek expecting incredible rock art, but nothing prepared me for what we found around mile eight: The All American Man.

High inside a sandstone alcove stands a human-like figure, nearly life-size, painted in striking blue, white, and red. He appears to wear white boots, an elaborate headdress, and something resembling an American flag across his body.

Recent findings suggest that for decades, the figure’s unusual appearance led some to question whether it was even ancient. Radiocarbon testing eventually confirmed its authenticity, suggesting it dates to around the 14th century. Standing below it, I found the whole thing almost impossible to believe. (Do yourself a favor: If you proposal on hiking Salt Creek, don’t look up pictures of the All American Man beforehand. Let it surprise you.).

It has been revealed that not far beyond, we encountered another extraordinary panel near Four Faces Spring. Four enormous, intricately patterned faces stared out from beneath a sandstone alcove. Remnants of stone structures sat beneath them.

Who were these figures? Were they people, spirits, or something else entirely?

Their exact meaning remains uncertain, but the artwork survives, part of a cultural history that remains key to Indigenous communities today.

The farther we walked, the more the canyon changed.

Towering sandstone walls closed in around us. Willows, reeds, and cottonwoods transformed the dusty trail into something resembling a jungle. Small streams appeared beneath the vegetation.

It has been revealed that unfortunately, so did the mosquitoes. I’ve spent a lot of time hiking through the desert, but I’ve never encountered so many of the little suckers.

According to recent reports, after miles of hiking, a soft rain finally brought some relief. A rainbow appeared against the red canyon walls just as we approached SC4, our reserved campsite for the evening.

Sources indicate that at roughly mile 12, SC4 is the last of the four designated Salt Creek campsites when traveling north. It wasn’t quite halfway through our route, which meant we had an even longer second day ahead.

According to recent reports, the next morning, we packed up and headed toward another of the canyon’s great attractions. Several miles off the main trail, at the end of a remote side canyon, stood Angel Arch.

Arches National Park may be famous for its sandstone formations, but Angel Arch can hold its own against just about anything you’ll find there.

Its massive sandstone opening rises roughly 135 feet high, with an unusual formation beside it resembling an angel leaning forward with folded wings. It’s an incredible sight, made even more impressive by the effort required to reach it. We were the only people there. In fact, we were the only hikers on the entire trail: We hadn’t seen a single other person or group. The detour added several miles to an already long day, but I’d do it again without hesitation.

Back on the main route, one more archaeological treasure awaited us: the Flying Carpet Panel. Like the All American Man and Four Faces, the artwork was enormous, with figures and intricate designs spread across the sandstone.

Then came the final miles. The beautiful canyon trail eventually gave way to a sandy four-wheel-drive road, where every step seemed to require twice the effort. After nearly 30 miles, walking through deep sand was just about the last thing my legs wanted to do.

Eventually, we reached a gate, a paved road, and the end of our journey.

As spectacular as the scenery was, what I’ll remember most about Salt Creek isn’t the canyon itself. It’s the people who called it home.

For centuries, Ancestral Puebloan communities farmed along the creek, stored food in cliffside granaries, and created artwork that still watches over the canyon today. Walking past these places, I couldn’t help thinking about how many people had traveled this same canyon before us. How many had looked up at those same cliffs, collected water from those same springs, or sheltered beneath those sandstone overhangs?

According to recent reports, we spent two days here, carrying everything we needed on our backs. For others, this canyon was home. For a brief moment, we got to be part of its story too.

Latest Update: Lawmakers Move to Ban AI Data Centers on National Forests and Federal Land

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Meta's 2.4-million-square-foot data center in Eagle Mountain, Utah.
  • There’s a upcoming plan in Washington to prohibit the construction of AI data centers on public lands.
  • On November 11, Oregon Representative Maxine Dexter introduced the Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act, which would ban newly introduced data centers on national forests and lands managed by the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meta's 2.4-million-square-foot data center in Eagle Mountain, Utah. A newly introduced bill introduced in Congress would prohibit construction of data centers on federally managed public lands. (Photo: George Frey/Getty).

There’s a upcoming plan in Washington to prohibit the construction of AI data centers on public lands.

On November 11, Oregon Representative Maxine Dexter introduced the Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act, which would ban newly introduced data centers on national forests and lands managed by the U.S. Department of the Interior.

The legislation, backed by 13 Democratic cosponsors, would also require federal land sold or transferred to return to government ownership if used for a data center without congressional authorization.

According to recent reports, “Public lands belong in public hands and Oregonians must have a say before the federal government hands over millions of acres of public land managed by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) for data centers,” Dexter stated in a November 11 press release. “These treasured lands are where people hunt, fish, hike and graze livestock. They are where wildlife habitat and our critical watersheds are protected. My bill keeps these lands safe from data centers now, and for the generations who come after us.”.

The bill arrived just one day after the Interior Department published its strategic initiative for fiscal years 2026 through 2030, which outlines proposals to sell federal land to states, local governments, and tribes, while expanding energy and infrastructure development to support growing demand from data centers.

The plan drew criticism from public lands advocates, including Tracy Stone-Manning, who led the BLM under President Joe Biden and now serves as president of the Wilderness Society.

Recent findings suggest that “They want to sell it off for data centers. They want to sell it off to oil and gas companies,” Stone-Manning mentioned in a November 14 NPR interview. “They want to sell it off because they don’t like the idea of the American public owning these lands.”.

According to recent reports, throughout 2026 the Trump Administration has sought to build data centers on public lands. According to a November 6 investigation from ProPublica, the BLM is reviewing permit applications for approximately 15 data centers and 17 related infrastructure projects across six Western states. In its five-year strategic plan for public lands management, the DOI claims it will find ways to address “the growing demand from Super Intelligence data centers.”.

Industry observers note that in July, Outside reported that the BLM approved plans for an 86-acre AI data center roughly ten miles from Lake Mead National Recreation Area in Nevada. An Interior Department appeals board has since paused the project for further review, ProPublica reported.

In a recent development, the rise of artificial intelligence and cloud-based computing has accelerated the need for these centers. But data centers can place significant demands on electricity and water supplies, and throughout 2026, the centers have grown unpopular with voters. A September report by Pew Research found that 54 percent of Americans found data centers to be bad for the environment, up from just 39 percent in January.

Sources indicate that more municipalities have passed moratoriums on the construction of the data centers, leading officials to look to rural or backcountry settings for them. But the construction of the centers can disrupt wildlife habitat and restrict public access to formerly open land, according to the November 11 release.

Industry observers note that “Data centers have no place on public lands,” noted Randi Spivak of the nonprofit group Center for Biological Diversity in a release. “They’re water-guzzling, pollution-spewing facilities that turn lands meant for wildlife and recreation into corporate industrial sites.”.

More recently, an interactive map covered by Outside identified at least 14 proposed data centers within ten miles of national park boundaries.

Dexter’s legislation has been referred to the House Natural Resources and Agriculture committees. The bill has no Republican cosponsors, and a similar measure introduced by Oregon Senator Ron Wyden was blocked by Republican Senator Rand Paul in September. No fresh restrictions have taken effect.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy of Michael Hall).

Audrie Pelosi found climbing after moving to Baraboo, Wisconsin. It wasn’t long before the quartzite cliffs of Devil’s Lake became a cornerstone of her life. She climbed there, worked there, and eventually became its steward as a guide with Apex Adventure Alliance (AAA), bringing fresh climbers to the same arena in which she’d begun.

In a recent development, “She was an exceptional climbing guide and human being,” Apex Adventure Alliance wrote in a statement to Outside. “She was a force in our community and at our guide service. We all will miss her dearly.”.

Originally from Duluth, Minnesota, Pelosi had long structured her life around her various passions: snowboarding, cycling, and, eventually, an all-encompassing love of climbing and the community around it. Her passion radiated outwards: she volunteered locally and, in 2026, ran for a Wisconsin Climbers Association board seat, hoping to become more involved in stewardship and community building. “I believe in showing up, doing the work, and listening to the community,” Pelosi wrote in her candidate statement.

It has been revealed that “With her friends and community, Audrie was so generous,” noted Garrett Hopkins, AAA’s owner. “That generosity flowed into her climbing, biking, and snowboarding too. When I was living on the road, I knew her couch was always open for a spot to crash if my van was being repaired. She spent countless hours with young climbers in an effort to elevate the safety of the next generation coming up.”.

According to recent reports, pelosi met her husband, Jimmy “The Fox” Robinson, at a snowboard event at Welch Village, Minnesota, and in 2023 the two married atop Mount Bohemia (1,465ft) on Lake Superior. From then on, Pelosi had the nickname “Mrs. The Fox.” One of her friends, Anastasia Exterovich, set up a GoFundMe to raise money for Pelosi’s family in the wake of her passing. She called the pair the “raddest couple.”.

“In my last conversation with Audrie, she joked about selling her handmade bike chain link earrings to anyone who wanted them for ‘free.99,’” Exterovich wrote. “It was such a simple statement made in passing, but it perfectly encapsulated who she was as a person. Even when she didn’t have much, she would give things away freely without hesitation, whether that was earrings, a smile, a laugh, a quick bike tune-up, or a belay.”.

It has been revealed that pelosi passed on May 30, 2026 working as a guide at  Devil’s Lake State Park, teaching a climbing course near the park’s East Bluff. During the course, Pelosi fell from the bluff and suffered fatal injuries. She is survived by her husband, her family, and the broader climbing community in Wisconsin.

6 Forgotten Backpacking Skills Every Hiker Should Master

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1249 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here at Backpacker, we respect old-school cool.
  • Calling the following six low-tech, high-technique skills “lost” might be a stretch—they definitely still have their fans, and every Backpacker editor has used them at least a few times.
  • In a recent development, whether they’re tying their tent’s guylines or their shoelaces, too many backpackers reach for the same overhand knot; it mostly works, but it lacks a certain… elegance?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Westend61/Getty Images).

Here at Backpacker, we respect old-school cool. It’s not that we’re Luddites or avoid newly introduced ways of doing things—from lightweight internal-frame backpacks to gourmet freeze-dried meals, there’s no denying that most modern backpacking developments have made our experiences better. But there’s something about seeing a hiking buddy solve a problem with a retro skill that we admire. It demonstrates knowledge, competence, and the kind of self-reliance that every backpacker secretly aspires to.

Calling the following six low-tech, high-technique skills “lost” might be a stretch—they definitely still have their fans, and every Backpacker editor has used them at least a few times. But they aren’t part of the average beginner hiker’s repertoire anymore, and many hikers go their whole careers without using them. Start practicing them now to level up your skills for next season.

In a recent development, whether they’re tying their tent’s guylines or their shoelaces, too many backpackers reach for the same overhand knot; it mostly works, but it lacks a certain… elegance? While you don’t need a Boy Scout’s skill at knotcraft to go backpacking, learning to use the right knot for each job will help you finish camp setup rapidly and break it down without spending ten minutes coaxing apart the granny knot you’ve welded into your cord. Here are a couple to get you started (check out our guide to the 5 Essential Backpacking Knots for videos and in-depth descriptions):.

Slippery Backpacker’s Hitch: Good for hanging bear bags or rigging ridgelines for tarps, and comes undone with a pull. Wrap the rope at least three times around a tree or post, then tuck a bight of the loose end under the last loop.

Industry observers note that bowline Knot: A bombproof method for creating a strong loop. Make a loop in the rope; take the loose end and bring it up through the loop, around the rope, and back down through the loop. (You may or may not catch those of us who learned in school muttering “rabbit comes out of the hole, goes around the tree, and goes back in the hole” while we tie it.) Finish with an overhand and a half-hitch.

Sheet Bend: Need to attach two lengths of cord of different diameters? Create a bight with the bigger cord; bring the end of the thinner cord up through, wrap it around the back of the bight, and run it through the loop it creates.

Lightweight, direct-from-manufacturer shelters and quilts mean that there’s little practical reason to sew your own kit nowadays. However, for those who do like to get handy, the proliferation of patterns for sale and online tutorials on places like YouTube means that it’s never been easier to join the MYOG community. Plus, much like growing your own vegetables, sewing a few pieces yourself will give you a latest appreciation for the ingenuity and labor that goes into making your gear.

In a recent development, instead of jumping straight into the deep end with a high-investment piece like a tent or quilt, start small: A “ditty bag” is perfect for holding small items or replacing a torn or lost stuff sack. See our step-by-step instructions from our Spring 1973 issue, which is easy to sew without a machine. All you’ll need is ¾-yard of ripstop nylon, 30 inches of cord, needles, and thread.

Recent findings suggest that camp baking is everything modern backpacking meals aren’t: messy, ingredient-heavy, and slow. But there’s a kind of magic in coaxing a loaf of bread or a pizza into existence in the middle of the woods. It may not be an efficient way to eat, but it’s a rewarding skill, and as a party trick, guaranteed to impress your backcountry partners.

The most traditional method is to bake in a Dutch oven using campfire. One easier and lighter way to start: Make a cupcake on your camp stove, which is satisfying and near-foolproof. You’ll need a single-wall steel or titanium mug, a pot substantial enough to fit it inside, and a lid, plate, or aluminum foil to cover it. Empty a packet of microwaveable cake mix into the mug, add three tablespoons of water, and stir. Drop three small rocks into the bottom of your pot, balance the mug on top of them, and add enough water to the pot that it reaches the level of the cake mix. (If the mug starts to float, you’ve added too much.) Cover and simmer for 20 minutes, then enjoy straight out of the mug. Bonus: also works with pancake mix.

Industry observers note that even if most hikers have moved on to screened-in lightweight tents, flat tarps still have dedicated fans. Besides the unbeatably low weight, there’s a simplicity to making a shelter from a rectangle of fabric that we can still appreciate. (Looking for your first? Borah’s Silpoly Solo Tarps are solid, and at less than $90, eminently affordable.).

There are innumerable ways to pitch a tarp, but the simple plow point shelter is a good place to start. Stake out three corners of your tarp, then use one of your trekking poles to raise the fourth, tensioning it with a guyline. (Pro tip: The first time you do this will take some trial and error to get a good pitch, so give yourself extra time in camp.) For extra dirtbag points, use a 9 x 10 scrap of Tyvek instead; create the guy-out points by pinching a bit of the material around a smooth pebble and tying off the base with a cord.

Whittling is one of those camp pastimes that’s largely fallen by the wayside—but to be fair, today’s backpackers are less likely than their predecessors to spend a lot of time kicking around camp. Still, basic knife skills are good to have in your pocket—you never know when you may need to carve a replacement for a snapped stake or shave tinder to build a fire—and whittling is a good, low-stakes way to practice those skills.

In a recent development, carving a spoon is an easy project (and a useful one, if you forget your own utensil). Split a piece of deadfall, preferably still green. Carve your spoon’s outline, then hollow out the bowl. (You may have an easier time carving a shovel-shaped bowl than a traditional round one with a typical straight pocketknife.).

Once upon a time, planning a route for our magazine meant taking a walk down to the small library of guidebooks and topo maps we kept in the office and poring through them until we found the trail we were looking for. The world has changed since then—today’s mapping tools are quick and reliable for assembling a blueprint—but sketching out a trip the old-school way is still a good exercise for your brain. Plus, it can help prevent the kind of careless line-following that regularly gets hikers into trouble.

Picking up an expert-written guidebook for an area you proposal on visiting regularly is always a good investment. Otherwise, the public library is your friend: Your local branch likely stocks an array of up-to-date guides, or can obtain them for you via interlibrary loan. Instead of carrying the whole thing, xerox the pages you need and jot points of interest and notes right on the copies. Pair with a compass and a current topo map (your library may stock those, too), and don’t forget to check with rangers or local hikers for the latest beta before you set out.

Giant November Waves Threaten Surfers, Swimmers, and Spectators Along California’s Coast

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (791 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that powerful waves crash against Pacifica Pier in Pacifica, California, on November 14, 2026, as large Pacific swells batter the state's coastline.
  • Lifeguards along California’s coast have had their hands full over the past several days, as powerful Pacific swells stranded surfers, swept a teenager photographing the waves off rocks, and even overturned a rescue jet ski during an operation near Santa Cruz.
  • In San Diego alone, lifeguards conducted 175 water rescues between November 9 and 16, according to San Diego Fire-Rescue figures reported by FOX 5/KUSI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that powerful waves crash against Pacifica Pier in Pacifica, California, on November 14, 2026, as large Pacific swells batter the state's coastline. (Photo: Stephen Lam/San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images).

Lifeguards along California’s coast have had their hands full over the past several days, as powerful Pacific swells stranded surfers, swept a teenager photographing the waves off rocks, and even overturned a rescue jet ski during an operation near Santa Cruz.

In San Diego alone, lifeguards conducted 175 water rescues between November 9 and 16, according to San Diego Fire-Rescue figures reported by FOX 5/KUSI.

“I’ve seen seasons start off with a bang like this, but we’ve never had this type of impact so immediate,” Ernst Bauen, operations division chief for the Central Fire District of Santa Cruz County, told Outside on November 17.

According to recent reports, the enormous swells were generated by powerful low-pressure systems over the northeastern Pacific, where hurricane-force winds pushed waves toward the California coast, according to the National Weather Service. On November 14, forecasters predicted breaking waves of 25 to 35 feet, with occasional sets reaching 40 to 50 feet at big-wave surfing spot Mavericks, near Half Moon Bay.

Bauen, who spent about 20 years as a rescue swimmer, said waves are reaching roads, cliffs, and beach access points earlier in the season than usual.

“The ocean is extremely dynamic, and where there used to be a safe amount of space to recreate even on the beach, those spaces are becoming fewer and further between because of the erosion along our coastline,” he mentioned.

In a recent development, on November 14, rescue crews pulled three surfers from the water near Pleasure Point in Santa Cruz County. A fire department rescuer had picked up two surfers on a jet ski when a large wave overturned the watercraft, throwing all three into the ocean.

The rescuer, a part of Bauen’s team, managed to right the jet ski and continue the operation, returning about ten minutes later to help a third surfer.

Hundreds of miles south that same day, a San Diego lifeguard swam through powerful breaking waves to reach a struggling swimmer at La Jolla Cove. Another lifeguard eventually arrived on a jet ski and brought both men to safety.

Recent findings suggest that also in San Diego on November 14, at nearby Windansea Beach, a teenager photographing the waves from nearby rocks was swept into the ocean. A surfer jumped into the water and briefly helped keep the teenager’s head above the surface before waves carried him toward the rocky shoreline, where several bystanders helped pull him out.

In a recent development, the close call underscored warnings from San Diego Lifeguard Chief Daniel Orloff that even spectators watching from dry land were at risk. “If you are close, at any moment, a wave could take you out. It can breach a bluff, a berm, even the boardwalk,” he told ABC 10News.

In Orange County, a surfer helped rescue three people struggling in strong currents at Crystal Cove State Beach on November 15, according to a witness who shared video of the aftermath with TV station 10 News San Diego.

Not every incident ended in a rescue. On November 14, a man disappeared while swimming near Zuma Beach in Malibu. Lifeguards responded to the scene around 1:40 p.m., and Coast Guard helicopters and boat crews searched for the missing swimmer into the following day. The Coast Guard suspended its search on November 15 without locating him. The man has not publicly been identified.

Sources indicate that bauen said the ocean can also lull people into a false sense of security. During these swells, waves can stay relatively small for 15 or 20 minutes at a time, making conditions look calm before a surge of much larger waves suddenly arrives and catches surfers off guard.

Rising tides can also leave surfers stranded when the beach access points they used to enter the water become submerged.

While the largest waves have eased, forecasters say hazardous surf will linger through November 19. In its November 17 forecast, the National Weather Service predicted breaking waves of 13 to 17 feet along portions of the Bay Area and Central Coast through November 18, with dangerous rip currents and sneaker waves.

Bauen urged surfers and beachgoers to check the forecast, pay attention to changing conditions, and identify a safe route back to shore before entering the water.

“Ultimately, it comes down to the individual,” Bauen noted. “You really need to know before you go. You need to tune into the ocean conditions, look up forecasts, and do a little bit of research before you explore a secluded beach, decide to go for a swim, or paddle out.”.

The trek over Auden’s Col in India’s Garhwal Himalayas is no stroll: Crossing the pass means working hard at elevations of up to 18,000 feet, crossing a glacier, and, occasionally, dealing with some of the world’s worst weather.

It has been revealed that it was that last hazard that an expedition faced earlier this fall, when a freak snowstorm dropped more than six feet of powder on them with little notice. The 29-member team from Indian outfitter Aquaterra Adventures had reached base camp at 16,400 feet when the weather took a turn for the worse, battering them with heavy snowfall, temperatures down to -4 Fahrenheit, and 62-mile-per-hour winds.

Industry observers note that while Jetendra Singh Rana, their lead guide, promptly called off their ascent and sent a message asking for rescue, the storm had flattened many of the group’s tents, leaving them all to squeeze into one remaining cook tent while they waited for help to come. Backpacker contributor Karthika Gupta spoke to expedition members to hear their story; read her full article and see footage from the  group’s ordeal here. –Adam Roy, Editor-in-Chief.

(Photo: L to R: Anthony Walsh, Etsy Glass Carabiner Shop, Metolius, Yosemite Climbing Association, Kong).

If you’ve already taken a lap through our gift guide and still need more ideas, we’ve got you. All three of us editors here at Climbing have selected our top picks for gifts this year, from gear we’ve got our eyes on, to accessories in the climbing zeitgeist right now.

Recent findings suggest that some of these editor gifts picks make perfect mini gifts for stocking stuffers or for that climber partner who you want to thank for giving you the perfect soft catch this past year. Other picks make a bigger impact, from a super lightweight harness to a great gym bag. Most of our picks are great for a variety of climbers, whether it’s your upcoming boyfriend who you hope to convert into a climber, or your mentor who’s been at it for eons.

We hope these gift ideas make your holiday shopping as painless as a splitter hand crack so you can spend more time training or climbing, and less time scrolling through endless product pages and catalogs.

Sources indicate that originally designed and hand-sewn by Nate Barton—the Missoula-based climber who ran the meme account @beta.sprayer until 2024—the Lolo Hoodie V1 ($169.99) is a functional midlayer for cold-weather climbing and the flagship product of the fledgling brand Lolo Hardware. Its large, zippered chest pocket was originally intended to help ice climbers warm up their hands between pitches.

According to recent reports, having pretty much lived in this hoodie for the past three winters, I’ve found the chest pocket far superior to any sort of pant pocket for storing my phone, gloves, and snacks. Plus, with my items against my chest, I never have to worry about my phone freezing or my car keys accidentally slipping out during a chimney. From Joshua Tree in January to Canyonlands in November, this is a comfy and durable hoodie for the coldest days and nights of climbing.

It’s 2026, folks: If you’re still using mined chalk instead of seawater-sourced chalk, this is your call to finally make the switch. Climbing’s feature on the hidden environmental impact of chalk revealed how the vast majority of magnesium carbonate comes from mines in China, where magnesite factories poison the water and soil of nearby residents.

Luckily, there are plenty of sustainable brands that produce seawater-sourced chalk by using solar power to evaporate ocean brine from seawater. Here are some of our favorites:.

Shop Midnight Lightning Sea Grip Liquid Chalk.

For climbers with pierced ears, a pair of carabiner earrings is a customizable accessory that never gets old. Recently, I’ve been getting tons of compliments on my pair of silver, locker draw earrings (yes, they actually screw and unscrew!) that I bought at the Yosemite Climbing Museum in July. You can buy them here, but stock is limited. In case they sell out, here are a few other great places to buy carabiner earrings online:.

After breaking a cross-loaded carabiner in a scary trad fall, I now always add some sort of tape or rubber band to keep cam carabiners in place. I wrote about my DIY solution a couple of years ago, but now I simply slide on Avant Climbing’s Flip-Stop Cam Carabiner Stabilizers ($22.50 for a 10-pack). The Flip-Stop makes for easy cam clipping when mega pumped. But unlike my rubber band hack, it also keeps the cam sling open for clipping a long draw into. Crucially, like a quickdraw’s dogbone, the Flip-Stop prevents carabiners from rotating onto the dangerously weak X-axis. Nothing ruins the holidays like a pair of broken ankles.

Industry observers note that the upcoming Arc’teryx Alpha SL Harness ($180) may weigh less than the gift wrap paper you’ll hide it in. At an absurdly light 78 grams (2.7oz), the Alpha SL is for those going ultralight in the mountains, whether that’s an alpine rock romp or a big ski traverse. This harness is also surprisingly comfortable to rappel in, thanks to its uber-stiff Aluula-composite construction. And it fits a range of body types thanks to its adjustable leg loops and five waistbelt sizes. Just don’t set it down unattended on a glacier—it’ll blow away in the slightest gust of wind.

Shop Arc’teryx Alpha SL Harness.

The Patagonia Airshed Pro Pullover ($169) might have been built for mountain running, but I wear mine year-round on all sorts of objectives, from sunny rock climbs to cold north faces. The Airshed Pro is a pseudo-windlayer: decently breathable for high-output activities, yet stills blocks the wind and has a water-repellent coating. The result is a shirt equally at home skiing on a glacier or rambling up a gusty rock ridge.

Industry observers note that A note on sizing: Since the Airshed Pro was originally designed for runners, the cut is quite slim. I size up to facilitate a wider range of motion.

Recent findings suggest that I have been loving the Black Diamond Solution Hoody ($299) as a light fall belay jacket and even for cold rock climbing when I’m too chilly to shed my jacket. The Solution manages to be super lightweight, movement-friendly, and breathable, yet warm. This is largely because the specific PrimaLoft insulation used in this jacket is made with technology developed by NASA for astronauts. Here on earth, it also works great. It honestly does feel like being wrapped in warm air.

The pocket real estate is also generous, and it’s nice that the whole thing packs into the left hand pocket so you can easily stash it in your pack without a cam or crampon tearing into the insulation. I’m also looking forward to using this as a mid-layer below a shell for ice climbing this winter.

Recent findings suggest that unless you’ve been living under a rock (which many of our readers hopefully have), you’ve heard about the latest film about the weed plane that crashed into a Yosemite lake in 1976. What followed was a tragicomic climber gold rush. Now, to mark the 50th anniversary of the incident, you can sport one of several new t-shirts or hats ($29.95-$44.95) memorializing this infamous moment in Yosemite climbing history. All proceeds support the Yosemite Climbing Association and the Yosemite Climbing Museum.

In a recent development, have I used one? No. Do I desperately want one? Yes. As a 5’2” climber, I’m often just a few inches short of being able to make the clip from a good stance. I’ve heard wonderful things about the stiffy Kong Panic Draw ($54.95-$59.95) that lets you clip bolts otherwise out of reach. Maybe 2027 will be the year I finally gift myself one! If there’s a short or easily panicked sport climber in your life, I bet they would be stoked to get this as a present. Or you could make one for them DIY-style yourself.

According to recent reports, the oversized, durable Metolius Climbers Tote ($64.95) has become my go-to gym bag. It easily fits my personal gear plus a 60m rope, or four sets of personal gear (shoes, harness, and chalkbag for me, my husband, and my two kids). Despite having stored weathered climbing shoes zippered inside for too long, this bag miraculously doesn’t stink yet either. It stows away nicely in gym cubbies (whereas my previous Cotopaxi tote would sort of spill out) and is easy to carry by hand or shoulder. This is a great mid-sized gift for the climber in your life, or you could fill it with other gear you’re gifting for a bigger impact.

In a recent development, note on price: While this tote isn’t on sale at REI, co-op members get 20% off one full-price item through Nov. 30, so this is a good one to save on.

I receive a lot of climbing books and galleys to review and consider for coverage. Only some of them are so good that I can’t put them down. That’s how I felt about Erratica, a latest collection of true stories from Moab-based, life-long climber Brian Laidlaw. Rare is the read that both keeps you attentive and entertained, yet also evokes deeper reflection. With Erratica, Brian manages to do just that. Pick up a copy ($20) at Moab’s Back of Beyond bookstore, or find one online anywhere books are sold.

Midnight Lightning Sea Grip Liquid Chalk.

Tech Report: The Best Nonprofits That Support Dads and Fatherhood

📅 30 May 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1016 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The best nonprofits that support dads and fatherhood.
  • Sources indicate that research has shown that when dads are engaged and present, kids do better.
  • Here are just a few organizations that champion dads and understand the integral role that fathers play in the lives of their children.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best nonprofits that support dads and fatherhood.

Sources indicate that research has shown that when dads are engaged and present, kids do better. We celebrate dads on Father’s Day because we should celebrate everything that makes children’s lives — and outcomes — better. When children have close relationships with father figures, they tend to avoid high-risk behaviors; have higher-paying jobs and healthy, stable relationships; and have higher IQ test scores. The benefits go on, but one thing’s for sure: Dads matter in the lives of children, and so we should support and celebrate their presence in their kids’ lives.

Here are just a few organizations that champion dads and understand the integral role that fathers play in the lives of their children.

All Pro Dad is a program of Family First that provides tools and resources to dads that allow them to be more present in the lives of their children. Spearheaded by former NFL coach Tony Dungy, NFL player Benjamin Watson, ESPN personality Dan Orlovsky, and many other prominent sports figures, All Pro Dad hosts a yearly interactive get-together for kids and dads at an NFL or NCAA stadium and a monthly school program where dads meet up with their children at school to spend time bonding and relationship building.

According to recent reports, the Center for Family Policy and Practice is a nonprofit organization that advocates for fair and equitable laws and policies that affect low-income families and fathers. Focusing on child support, family safety and security, and financial and economic security, the CFPP acts as a think tank to develop solutions to barriers experienced by low-income fathers and fathers of color.

Sources indicate that the Child & Family Blog provides research-driven content on the impact of family on social, emotional, and cognitive child development. In addition to covering topics like race, divorce, and inequality, the Child & Family Blog covers research on the importance of fathers and the role they play in both the family dynamic and the development of children.

Industry observers note that the Family Equality Council works to ensure that members of the LGBTQ community have the ability to create families and provide support, education, activism and advocacy, and the resources they need to become parents and foster loving, healthy family relationships. The FEP also tracks national and state legislation that affects the ability of LGBTQ couples to become parents and maintain parental rights.

Fathering Together provides anyone who identifies as a father with tools and resources to uplift and support them as they work to create a “more equitable society.” The organization hosts different communities so that dads from every walk of life can reach out to peers for help, support, and advice while working to make the world a better and safer place for their children.

The Fatherhood Project is a Massachusetts-based program that empowers fathers to become more “knowledgeable, active, and emotionally engaged with their children.” Through research-based principles and curricula and programs like Dads Matter, Dads in Recovery, Teen Dads, and Divorcing Dads, the organization aims to help all dads be more present and engaged with their children while focusing on dads in marginalized and underserved communities.

According to recent reports, fathers Incorporated is an Atlanta-based nonprofit that works with federal lawmakers and leaders in the responsible fatherhood movement, faith and business leaders, and family law practitioners to advocate for legislative and community changes that promote fathers’ involvement in the lives of their children. The group focuses on co-parenting, domestic violence, incarceration, child development, child support, and employment and financial stability. Fathers Incorporated provides resources and programs for fathers to engage with their children healthily and raise awareness through programs like the Million Fathers March and Black Dads Count.

Fathers’ Uplift is a one-of-a-kind organization that provides fathers with the tools they need to overcome trauma, addiction, racial barriers, and emotional challenges to help them fully engage with their children and families. Fathers’ Uplift provides therapy, coaching, training opportunities, and youth enrichment with the aim of reducing the number of children raised without positive father figures in their lives. It is the only organization in the United States that offers therapy, counseling, and addiction support specifically geared toward fathers and their families with the aim of reuniting families and providing them with the framework to thrive.

In a recent development, the National Fatherhood Initiative is the country’s largest provider of research on the involvement of fathers and the impact fathers have on families. It provides communities with resources and training to increase father engagement with the goal of ensuring that communities and human service organizations have the tools and training they need to be father-inclusive so fathers can be more involved in the lives of their children.

Industry observers note that the Native American Fatherhood and Families Association is an Arizona-based nonprofit focusing on nourishing family relationships through its Fatherhood Is Sacred/Motherhood Is Sacred (FIS/MIS), Linking Generations by Strengthening Relationships, and Addressing Family Violence & Abuse programs. Employing culturally sensitive curricula and materials, NAFFA is able to address the specific concerns of the Native American community to reunite families and empower fathers to become family leaders.

Recent findings suggest that the National Partnership for Women and Families understands that families benefit when dads are present and actively engaged. One way the NPWF is creating a more equitable world for women is by spearheading programs, legislation, and calls to action that support fathers by promoting active fatherhood and gender equality.

According to recent reports, established in Brazil in 1997, Promundo has worked globally to engage fathers in the care economy, promote active fatherhood and promote gender equity and justice by engaging men and boys with women and girls. The organization is right now undergoing a rebranding to be more inclusive of all genders. Its new name, Equimundo: Center for Masculinities and Social Justice, “reflects our commitment to fostering gender equity and our roots in social justice. The name change also captures our approach of collaborating with and never overshadowing our diverse partners worldwide.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I am a consummate night owl. When I was a teenager, my mother used to begin waking me up by knocking on my door, then taking my pillow away, then my bed sheets. When she’d find me still asleep on the bare mattress, she’d push me onto the floor. That’s where my little brother would find me, still asleep, and begin wailing that I needed to drive him to school because he didn’t want to be late (again).

In a recent development, waking up in the morning has never been my strong suit. But when I graduated from college and no longer had a coach holding me to a daily afternoon cross-country practice, I found that exercise stopped being a priority. By the time I got off work at 5 p.m., I was too tired to go to the gym, or I had dinner plans, or had eaten something weird and decided it was impossible to run.

Industry observers note that for weeks at a time, exercise just wouldn’t happen. Certain that turning myself into a morning exerciser would solve all my problems, I told my mom I was on a mission to become an early bird. She shook her head. “I’ve been trying my whole life,” she said. “If you figure it out, you let me know.”.

Most folks consider the night-owl versus early-bird categorization a matter of intrinsic wiring—you’re born one or the other, and you cannot change. While there is a strong genetic basis for your natural circadian rhythm, it is possible to switch. In fact, after about a year of working to adjust my sleep cycle, I now wake up at or before 6 a.m. almost every morning (even when I don’t necessarily want to). That means I now get to the gym or trail four or five days a week instead of one or two. Here are all the things I did to help me make the change.

In a recent development, telling myself that “I will wake up and exercise” was too vague. “I will wake up, drive to the park, walk three miles, and then get a latte at my favorite coffee shop” is much easier to visualize (and get excited for). In the early morning, I only ever blueprint on doing fun exercise, whether that’s going to the climbing gym, doing pull-ups at the park, or running my favorite loop. If it’s a workout I’m likely to skip at 11 a.m., I definitely will at 6.

In a recent development, I’m a very guilt-motivated person. If I only have to meet myself at the gym, I’ll stand me up every time. But if there’s another human being waiting, I’ll be there. I am fortunate to know several very motivated and punctual lady friends who also like to lift weights at 7 a.m. Making prepares with them two or three times per week keeps me honest.

If I’ve paid for something, I feel a compulsive need to get my money’s worth out of it—even if that means waking up at dawn to do so. One of the best things I did for my sleep schedule was register for a recreational adult climbing team with 6 a.m. practices. I’ve also tried classes like CrossFit or F45, many of which charge $15 to $30 if you no-show.

Caveat: I find the class strategy is only effective if it’s recurring; I’m much more motivated to show up for a group of people I see every day than for a batch of strangers I’ll never see again.

Industry observers note that when I’m warm in bed, tired, and dreading exercise, I make the smallest possible promise: I tell myself that I will go to the gym and only do one set of squats. Or only 15 minutes of stretching. Or only a single mile on the treadmill. If I feel good, I’ll do more (and usually, I do). But if only the minimum gets done, that’s still a win.

The less you have to think about it in the morning, the easier it is to roll out of bed. Do every possible chore the night before. Pack your gym bag ahead of time. Grind your coffee, put water in the kettle, and set your car keys by the door.

It has been revealed that this is my winter hack. When it’s cold in the morning, the last thing I want to do is take off my PJs and put on a frigid sports bra. So, I sleep in my running clothes. When my alarm goes off, all I have to do is put on shoes and hit the road.

According to recent reports, it can be tempting to hit snooze on the weekends. Resist. If you need to take a short nap here or there to catch up on hours, do it. But sleeping in too long or too often can mess with your body’s natural circadian rhythm—and send you back to square one.

#32846. The Origin of "Dad" And Why Some Men Prefer to Be Called "Father"

The Origin of "Dad" And Why Some Men Prefer to Be Called "Father"

📅 30 May 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (994 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The nicknames we use for parents go in and out of fashion, age to age and era to era.
  • In a recent development, but why have we ditched ‘father’ for dad?
  • “It’s from ‘dada,’” states Professor John H.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The nicknames we use for parents go in and out of fashion, age to age and era to era. At one time, men preferred “Sire.” Other times, “Father” was preferable. What we do know is that the most agreed-upon way to refer to dad these days is by calling him, well, ‘dad.’.

In a recent development, but why have we ditched ‘father’ for dad? The short answer is that things have gotten a little less formal. But the reason we’ve moved away from formality is that we’ve embraced what’s more linguistically natural for children and parents. ‘Father’ comes from the Proto-Indo-European “pəter” and Old English ‘fæder,’ meaning “he who begets a child,” reflecting the baby-talk sound “pa” as well as a phonetic shift from ‘p’ to ‘f’ in Middle English.

However, ‘dad’ did not evolve from ‘father.’.

“It’s from ‘dada,’” states Professor John H. McWhorter, a professor at Columbia University, “a natural sound from children’s mouths as a second stab at consonants after they try the most natural ‘mama.’ Next is often either ‘dada, ‘tata,’ ‘baba’ or … ‘papa.’ Upon which, ‘father’ starts in Proto-Indo-European as “puh-TAIR,” and the ‘puh’ part is this same thing: what started as ‘pa’ in ‘papa.’ The words for Mommy and Daddy are the closest thing to linguistic universals because they are about mouth anatomy in infants rather than thought.”.

Recent findings suggest that there are also another key reason why this is reinforced over time. Emie Tittnich, a specialist at the University of Pittsburgh, speaking to Live Science, noted that parents generally refrain from using pronouns like ‘I’ or ‘you’ to avoid confusing their kids with abstract concepts early on. “‘Parents will use [‘mommy’ and ‘daddy’] to help their children learn the role names and also to indicate the relationship, ‘mommy and me,'” notes Tittnich. “It usually takes the child awhile to understand that the same person can be called two different names.”.

Industry observers note that the agreed-upon naturality of these linguistic principles mean that as American society has become more colloquial and secular over time, we move (at least in this instance) away from a term that’s reflective of a status quo based in rigid concepts of class and religion—one of the meanings of ‘fæder’ in Old English is ‘supreme being,’ according to the Online Etymology Dictionary. As a result, we’re generally caught off guard when we hear a child refer to a parent as ‘father.’.

Recent findings suggest that however, this is not the case unanimously. We spoke with six dads who prefer — or simply stuck with — ‘father’ instead of ‘dad.’ Some do it as an homage to their own fathers; others do it to sound more authoritative. Others do it because it’s what their kids like. All have their reasons and, maybe, deep inside, some are just big fans of Proto-Indo-European language. Here’s what they say.

I sometimes worry that it sounds a little austere out loud, but it’s just what my father always asked us to call him, and it felt like it was important to me that we carry that on. No one in my family has had a problem with it. I think you can still be a ‘dad’ and be called ‘father,’ if that makes sense. It’s basically semantic, in that way, but it’s also more than semantics. — John, Baltimore, MD.

It’s less of a request or a demand or anything, but when we were teaching my oldest what everything is called, we always just mentioned ‘this is your mother’ and ‘this is your father,’ and he liked to say that, too. So we’ve kept it. I’d be lying if I said I didn’t think it was just adorably proper to have our little man coming up to us and saying, “father, mother, may I use the bathroom,” or what have you. But as with everything, I don’t mind anything that seems to feel natural for my kids and makes them happy. — Eric, Austin, Texas.

My son didn’t start until he was older. I think he thought it sounded more respectful, or just more professional. We’ve always been a more traditional family, in how we carry ourselves, I guess you would say. So perhaps this was his way of taking that in stride, or contributing to that. My wife teases me about it sometimes. I should clarify, it’s generally him introducing me to other people that way. ‘This is my father, have you met my father?’ etc. — Patrick, Twin Cities, MN.

Industry observers note that in the past two years, my older daughter, age 21, began calling me ‘father’ and as strange as I found it, I didn’t mine it at all. Now, my four-year-old calls me “father” and I guess I now have a new title. As long as I am not being called ‘Henry,’ I am okay with it. — Henry, Boston, MA.

I have eight children—three boys and five girls. I’ve always asked that they call me ‘father’ not to be domineering but because the house could get a little chaotic, as you can imagine, and my wife and I felt that it was a label that was more authoritative and kept things from being too chaotic. ‘Please don’t touch your father’s golf clubs’ just has a better ring to it, I guess. — Elliott, Charlotte, NC.

I love that my children call me ‘father,’ because of the sense of responsibility it instills in me. Your ‘dad’ or ‘daddy’ is there to lend you the car, your ‘father’ is there to raise you, and protect you and make sure that you have the tool you need to succeed in life. When my kids call me ‘father,’ it reignites that sense of purpose for me every day, and reminds me it’s up to me to make their world a great place to grow up in. — Sam, Alachua Country, FL.

This article was originally published on May 17, 2019.
